- **2.** Inform the surgeon; stop unnecessary fluids or implicated transfusion/infusion. Continue life-saving blood or appropriate anaphylaxis resuscitation rather than stopping all fluids indiscriminately.
- **3.** Apply/titrate PEEP and lung-protective ventilation; suction obstructing frothy secretions as necessary. Check haemodynamics because PEEP can worsen RV dysfunction and venous return.
- **4.** Find the mechanism with ECG, ABG, point-of-care echo/lung ultrasound, clinical timeline (transfusion? airway obstruction? drug?), BP and rhythm. Check for ischaemia, acute MR, fluid excess, anaphylaxis, aspiration, TRALI/TACO and pulmonary embolism.
- **5.** Treat phenotype: vasodilator if hypertensive; diuretic if overloaded; vasoactive/inotropic support if low output; cardioversion if an unstable tachyarrhythmia; reperfusion if ACS; adrenaline if anaphylaxis.
- **6.** Decide whether to finish or abbreviate surgery and plan ICU/HDU, ventilation and serial cardiac evaluation.

## Postoperative implications and special mechanisms

- Observe for recurrence of oedema, oxygen/ventilatory requirements, arrhythmia, myocardial injury, renal failure and response to diuresis.
- Use a repeat echo for an unresolved structural or low-output question, not merely to document that B-lines were present.
- Arrange medication review and fluid balance plans; acute hydrostatic oedema in a patient with valve disease may be the first sign that valve intervention is now required.

**Negative-pressure pulmonary oedema:**

- Very negative inspiratory pressures against an obstructed airway abruptly increase venous return and pulmonary capillary transmural pressure, with associated sympathetic and permeability effects.
- It typically begins soon after obstruction and often improves over 12–48 h once obstruction is relieved and supportive CPAP/PEEP is given.
- Diuretics are not routine in a euvolaemic patient.

- **Re-expansion pulmonary oedema:** may follow rapid lung re-expansion after large effusion or pneumothorax drainage. Manage supportively; avoid uncontrolled suction and follow pleural-procedure protocols. BTS guidance on cautious pleural-fluid drainage is not a rigid identical rule for all chest drains.

**Exam synthesis.** First decide whether the oedema is hydrostatic, permeability-related or obstruction-related; then support oxygenation with appropriate positive pressure and treat the specific circulatory/airway cause.

items.title: 7. Valvular heart disease
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (valvular heart disease component); SS_CS 1.4 (valve pathology and filling status)
items.body:
## Why it matters: every valve lesion imposes a particular loading problem

- **A narrowed valve obstructs forward flow; an incompetent valve allows regurgitant flow.** Both eventually cause ventricular and atrial remodelling, raised filling pressures, pulmonary hypertension, AF and myocardial ischaemia—but the optimal anaesthetic strategy can be **opposite**.
- In aortic stenosis (AS) maintaining systemic pressure protects coronary perfusion; in aortic/mitral regurgitation (AR/MR) unnecessarily increasing SVR worsens regurgitant or forward-flow haemodynamics.
- In mitral stenosis (MS), slowing the heart markedly improves transmitral filling time, while in AR profound bradycardia increases regurgitant time.

- **Every preoperative valve assessment should answer five questions:** (1) what lesion and mechanism? (2) how severe by integrated echo criteria? (3) symptoms and stability? (4) effect on LV/RV, pulmonary pressure and rhythm? (5) has the patient reached a threshold for valve intervention before elective non-cardiac surgery? [R11, R12]

| Lesion | Main pathophysiology | High-yield haemodynamic direction |
|---|---|---|
| **AS** | LV pressure overload, concentric LVH, high LVEDP, limited flow reserve | **Preserve perfusion pressure, sinus rhythm, adequate preload; avoid tachycardia and abrupt vasodilation.** |
| **AR** | LV volume overload, low aortic DBP, increased LV volume | **Avoid bradycardia and excessive afterload; maintain forward flow**, appropriate high-normal HR. |
| **MS** | LA–LV filling obstruction, high LA/PA pressure, AF/RV risk | **Rate control, diastolic filling time, sinus rhythm if possible, low PVR**, cautious fluid. |
| **MR** | LV ejects into LA, volume overload; EF may overstate true function | **Avoid marked bradycardia/high SVR; preserve forward flow**, avoid congestion. |

- **Important distinction:** “maintain preload” means avoid demonstrated underfilling; it is not a license to make patients with AS, MS or HCM deliberately hypervolaemic.

## 7A. Aortic stenosis

### Why it matters

- Severe AS restricts the ability to increase stroke volume across a calcified valve.
- The chronically pressure-loaded LV hypertrophies, develops diastolic dysfunction and a higher LVEDP.
- **Coronary perfusion falls when aortic DBP falls or LVEDP rises**, while myocardial demand is high because wall stress and LV mass are increased.
- Induction-induced vasodilation, tachycardia, AF and significant hypovolaemia can therefore precipitate myocardial ischaemia, pulmonary oedema or collapse.
- This is why severe symptomatic AS deserves a higher level of perioperative planning than an incidental murmur.

### Preoperative implications: determine severity, symptoms and whether the valve needs treatment

Ask about **exertional angina, syncope/presyncope and dyspnoea/heart failure**, functional decline and recent symptoms; auscultate for ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids, slow-rising low-volume pulse, soft/absent A2 and signs of congestion. Murmur intensity alone does not grade severity, particularly with low flow.

- **Echocardiographic severe high-gradient AS:** **peak velocity ≥4 m/s**, **mean gradient ≥40 mmHg**, **AVA ≤1.0 cm²** (indexed ≤0.6 cm²/m²); dimensionless velocity index **<0.25** supports severity. AVA = LVOT area × LVOT VTI / AV VTI. Use integrated echo rather than selecting one inconsistent number; gradients change with flow, pressure and output. [R11]

**Low-flow low-gradient AS:**

- AVA may be ≤1.0 cm² despite mean gradient <40 because little blood crosses the valve; **stroke-volume index ≤35 mL/m²** defines conventionally low flow.
- Classical LFLG involves reduced EF; paradoxical LFLG occurs with preserved EF but small stiff hypertrophied LV.
- Review BP, accurate LVOT measurement and flow; in selected reduced-EF cases use low-dose dobutamine stress echo, and CT valve calcium may resolve discordant severity.
- **A “low gradient” does not automatically mean mild AS.**

**When to proceed:**

- Severe symptomatic AS usually merits Heart Team review and valve intervention before elective major surgery if feasible; decompensated disease warrants delay.
- Symptom-free severe AS with preserved LV function may proceed for necessary surgery with informed risk assessment, close monitoring and the ability to rescue hypotension.
- For time-sensitive non-cardiac surgery, TAVI or balloon aortic valvuloplasty may be considered as a bridge in selected patients.
- Choice of SAVR/TAVI depends on age, anatomy, vascular access, anticipated durability, surgical risk and patient preferences—not age alone. [R11]

### Intraoperative implications

- **Preload:** maintain a normal filling state; avoid haemorrhage/dehydration, but a stiff LV is vulnerable to fluid overload. Use reassessed boluses rather than routine preloading.
- **Heart rate:** avoid fast rates (short diastole and coronary perfusion) and excessive bradycardia (reduces output). A roughly **60–80/min** teaching range may be useful but adjust to baseline, EF and rhythm; there is no obligatory target.
- **Rhythm:** maintain sinus rhythm where possible; loss of atrial contraction in a stiff LV may abruptly reduce filling. Treat unstable AF/SVT promptly, including synchronised cardioversion.
- **Afterload/perfusion:** prevent sudden falls in SVR and aortic DBP. Vasopressors such as **phenylephrine, metaraminol or noradrenaline** are frequently required; which is preferable depends on HR, contractility and vasodilatory versus low-output physiology. Avoid severe hypertension that increases wall stress.
- **Technique:** place arterial monitoring before induction for significant disease/major procedures; slow titrated GA with vasopressor available is common.
  - A dense single-shot spinal can cause dangerous abrupt sympathectomy; incremental epidural or selected low-dose neuraxial techniques may be possible with monitoring, careful block onset and pressure support, not categorically banned in every AS patient.
- **Complications:** recognise myocardial ischaemia, AF, pulmonary oedema and refractory hypotension. Use echocardiography to identify reduced contractility or other causes of collapse rather than only giving fluid.

### Postoperative implications

Major risk persists with pain, bleeding, vasodilation and arrhythmia. Ensure stable perfusion, cautious fluids, controlled heart rate, analgesia and an appropriately monitored ward/HDU/ICU bed for severe lesions or major surgery. Reassess valve symptoms and cardiology plan if perioperative failure occurs.

## 7B. Aortic regurgitation

### Why it matters

- During diastole an incompetent aortic valve permits aortic blood to return to the LV.
- Chronic AR creates **LV volume overload**, eccentric dilatation and a high stroke volume; the enlarged ventricle may initially compensate with preserved EF but eventually fails.
- Because blood escapes from the aorta in diastole, **diastolic aortic pressure can be low**, reducing coronary supply.
- **Slow heart rates prolong diastole and the opportunity for regurgitation**, while high SVR increases the pressure favouring retrograde flow.
- This is why AR haemodynamics differ fundamentally from AS.

**Acute severe AR** (endocarditis or an aortic-root process) is far more dangerous: a non-dilated LV cannot accommodate the sudden regurgitant volume, so LVEDP and LA pressure rise sharply → pulmonary oedema and shock. No long history of symptoms is required.

### Preoperative implications

- Assess breathlessness, angina, exercise limitation and signs of heart failure; look for a wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse and early diastolic decrescendo murmur.
- Echo should define mechanism (cusp versus root), severity, LV size and EF, aortic-root/ascending-aorta diameter and associated lesions.
- Severe AR indicators include **regurgitant volume ≥60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction ≥50%, EROA ≥0.30 cm²**, vena contracta generally >0.6 cm and holodiastolic reversal in the descending aorta; integrate because each is load dependent.
- Chronic severe AR with symptoms, important LV dysfunction or dilatation warrants valve evaluation before major elective surgery.
- 2025 ESC guidance has both established intervention triggers (e.g. LVEF ≤50%, LVESD >50 mm/indexed >25 mm/m²) and earlier consideration thresholds in carefully selected low-risk asymptomatic patients; avoid treating early-consideration criteria as automatically mandatory surgery. [R11]

### Intraoperative implications

**Avoid bradycardia; preserve forward flow with low–normal afterload:**

- A high-normal HR, frequently around 80–100/min as a teaching guide, can shorten diastolic regurgitant time, but avoid clinically important tachycardia if CAD or LV dysfunction coexists.
- Maintain appropriate filling without overload, preserve contractility and avoid severe vasoconstriction.
- Neuraxial afterload reduction is often relatively favourable if BP is supported; GA with controlled induction is also appropriate.
- Treat major hypotension using the true mechanism—some vasopressor support may still be necessary to perfuse organs, but indiscriminate high-dose alpha agonism increases regurgitant flow.
- **An IABP is contraindicated in important AR** because balloon diastolic augmentation increases regurgitation.
- Manage acute severe AR with urgent surgery/Heart Team care and haemodynamic support, not routine outpatient optimisation.

### Postoperative implications

Avoid bradycardia, large afterload rises, recurrent hypertension and fluid excess. Watch for pulmonary oedema, myocardial ischaemia, LV dysfunction and arrhythmias; severe lesions require monitored recovery and a definitive valve plan.

## 7C. Mitral stenosis

### Why it matters

- The stenotic mitral valve obstructs diastolic filling of the LV.
- LA pressure rises; pulmonary venous pressure then rises, causing **pulmonary oedema**, pulmonary arterial hypertension and eventually RV failure.
- The LV may be small and underfilled even while lung capillaries are congested.
- **Tachycardia sharply worsens MS:** diastole becomes shorter, so the same flow must cross a narrowed orifice in less time, increasing the LA–LV gradient and pulmonary venous pressure.
- AF is especially dangerous because it combines tachycardia, loss of effective atrial contraction and a risk of left atrial thrombus/stroke.

Rheumatic disease remains particularly important in Australia and New Zealand. MS may become evident only in pregnancy or during surgical stress when CO increases, and a patient with severe MS may become critically hypoxic despite normal LV EF.

### Preoperative implications

Ask about exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, recurrent pulmonary oedema, embolic history, AF and exercise limitation. Examine for a loud S1, opening snap and low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, signs of pulmonary hypertension/right failure and irregular pulse. Review anticoagulation and rate control carefully.

- Echo includes **mitral valve area (MVA), mean transmitral gradient with HR stated**, LA size/thrombus, pulmonary pressure, RV function and associated MR.
- In current intervention-oriented guidance **MVA ≤1.5 cm² is clinically significant MS**; traditional echo grading sometimes calls **<1.0 cm² severe**, so state which classification is being used.
- The mean gradient depends strongly on rate/flow; a gradient >10 mmHg may indicate severe haemodynamic obstruction but cannot be interpreted without HR and output.
- Pressure half-time can estimate area (**MVA ≈220/PHT**) but becomes unreliable with altered compliance, AR or after intervention. [R11, R12]

- Optimise rate (often beta-blocker; selected diltiazem/digoxin according to EF/AF), control AF, relieve congestion cautiously, treat anaemia/infection and assess pulmonary hypertension.
- Severe symptomatic MS may need balloon mitral commissurotomy or surgery before elective major surgery.
- **Rheumatic moderate/severe MS with AF or LA thrombus usually requires a VKA rather than DOAC**; plan interruption/bridging according to thrombosis, bleeding and neuraxial risk.

### Intraoperative implications

- **Rate and rhythm first:** prevent sympathetic tachycardia from anxiety, intubation, pain and emergence. Slow–normal rates often allow longer diastolic filling; do not assume all patients must be <70/min. Preserve sinus rhythm if possible; unstable AF warrants urgent cardioversion.
- **Preload:** adequate but not generous. A small increase in LA pressure may flood the lungs while the LV still receives limited flow; fluid must be guided carefully.
- **SVR and PVR:** maintain systemic perfusion; avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, high airway pressures, hypothermia and nitrous oxide when pulmonary hypertension is significant.
- **Monitoring/technique:** arterial line for severe disease/major surgery; early echo for instability. GA is feasible with smooth intubation and rate control. Gradual neuraxial techniques are possible but rapid SVR reduction can compromise already-limited cardiac output.
- **Laparoscopic surgery:** pneumoperitoneum may raise intrathoracic pressure, reduce venous return and increase CO₂/PVR; steep Trendelenburg can worsen congestion. Use gentle positioning, consider low insufflation pressure and discuss alternative procedures when severe disease is unstable.

### Postoperative implications

Aggressive prevention of tachycardia, pain, hypoxaemia and fluid overload is important. Watch AF, pulmonary oedema and right-sided failure; resume anticoagulation with an explicit bleeding/neuraxial plan and observe severe disease in a monitored setting.

**Pregnancy exam extension:**

- Gestational increases in CO can unmask severe MS, particularly in late pregnancy and around autotransfusion after delivery.
- Rate control, diuresis for congestion, pregnancy-heart-team care and carefully titrated early neuraxial analgesia are important.
- Avoid abrupt vasodilation; maternal and fetal needs require individual plans rather than a universal delivery mode.
- This has historically featured in ANZCA questions and overlaps the obstetric study sets.

## 7D. Mitral regurgitation

### Why it matters

- The LV ejects part of its stroke volume into the **low-pressure left atrium** rather than forward into the aorta.
- Chronic MR causes LA and LV volume loading, eccentric remodelling, AF and eventually pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction.
- A normal-looking LVEF may be deceptive: it includes the easy backward ejection, and **LVEF ≤60%** in severe primary MR can already signify impaired LV contractile reserve.
- Excess systemic resistance makes forward flow relatively less favourable and increases regurgitant fraction.

**Acute severe MR** after papillary muscle or chordal rupture has a small non-compliant LA, so pressure rises abruptly and the patient develops flash oedema or shock, sometimes with an unexpectedly soft murmur.

### Preoperative implications

- Define **primary structural MR** (prolapse/flail, endocarditis, rheumatic, chordal rupture) versus **secondary functional MR** (LV dilation/dyssynchrony/ischaemia or atrial annular dilation).
- Take symptom history, functional capacity, pulmonary oedema/AF history; examine for pansystolic apical murmur to axilla, displaced apex and signs of failure.
- Echo quantifies mechanism and severity with **EROA, regurgitant volume, vena contracta, pulmonary venous flow**, LV size/function, LA size and pulmonary pressure.
- In severe primary MR, **EROA ≥0.40 cm², regurgitant volume ≥60 mL/beat, vena contracta ≥0.7 cm** and pulmonary vein systolic reversal support severe disease; use integrated measures.
- An **EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm** is an important LV decompensation/intervention threshold in severe primary MR. [R11, R12]

Symptomatic severe MR, acute MR or established LV deterioration requires valve/cardiology review before elective major surgery. Secondary MR management starts with optimised HF therapy and CRT where indicated; selected patients benefit from TEER/repair. Interpreting TOE under GA requires remembering that anaesthetic afterload reduction can **underestimate awake MR severity**.

### Intraoperative implications

- Maintain euvolaemia, a **normal to high-normal HR** if tolerated, adequate contractility and **low to normal SVR** to favour forward flow.
- Avoid marked bradycardia and severe afterload increases, while still protecting coronary/renal perfusion.
- GA or a carefully titrated regional/neuraxial technique may be suitable; unlike severe stenosis, modest afterload reduction can be helpful.
- If hypotension occurs, treat the cause and use enough noradrenaline/vasopressin to preserve perfusion, but do not indiscriminately raise afterload without reassessing forward output.
- Significant pulmonary hypertension requires RV protection: avoid hypoxia, acidosis, hypercarbia and excessive lung distension.
- In acute MR, seek immediate echo and cardiac surgical advice; afterload reduction works only if BP is adequate, and selected support may bridge to intervention.

### Postoperative implications

Watch congestion, AF, myocardial injury and LV failure. After surgical correction of severe MR, the low-impedance regurgitant outlet is removed: **afterload mismatch** can unmask true LV systolic dysfunction even when preoperative EF looked reassuring. Repeat echo and targeted inotropic/afterload support may be required.

## 7E. Prosthetic valves: the haemodynamic problem becomes an anticoagulation problem

A mechanical valve is durable but thrombogenic; a bioprosthesis generally needs less lifelong valve-specific anticoagulation but may degenerate. A previous valve intervention is not synonymous with cure: assess prosthetic function, valve gradients, anticoagulation, structural deterioration, endocarditis and ventricular disease before surgery.

| Valve type | Typical long-term antithrombotic principle | Clinical risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical AVR** | **Lifelong warfarin/VKA**; target INR depends on valve model and patient risks (often target 2.5 with modern bileaflet and no additional risk). | Thrombosis, embolic stroke and bleeding; DOACs are not suitable. |
| **Mechanical MVR / higher-risk valve** | Lifelong VKA, commonly higher target such as INR 3.0 (range often 2.5–3.5), individualised. | Higher thrombosis risk and importance of interruption plan. |
| **Surgical bioprosthesis** | Early aspirin or VKA depending on position, AF and operative guidance; OAC often used for initial mitral/tricuspid cases. | Early thrombosis versus bleeding; later degeneration. |
| **TAVI** | With no OAC indication, current European guidance generally favours **single antiplatelet therapy**, not routine DAPT/DOAC solely for the TAVI. | Bleeding, vascular injury, paravalvular leak, conduction disease. |

**Perioperative warfarin:**

- Minor low-bleeding-risk procedures may permit continued therapeutic warfarin.
- If interruption is required, warfarin is commonly stopped ~5 days before and INR checked; use **individualised bridging**, not an automatic “bridge every mechanical valve” rule.
- **CHEST 2022 conditionally suggests against routine bridging** even in mechanical valves (very low-certainty evidence), while valve/ACC guidance supports specialist consideration in selected very-high-risk patients (mechanical mitral or older valve, recent embolism, marked LV dysfunction).
- Always agree the plan with cardiology/haematology and the surgical and regional teams. [R13, R14]

- If urgent reversal is needed for major surgery or life-threatening bleeding, **4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K** according to weight/INR/local protocol is usually preferred; vitamin K alone is too slow and FFP is less concentrated.
- Resumption is determined by haemostasis and thrombotic risk: warfarin may be restarted 12–24 h when safe; therapeutic heparin after high-bleeding-risk surgery often requires **48–72 h** and strict catheter timing.
- A therapeutic LMWH dose needs **at least 24 h** before neuraxial needle placement, with longer assessment in renal impairment; apply the full current ASRA/ANZCA policy rather than one shortcut interval. [R14]

### Mechanical valve in pregnancy: a predictable advanced viva

- Maternal valve thrombosis can be fatal, while warfarin crosses the placenta and carries embryopathy/bleeding risks; LMWH avoids fetal transfer but inadequate anti-Xa exposure increases valve thrombosis.
- A multidisciplinary pregnancy heart team chooses between VKA and carefully monitored dose-adjusted LMWH/UFH (including 4–6 h postdose anti-Xa monitoring when indicated), informed by valve position, warfarin requirements and fetal/maternal priorities.
- Near delivery, controlled transition to heparin allows a planned birth and neuraxial approach; avoid delivery on full warfarin if possible.
- **Do not use a universal restart time for therapeutic LMWH after caesarean or a blanket bridging rule**—haemostasis, neuraxial catheter removal and valve risk determine the schedule.
- This subject was explicitly examined in ANZCA 2023.1. [E2]

## 7F. Comparing lesions in a medical viva: test yourself

| Question | AS | AR | MS | MR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Why does tachycardia matter? | Shortens LV filling and coronary perfusion | May be helpful up to a point; avoid excessive tachycardia/ischaemia | **Particularly harmful:** raises LA–LV gradient and oedema | Avoid marked bradycardia; excessive tachycardia may still harm |
| Is fluid loading helpful? | Only if truly underfilled; stiff LV | Maintain preload, not overload | Particularly dangerous if LA pressure high | Adequate but not excessive |
| What about increasing SVR? | Prevent collapse in coronary pressure; excessive SVR also adds stress | Worsens regurgitant pressure gradient | Preserve perfusion but does not relieve valve obstruction | Increases regurgitant fraction; avoid needless rise |
| Important rhythm issue | Sinus/atrial filling | Avoid excessive bradycardia | AF with RVR and embolic risk | AF from LA enlargement |
| What is the dangerous postoperative event? | Ischaemia, hypotension, arrhythmia | Oedema, LV failure | AF, pulmonary oedema/RV failure | HF/AF, low output after repair |

**Exam synthesis.** Do not memorise “full, slow, high” or “full, fast, forward” without understanding why. Start with whether the lesion is pressure or volume loading, which chamber is congested, where flow is obstructed or regurgitant, and what heart-rate/afterload change improves genuine forward cardiac output.

items.title: 8. Cardiomyopathy
items.body:
## Why it matters: different cardiomyopathies fail in opposite ways

- Cardiomyopathy describes disease of myocardial structure or function that cannot be explained solely by ordinary loading conditions or coronary obstruction.
- The label must be refined: is this ventricle **weak and dilated**, **thick with dynamic obstruction**, **stiff and restrictive**, or **electrically unstable**?
- A vasodilator can improve output in dilated cardiomyopathy yet provoke collapse from dynamic LVOT obstruction.
- A fluid bolus may help a genuinely underfilled HOCM ventricle but flood the lungs in restrictive amyloidosis.
- **Identify the mechanism before prescribing a generic “cardiac” anaesthetic.** [R15]

| Phenotype | Central abnormality | Dominant perioperative danger |
|---|---|---|
| **Dilated (DCM)** | Dilated LV and impaired contraction; often secondary MR and arrhythmia | Vasodilation or myocardial depression → low output; fluid overload |
| **Hypertrophic (HCM)** | Unexplained LVH, diastolic dysfunction ± dynamic LVOT obstruction | Tachycardia, vasodilation, decreased LV volume or increased contractility → obstruction/collapse |
| **Restrictive (RCM)** | Very stiff ventricle with limited stroke-volume reserve, often preserved EF | Underfilling or fluid excess, arrhythmia, hypotension with induction |
| **Arrhythmogenic** | Fibrotic/fatty myocardial disease, ventricular arrhythmias | VT/VF and sudden death, possibly before severe pump dysfunction |
| **Takotsubo** | Stress-related usually reversible regional ventricular dysfunction | Mimics ACS; may develop shock and/or dynamic LVOTO |
| **Peripartum** | New systolic dysfunction during late pregnancy/postpartum | HF, thrombus/embolism, labour and postpartum fluid shift |

## 8A. Dilated cardiomyopathy

### Why it matters

- The LV is dilated and has impaired systolic force.
- Stroke volume may be preserved at rest by an increased end-diastolic volume and sympathetic tone, but the patient is **sensitive to loss of contractility, increases in afterload or inadequate coronary perfusion**.
- Mitral annular dilation causes functional MR and increases pulmonary pressure.
- Circulatory transit may be prolonged, changing the apparent onset of some IV drugs.
- A dilated LV may contain thrombus, while atrial and ventricular arrhythmias are common.

- Causes include familial/genetic disease, myocarditis, cardiotoxic chemotherapy (anthracyclines), alcohol, tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, peripartum disease and idiopathic disease; exclude ischaemic or severe valve causes.
- TTE evaluates LV/RV size, EF, regional function, MR and intracardiac thrombus; ECG/Holter identify arrhythmia, and cardiac MRI may characterise fibrosis/scar.
- **An EF below a particular number is not by itself an indication for therapeutic anticoagulation in sinus rhythm**; seek documented thrombus, AF or another established indication.

### Preoperative implications

- Define symptoms and NYHA status, recent admissions, congestion, prior arrhythmia/syncope and family history.
- Review GDMT, device therapy, anticoagulation and functional reserve; obtain recent/clinically indicated TTE and electrolytes/renal function.
- Defer elective surgery when decompensated; optimise volume and drugs.
- Patients with a pacemaker/ICD/CRT need a **specific device plan:** model, indication, pacing dependence, battery/interrogation, magnet response, likelihood of electromagnetic interference and safe reactivation, rather than assuming every magnet affects all devices equally.
- Detailed CIED work is in Set 12.

### Intraoperative implications

**Preserve forward output without causing congestion:**

- Titrate induction slowly; consider arterial monitoring before induction in severe disease, echo/cardiac-output monitoring for major surgery, and noradrenaline support for vasodilation.
- Avoid excessive afterload and negative inotropy; dobutamine/milrinone may help genuine low output but can worsen hypotension/arrhythmia and should not be given simply for low EF.
- Fluids are cautious and response-guided.
- Neuraxial afterload reduction may benefit a compensated DCM patient but a sudden sympathectomy can produce collapse; match technique to disease, surgical demands and antithrombotics.

### Postoperative implications

Monitor low output, pulmonary oedema, AKI, AF/VT and myocardial injury. Avoid unplanned fluid loading, restart HF therapy when stable, and ensure any ICD therapies suspended for surgery are restored before leaving monitored care. Patients with advanced disease may need HDU/ICU even after apparently uncomplicated surgery.

## 8B. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and dynamic LVOT obstruction

### Why it matters

- HCM commonly results from sarcomere disease causing unexplained LV hypertrophy (in adults, **wall thickness ≥15 mm**, or less in a strong family/genetic context) and impaired relaxation.
- In obstructive HCM the anterior mitral leaflet moves towards the hypertrophied septum in systole (**systolic anterior motion, SAM**), causing dynamic narrowing and often posteriorly directed MR.
- A combination of **flow drag and geometry** contributes; the old isolated “Venturi effect” explanation is incomplete. [R16]

- The obstruction is **dynamic:** it worsens when the LV cavity becomes smaller (hypovolaemia, venodilation, excessive PEEP), when systemic afterload falls (vasodilation), when HR rises (less filling) or when contractility increases (catecholamines, inotropes).
- Conversely, restoring systemic pressure, correcting genuine underfilling and reducing excessive contractility can lower the gradient.
- These facts explain why the “usual” rescue for hypotension—adrenaline, ephedrine or dobutamine—may **make obstructive shock worse**.

- The obstruction is considered present at a peak LVOT gradient **≥30 mmHg**, and **≥50 mmHg** at rest or with physiological provocation is important for symptom-related treatment decisions.
- Look also for diastolic dysfunction, myocardial ischaemia despite normal coronaries, AF, ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death risk.
- Not all HCM is obstructive; absence of a resting gradient does not exclude inducible obstruction with exertion or anaesthesia. [R16]

### Preoperative implications

- Assess exertional dyspnoea, angina, syncope/presyncope, palpitations, episodes of AF and a family history of premature sudden death.
- Examine for systolic murmur that increases with standing/Valsalva and often decreases with squatting or increased afterload.
- ECG may show LVH, repolarisation changes or deep Q waves.
- TTE should report LV thickness, cavity size, **LVOT gradient at rest and with provocation**, SAM, MR, filling pattern and function.
- CMR (late gadolinium enhancement/apical aneurysm) and rhythm monitoring contribute to risk assessment.
- Review beta-blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, disopyramide or myosin-inhibitor treatment and ICD status.

- For symptomatic obstructive HCM, **non-vasodilating beta-blockers** are first-line; verapamil/diltiazem are alternatives in appropriate patients, while disopyramide or cardiac myosin inhibitors (e.g. mavacamten) and septal reduction (myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) are selected specialist treatments.
- Mavacamten can depress EF and interacts with several drugs; serial echo is required.
- Patients with refractory symptoms, significant gradient or recent arrhythmia merit specialist optimisation before elective surgery.
- SCD prevention is based on risk factors such as previous arrest/VT, unexplained syncope, family history, massive hypertrophy, NSVT, apical aneurysm, EF <50% and extensive scar—not solely an elevated LVOT gradient.

### Intraoperative implications: make the LV bigger, slower and less hypercontractile without flooding it

| Variable | Aim | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Maintain normal filling; correct demonstrated hypovolaemia | A small cavity narrows the LVOT and exaggerates SAM. |
| SVR | **Maintain systemic vascular resistance and coronary pressure** | Vasodilation makes obstruction worse. |
| Contractility | Avoid excessive beta-agonist stimulation | Strong ejection accelerates flow and worsens SAM/LVOTO. |
| HR | Low-normal rate, usually sinus rhythm; prevent tachycardia | Allows filling and coronary perfusion; reduces oxygen demand. |
| Rhythm | Preserve atrial contribution; rapidly treat unstable AF | The stiff hypertrophied LV may be dependent on atrial filling. |

**Induction:**

- Titrate gently, with arterial pressure monitoring for substantial obstruction; have phenylephrine or vasopressin available and assess volume.
- Avoid strong sympathetic surges, large propofol/neuraxial vasodilatory swings and routine ephedrine/adrenaline/dobutamine for hypotension.
- Other agents are not absolutely forbidden—what matters is the haemodynamic effect and phenotype.
- In a patient with severe obstruction, abrupt single-shot spinal sympathectomy is hazardous; incremental epidural or carefully selected low-dose techniques may be feasible with monitoring and a rescue plan.

**If hypotension develops, ask:**

- Is it LVOTO?
- Use bedside echo if persistent: small hyperdynamic LV, SAM, dynamic colour-flow/Doppler LVOT gradient and MR support obstruction.
- Restore vascular tone with **phenylephrine (e.g. 50–100 µg titrated IV boluses)** or vasopressin where suitable, correct genuine underfilling with small reassessed fluid and reduce tachycardia/hypercontractility once pressure is supported.
- Esmolol may improve severe tachycardic LVOTO in expert hands, but **never give beta-blocker blindly for undifferentiated shock**.
- If no LVOTO is present and global pump failure dominates, inotropic management differs completely.

### Postoperative implications

Prevent sympathetic surges, dehydration, AF and pain; avoid forced tachycardia and fluid overload. Restart beta-blockade when safe and observe patients with severe obstruction or high arrhythmic risk in monitored recovery. Be prepared for dynamic LVOTO during mobilising, haemorrhage, sepsis or postoperative diuresis.

**Pregnancy/labour extension:**

- The increased plasma volume can enlarge the LV and lessen obstruction, but reduced systemic resistance, tachycardia, pain and post-delivery haemorrhage can worsen LVOTO.
- Early **slowly titrated epidural** analgesia with vasoactive support may attenuate labour stress; avoid sudden sympathectomy and excessive oxytocin boluses.
- Delivery planning should follow a pregnancy heart team and maternal symptoms.
- Past ANZCA SAQs have specifically tested HCM in pregnancy and for urgent fracture surgery. [E2]

## 8C. Restrictive cardiomyopathy and amyloidosis

### Why it matters

- A restrictive ventricle is very **stiff** but may have preserved EF.
- The stroke volume is relatively fixed, and filling pressure rises precipitously with excess fluid.
- Bradycardia can markedly decrease cardiac output when stroke volume cannot rise to compensate, while tachycardia limits diastolic filling and promotes ischaemia.
- Atrial contraction may be essential.
- Major causes include amyloidosis (AL/ATTR), sarcoid, haemochromatosis, radiation injury, endomyocardial fibrosis and infiltrative/storage disease.

- Amyloidosis may present with enlarged atria, apparently thick ventricular walls but low ECG voltage, conduction disease, AF, autonomic neuropathy and hypotension.
- It may involve kidneys, airways, GI tract and coagulation.
- Echo may show restrictive filling and a characteristic apical-sparing strain pattern; CMR and disease-specific testing help distinguish infiltrative disease from hypertensive LVH or constrictive pericarditis.

### Preoperative implications

- Ask syncope, orthostatic symptoms, exertional reserve, HF episodes, arrhythmia, pacing, renal/GI dysfunction and amyloid subtype/treatment.
- Review echo filling pressures, biatrial enlargement, RV involvement, conduction system and anticoagulation.
- Differentiation from **constrictive pericarditis** is important because the management and potential reversibility differ; dynamic septal motion, respiratory Doppler and cross-sectional imaging assist.
- Optimise congestion carefully without rendering the patient underfilled.

### Intraoperative implications

**Maintain a narrow physiological window:**

- Enough venous return for output but avoid preload excess, preserve a suitable HR and sinus rhythm, and prevent abrupt falls in vascular tone.
- Arterial monitoring and vasopressor readiness are valuable in advanced disease.
- Slow induction with selected etomidate or carefully titrated alternatives may be appropriate; positive-pressure ventilation can markedly reduce venous return.
- In some amyloid patients autonomic neuropathy limits compensatory vasoconstriction; vasopressor choice and dosing require close titration.
- Avoid reflex large fluid boluses for hypotension.
- Digoxin and non-DHP CCBs may be poorly tolerated in some amyloid phenotypes but are not universal absolute prohibitions in all clinical settings—seek specialist input.

### Postoperative implications

Watch conduction disease, arrhythmia, hypotension, renal injury and sudden congestion; restart cardiac medications after assessing perfusion/renal function. Advanced RCM may require monitored recovery and access to pacing or vasoactive support.

## 8D. Other important cardiomyopathies

**Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy:**

- Fibrofatty/fibrotic myocardial replacement (may involve RV and LV) predisposes to VT/VF and sudden death, sometimes before obvious systolic impairment.
- Ask about exertional syncope, family sudden death, prior VT, ICD and exercise history; review ECG, ambulatory rhythm, CMR and genetic assessment where relevant.
- Continue specialist beta-blocker/antiarrhythmic therapy, avoid catecholamine surges and have defibrillation/device management ready.
- Not all patients automatically require ICD implantation.

**Takotsubo cardiomyopathy:**

- Stress-associated regional LV dysfunction can mimic ACS with ECG/troponin changes and acute pulmonary oedema.
- Apical ballooning is common but not exclusive; obstructive CAD may coexist.
- First **exclude acute coronary occlusion**.
- If shock occurs, distinguish pump failure from **dynamic LVOTO**, because a catecholamine inotrope may worsen obstruction in the latter.
- Treat genuine LV failure with cautious haemodynamic support and consider MCS for refractory cases.
- LV thrombus and arrhythmias occur; recovery often follows over weeks but risk is not always trivial.

**Peripartum cardiomyopathy:**

- Otherwise unexplained HF with **LVEF <45%** developing in late pregnancy or the postpartum period.
- Evaluate decompensation, ventricular thrombus and embolic risk.
- Pregnancy alters drug safety: ACEi/ARB/ARNI and SGLT2i are contraindicated during pregnancy; use specialist pregnancy-compatible therapy, diuretics where needed, and tailored anticoagulation for AF/thrombus or marked dysfunction.
- Bromocriptine is a selected expert option that suppresses lactation and requires thromboprophylaxis.
- Labour/delivery and postpartum haemodynamic shifts demand multidisciplinary planning.

**Cardiotoxic and inflammatory cardiomyopathy:**

- Alcohol, anthracyclines, trastuzumab and myocarditis can produce DCM-like physiology or arrhythmias.
- Assess current EF and strain, cardiac symptoms, drug exposure, inflammation and QT/rhythm risk.
- Anthracycline toxicity risk increases with cumulative dose but can occur below old “safe” cut-offs; prior therapy does not eliminate later risk.
- Treat the actual ventricular phenotype and ensure appropriate cardio-oncology follow-up.

**Exam synthesis.** The most informative first question is “What is the shape and function of this ventricle, and is there dynamic obstruction?” A low EF, a small hyperdynamic LV with SAM, and a stiff amyloid ventricle need different responses to hypotension.

items.title: 9. Cardiac and great-vessel anatomy for ultrasound
items.body:
## Why it matters

- **Cardiac ultrasound is a set of anatomical cuts through a moving 3-D organ.** To interpret a chamber, valve, effusion or regional wall-motion abnormality correctly, first orient the probe and identify the neighbouring structures.
- The aim is not to memorise an anatomy atlas; it is to know which structures should appear in each standard view and what clinical problem each answers.

## 1. Four chambers, four valves and the fibrous skeleton

- The **RV is the most anterior chamber**, immediately behind the sternum.
- It is normally thin walled and crescentic in short axis, with prominent trabeculations and a moderator band.
- The **LV** is a thick-walled ellipsoid; its myocardium is commonly divided into 17 echo segments.
- The **LA lies posteriorly** against the oesophagus—one reason TOE visualises the LA, mitral valve and left atrial appendage well.
- The **RA** receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, with the crista terminalis and fossa ovalis as important landmarks.

| Structure | Features on imaging | Clinical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Mitral valve** | Anterior and posterior leaflets (scallops A1–3/P1–3), chordae and two papillary muscles | MR mechanism, MS area, SAM in HOCM; mitral and aortic valves share fibrous continuity. |
| **Aortic valve** | Three cusps: right coronary, left coronary, non-coronary; coronary ostia arise from sinuses | Short-axis cusp morphology; long-axis gradient, root dimensions, AR. |
| **Tricuspid valve** | Septal/anterior/posterior leaflets; insertion normally more apical than mitral | TV offset distinguishes RV and LV in apical 4-chamber; TR Doppler estimates RV pressure under appropriate assumptions. |
| **Pulmonary valve** | Anterior and cephalad relative to AV, outflow from infundibulum | RVOT and pulmonary artery flow; pulmonic regurgitation/stenosis. |
| **Pericardium** | Fibrous/serous sac around heart; small physiological fluid may occur | Effusion/tamponade: RA systolic and RV early-diastolic collapse are supportive, but pressure/respiratory context matters. |

- The **interatrial septum** contains the fossa ovalis; PFO is common and relevant to bubble studies and paradoxical embolism.
- The **left atrial appendage** is an important thrombus source in AF and is better assessed with TOE than routine TTE.
- Papillary muscles anchor the mitral leaflets: the **posteromedial** often receives a single PDA blood supply and is vulnerable after inferior MI; the anterolateral muscle usually has dual LAD/LCx contribution.
- This anatomical fact explains post-MI papillary muscle rupture and acute severe MR.

## 2. Coronary anatomy and regional wall motion

| Coronary vessel | Typical course and territories | Echo/ECG application |
|---|---|---|
| Left main | From left coronary sinus, dividing into LAD and LCx | Left-main disease may jeopardise large LV territory. |
| LAD | Anterior interventricular groove to apex | Anterior wall, apical and anterior septal motion; V1–V4 patterns. |
| LCx | Left atrioventricular groove | Lateral/inferolateral LV; lateral ECG leads, sometimes inferior/posterior territory. |
| RCA/PDA | RCA in right AV groove; PDA from RCA in right-dominant (most) hearts or LCx in left-dominant | Inferior LV, RV, AV nodal supply; inferior MI and associated bradycardia/RV infarction. |

The **17-segment model** contains 6 basal, 6 mid, 4 apical segments and the true apex. Coronary territories vary with dominance and wrap-around LAD; a regional wall-motion abnormality **suggests**, but does not prove, the culprit artery. Consider old scar, pacing, conduction abnormalities, afterload and cardiomyopathy as mimics of acute ischaemic wall-motion changes.

## 3. Great vessels and why anatomy matters in the operating theatre

- The ascending aorta arises from LVOT and continues to the arch, giving the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.
- The descending thoracic aorta lies posterior/left of the heart and is well visualised by TOE; the **distal ascending aorta has a recognised TOE blind spot** from intervening tracheal air.
- The IABP tip is normally positioned just distal to the left subclavian origin; positioning too proximal risks arch-vessel occlusion, too distal compromises visceral/renal arteries.

- The pulmonary artery exits the RV anteriorly, then bifurcates; the **PA catheter** follows RA → RV → PA → wedge position.
- The SVC enters the RA superiorly and the IVC inferiorly; a CVC tip for many standard lines is targeted at the **lower SVC/cavoatrial region** according to local protocol.
- Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the LA and Doppler pulmonary-venous flow can assist MR/diastolic assessment.

## 4. A systematic TTE scan

- **Parasternal long axis (PLAX):** with the probe left parasternal, see RV anteriorly, LV, septum and posterior wall, LVOT, aortic root/valve, mitral valve, LA and descending aorta behind LA. Use for LV size, gross function, pericardial fluid, AR and root size.

**Parasternal short axis (PSAX):**

- Rotate to slice the heart from base to apex.
- At aortic-valve level the three-cusp “Mercedes” appearance identifies the AV
- At mitral level the valve orifice can be seen (“fish mouth” in MS)
- At papillary level a circular LV shows septal/anterior/lateral/inferior regional motion and may display RV-pressure-induced septal flattening (D-shaped LV).

**Apical 4-chamber (A4C):**

- Align with the true LV apex, showing both atria/ventricles and mitral/tricuspid valves.
- Tricuspid insertion is more apical.
- Use for EF (with A2C), global RV, TAPSE and valve regurgitation.
- **Apical 5-chamber** tilts anterior to reveal LVOT/AV for Doppler gradients; 2-chamber shows LA, LV anterior/inferior walls and MV; 3-chamber resembles PLAX from the apex.

- **Subcostal four-chamber:** useful in supine patients, often for RV, pericardial effusion and gross LV function. **Subcostal IVC** estimates RA pressure trends but **IVC collapse alone does not diagnose volume responsiveness**. **Suprasternal notch** shows arch and branch vessels in suitable patients.

## 5. Essential TOE views and clinical questions

Because the oesophagus lies behind the LA, the transoesophageal probe produces mid-oesophageal (ME) views at different multiplane angles; advancement gives transgastric (TG) and deep TG views.

| View | Approximate angle | What to identify / answer |
|---|---|---|
| ME 4-chamber | 0–20° | Both ventricles and atria, MV/TV, septum, gross function. |
| ME 2-chamber | 80–100° | LV anterior/inferior walls, MV and LA/LAA region. |
| ME long-axis | 120–160° | LVOT, AV, MV, LA and proximal ascending aorta. |
| ME AV short-axis | 30–60° | Three cusps, AV morphology and coronary ostial region. |
| ME bicaval | 90–110° | SVC, IVC, RA, interatrial septum and PFO/catheter relation. |
| ME RV inflow–outflow | 50–70° | TV, RVOT, pulmonary valve and PA. |
| TG mid-papillary short-axis | 0° | Global mid-LV circumferential wall motion; useful in instability but does not cover all segments. |
| Deep TG long-axis | 0–20° | Align CW Doppler through AV/LVOT to estimate gradient. |
| Descending aortic SAX/LAX | 0°/90° | Atheroma, dissection, IABP location. |

**Focused echo during collapse should answer five questions rapidly:**

- (1) is there tamponade?
- (2) is the LV severely impaired or hyperdynamic?
- (3) is the RV dilated/pressure loaded?
- (4) is the LV underfilled, obstructed or congested?
- (5) is there a major valve lesion or new regional wall-motion problem?
- A focused view is not a substitute for comprehensive echo when a management-changing diagnosis is unclear.

**Exam synthesis.** Identify the chambers and valves first; relate standard TTE/TOE views to the physiological question (output, valve severity, regional function, RV pressure, tamponade) rather than memorising probe angles without anatomical orientation.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
> These are deliberately placed **after** the teaching chapters. For each study, remember the clinical question, main result and what it does not prove; do not memorise percentages divorced from the trial population and endpoint.

## Perioperative cardiac risk, medication and myocardial injury

- **T1 ·** [POISE: perioperative metoprolol (2008)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18479744/)
  - In 8,351 patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery, fixed high-dose extended-release metoprolol started immediately before surgery reduced perioperative MI (4.2% versus 5.7%) but increased total mortality (3.1% versus 2.3%) and stroke (1.0% versus 0.5%).
  - **Clinical lesson:** continue established beta-blockers; do not initiate a large fixed dose on the day of surgery. This does not imply beta-blockers are harmful when introduced cautiously for a genuine chronic indication well before surgery.
- **T2 ·** [POISE-2: aspirin (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1401105) and [clonidine (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1401106)
  - A factorial RCT involving approximately 10,000 patients: perioperative aspirin did not reduce death or nonfatal MI (7.0% versus 7.1%) but increased major bleeding (4.6% versus 3.8%).
  - Clonidine did not confer primary cardiovascular benefit and increased clinically important hypotension (47.6% versus 37.1%).
  - **Lesson:** do not routinely initiate either for perioperative cardioprotection. Recent coronary stents and other specific antiplatelet indications require separate decisions; stopping chronic clonidine is a different issue from starting it.
- **T3 ·** [CARP: coronary revascularisation before major vascular surgery (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa041905)
  - Among 510 selected patients with stable CAD, prophylactic coronary revascularisation did not improve mortality (22% versus 23% over median 2.7 years) or postoperative MI (12% versus 14%).
  - **Lesson:** do not send stable patients for PCI/CABG simply to clear them for surgery; patients with standard independent indications such as significant left-main disease remain different.
- **T4 ·** [VISION: postoperative high-sensitivity troponin and outcomes (2017)](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2620089)
  - Prospective cohort of 21,842 patients: postoperative myocardial injury/MINS was common (approximately 17.9% by the assay-specific study definition) and usually clinically silent (over 90% without ischaemic symptoms). Increasing peak hs-troponin T predicted increasing 30-day mortality.
  - **Lesson:** selected high-risk patients benefit from consideration of surveillance; the association alone does not prove screening or a specific treatment improves survival.
- **T5 ·** [MANAGE: dabigatran after MINS (2018)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29900874/)
  - In 1,754 patients with MINS, dabigatran 110 mg twice daily reduced a composite of major vascular complications (11% versus 15%).
  - **Lesson:** anticoagulation is a potential selected strategy after haemostasis is secured and bleeding/renal risks considered, not automatic treatment of every raised postoperative troponin. Early termination and high discontinuation limit generalisability.
- **T6 ·** [STOP-or-NOT: continuation of renin–angiotensin inhibitors (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11365013/)
  - Among 2,222 patients, continuing versus stopping a RAS inhibitor 48 hours preoperatively produced a similar 28-day composite of death/major complications (22% both groups), with more intraoperative hypotension after continuation (54% versus 41%).
  - **Lesson:** either strategy can be defensible based on indication, BP and the chosen guideline; no proven universal policy.
- **T7 ·** [METS: measurement of exercise tolerance before surgery (2018)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Measurement+of+Exercise+Tolerance+before+Surgery+METS+Lancet+2018)
  - Prospective 1,401-patient study: clinician-estimated functional capacity was poorly sensitive for low CPET capacity, whereas the structured Duke Activity Status Index was associated with the primary 30-day death/MI outcome.
  - **Lesson:** ask structured functional questions; subjective “good exercise tolerance” alone does not validate low cardiac risk.
- **T8 ·** [POISE-3 blood pressure strategy (2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=POISE-3+hypotension+avoidance+hypertension+management+trial+2023)
  - A bundled hypotension-avoidance strategy (withholding selected antihypertensives and targeting intraoperative MAP ≥80) did not significantly improve 30-day vascular outcomes compared with a hypertension-avoidance/continuation bundle (MAP ≥60; approximately 13.9% versus 14.0%).
  - **Lesson:** there is no single RCT-proven higher MAP target for all patients; the trial cannot isolate the independent effect of each component of the bundle.

## Acute myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock

- **T9 ·** [SHOCK: early revascularisation for MI-related cardiogenic shock (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199908263410901)
  - Emergency revascularisation did not significantly change the prespecified 30-day mortality endpoint but improved survival at 6 and 12 months.
  - **Lesson:** urgent culprit-artery reperfusion is foundational therapy for infarction-related cardiogenic shock; vasoactive support alone does not repair the cause.
- **T10 ·** [CULPRIT-SHOCK (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1710261)
  - In 706 patients with multivessel CAD and MI-related shock, culprit-only PCI (with potential later staged treatment) reduced the composite of death or severe renal failure requiring renal replacement at 30 days versus immediate multivessel PCI (45.9% versus 55.4%).
  - **Lesson:** avoid routine immediate non-culprit PCI in shock; selection still depends on coronary anatomy and the individual patient.
- **T11 ·** [IABP-SHOCK II (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1208410)
  - In infarction-related shock managed with early revascularisation, routine IABP did not reduce 30-day mortality (39.7% versus 41.3%).
  - **Lesson:** an IABP may have selected bridging/mechanical-complication indications but is not a routine survival-improving treatment for uncomplicated post-MI shock.
- **T12 ·** [DOREMI: milrinone versus dobutamine (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2026845)
  - Among 192 patients with cardiogenic shock, there was no statistically significant difference in the primary composite outcome.
  - **Lesson:** choose/titrate based on haemodynamics, arrhythmia, renal clearance and beta-blockade, rather than claim either inotrope improves survival.
- **T13 ·** [DanGer Shock: Impella CP for selected STEMI shock (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572)
  - In selected patients, 180-day death was lower with a microaxial LV pump (45.8% versus 58.5%), but severe bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal-replacement complications increased.
  - **Lesson:** a shock-team device option in the right phenotype, not an indication for universal device insertion; balance benefit against procedural harm.
- **T14 ·** [ECLS-SHOCK: early VA-ECMO in MI shock (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227)
  - Among 417 analysable participants, 30-day mortality was not lower with routine early extracorporeal life support (47.8% versus 49.0%), while moderate/severe bleeding and vascular complications were higher.
  - **Lesson:** rescue support should be phenotype- and expertise-guided; VA-ECMO itself may increase LV afterload and requires assessment for unloading.

## Heart failure and pulmonary oedema

- **T15 ·** [DAPA-HF: dapagliflozin in HFrEF (2019)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31535829/)
  - In 4,744 symptomatic patients with LVEF ≤40%, dapagliflozin reduced worsening HF or cardiovascular death compared with placebo (16.3% versus 21.2%), independent of diabetes status.
  - **Lesson:** SGLT2 inhibition is a core chronic HF therapy; **withhold perioperatively for ketoacidosis risk** and restart only after clinical recovery and eating.
- **T16 ·** [ESCAPE: pulmonary artery catheter in decompensated HF (2005)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=ESCAPE+trial+pulmonary+artery+catheter+heart+failure+JAMA+2005)
  - Routine PAC-guided therapy did not improve the primary outcome of days alive outside hospital during the first 6 months in patients hospitalised with severe HF, versus careful clinical assessment.
  - **Lesson:** invasive pressures are useful for particular diagnostic questions, especially uncertain/refractory shock, not routinely for every decompensation. Static filling pressures do not measure fluid responsiveness.
- **T17 ·** [3CPO: CPAP/NIV in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0707992)
  - Randomised comparison of oxygen, CPAP and bilevel NIV found faster relief of distress and physiological abnormalities with non-invasive support, without a significant difference in the primary seven-day mortality outcome.
  - **Lesson:** use early CPAP/NIV for appropriate respiratory distress but monitor for failure; the neutral mortality outcome does not establish universal equivalence of all modes.
- **T18 ·** [DOSE: IV furosemide strategies in decompensated HF (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1005419)
  - Bolus versus infusion and lower versus higher doses did not show significant differences in the coprimary symptom/renal endpoints; higher-dose regimens produced more transient creatinine increases while facilitating decongestion.
  - **Lesson:** titrate loop diuretic to urine output, natriuresis, symptoms and renal response, not an assumed universally superior administration mode.
- **T19 ·** [ADVOR: acetazolamide added to IV loops (2022)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36027559/)
  - In 519 patients with acute decompensated HF and congestion, IV acetazolamide increased successful early decongestion (42.2% versus 30.5%).
  - **Lesson:** selected sequential nephron blockade can help diuretic resistance, with electrolyte and renal surveillance.
- **T20 ·** [PARADIGM-HF: sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1409077)
  - The ARNI reduced the combined cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation outcome in selected ambulatory HFrEF patients (21.8% versus 26.5%).
  - **Lesson:** know the rationale for foundational RAAS/ARNI therapy; assess perioperative BP and renal function; an ACEi↔ARNI switch needs a ≥36-hour ACEi washout, not a universal 36-hour preoperative ARNI interruption.
- **T21 ·** [EMPEROR-Preserved (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2107038)
  - Empagliflozin lowered cardiovascular death/HF hospitalisation in symptomatic HF with EF >40% (13.8% versus 17.1%), mainly through fewer hospitalisations.
  - **Lesson:** do not misstate composite benefit as proof of mortality reduction in every HF phenotype.
- **T22 ·** [DELIVER (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2206286)
  - Dapagliflozin lowered worsening HF or cardiovascular death in mildly reduced/preserved EF (16.4% versus 19.5%).
  - **Lesson:** SGLT2 inhibition is useful across much of the EF range, but historical trial EF definitions do not automatically match the 2026 ESC classification.

## Valve disease and cardiomyopathy

- **T23 ·** [PARTNER 3: TAVI versus surgery in low-risk severe AS (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1814052)
  - In selected anatomically suitable low-risk patients, transcatheter treatment improved the one-year composite of death, stroke or rehospitalisation versus surgery.
  - **Lesson:** TAVI is a legitimate option beyond inoperable/high-risk patients, but anatomy, life expectancy, valve durability and later re-intervention matter; early results are not a universal mandate for TAVI.
- **T24 ·** [COAPT: transcatheter mitral repair in secondary MR (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1806640)
  - In carefully selected symptomatic HF with moderate-to-severe/severe secondary MR despite maximally tolerated therapy, edge-to-edge repair reduced HF hospitalisation and mortality relative to medical management.
  - **Lesson:** intervention decisions depend on the mechanism of MR and optimised background HF/CRT, not solely a large colour-Doppler jet.
- **T25 ·** [EXPLORER-HCM: mavacamten for obstructive HCM (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32871100/)
  - A myosin inhibitor improved the composite of exercise capacity/NYHA functional class in symptomatic obstructive HCM (approximately 37% versus 17%).
  - **Lesson:** understanding negative inotropy matters in LVOT obstruction; treatment requires serial LVEF/gradient monitoring because excessive systolic suppression is possible.

items.title: Hypotension after induction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
items.source: Example drafted by Claude from the Set 11 chapter 6 notes. Check against your own sources.
items.stem: A 45-year-old man with known hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is booked for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Five minutes after induction his BP is 70/40 and his heart rate is 95.

points: Treat with a pure alpha-agonist: phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms, or vasopressin
Fluid bolus and leg elevation to restore preload
Reduce the volatile concentration
Treat tachycardia (esmolol)
Do NOT give ephedrine or inotropes
Check for another cause: bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, ischaemia, arrhythmia

stages.prompt: Explain why those measures work and why ephedrine would make things worse.
points: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy narrows the LV outflow tract
In systole the anterior mitral leaflet is pulled toward the septum (SAM, Venturi effect and drag), worsening obstruction and causing posterior-directed MR
Obstruction is dynamic: worse with reduced LV volume (hypovolaemia, vasodilation), increased contractility, tachycardia, and reduced afterload
Diastolic dysfunction from LVH raises LVEDP, so supply-demand mismatch causes ischaemia despite normal coronaries
Ephedrine and beta-agonists raise contractility and heart rate, which increases the gradient

stages.prompt: His BP stays low despite phenylephrine. What next?
points: Use TOE to confirm SAM and LVOT obstruction
Start vasoconstrictor infusions (phenylephrine, vasopressin, noradrenaline)
Keep excluding other causes of hypotension
Call for help and tell the surgeon
Still avoid inotropes

stages.prompt: The surgeon wants to proceed with pneumoperitoneum. What are your concerns?
points: Insufflation raises SVR (helpful) but reduces venous return, especially head-up (harmful)
Slow insufflation at low pressure
Head-down tilt and fluid loading to maintain preload
Keep rate low-normal and sinus rhythm; treat AF early (cardiovert, amiodarone or beta-blocker; avoid digoxin)

items.title: What determines myocardial oxygen supply and demand?
items.q: What determines myocardial oxygen supply and demand?
items.a:
- Supply: coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic minus LVEDP), diastolic time, arterial oxygen content (Hb, SaO2), vessel patency.
- Demand: heart rate, wall tension (preload, afterload, radius, thickness), contractility.
- Oxygen extraction is already about 70 to 80% at rest, so increased demand is met predominantly by increased flow; extraction reserve is limited, not absent.
- Worst case: tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia and LVH together.

> **Closing point:** Tachycardia hurts both sides: it shortens diastole and raises demand.

items.title: State the six RCRI predictors.
items.q: State the six RCRI predictors.
items.a:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular).
- Ischaemic heart disease.
- Heart failure.
- Cerebrovascular disease.
- Insulin-treated diabetes.
- Creatinine above 177 micromol/L.

> **Closing point:** Risk of a major cardiac event climbs with each point; it supports decisions and consent but does not dictate them.

items.title: How do you assess functional capacity?
items.q: How do you assess functional capacity?
items.a:
- **<4 METs** is the traditional threshold for poor functional capacity, but a question about climbing two flights of stairs is only a screening clue—not an exact MET measurement.
- The **Duke Activity Status Index (DASI)** is structured; **DASI >34** has been associated with lower perioperative risk in the METS cohort (not a diagnostic pass/fail threshold).
- CPET objectively measures exercise capacity when the result will change a decision; it is not routine for every patient.
- Clinician-estimated exercise tolerance performed poorly in METS; interpret function alongside symptoms, frailty, procedure and active disease.

> **Closing point:** Use a structured assessment when uncertainty matters; neither stair climbing nor DASI alone decides whether surgery proceeds.

items.title: Give the minimum delay before elective surgery after coronary stenting.
items.q: Give the minimum delay before elective surgery after coronary stenting.
items.a:
- Balloon angioplasty alone: about 2 weeks.
- Bare-metal stent: at least 1 month (preferably 3).
- Drug-eluting stent, stable disease: at least 6 months.
- Drug-eluting stent after ACS: at least 12 months for elective surgery requiring interruption; selected time-sensitive surgery may be considered from 3 months after DES when delay is more harmful.
- Keep aspirin; stop the P2Y12 inhibitor only by joint decision.

> **Closing point:** Premature DAPT cessation is the biggest driver of stent thrombosis.

items.title: When should you stop each P2Y12 inhibitor before surgery?
items.q: When should you stop each P2Y12 inhibitor before surgery?
items.a:
- Clopidogrel 5 to 7 days (irreversible).
- Prasugrel 7–10 days (irreversible).
- Ticagrelor 3 to 5 days (reversible).
- Cangrelor: IV specialist bridge; neuraxial needle placement ≥3 h after stopping, first dose ≥8 h after catheter removal. Ticagrelor requires 5 days for neuraxial placement, distinct from some surgical intervals.
- Platelet transfusion works only once the active drug has cleared.

> **Closing point:** Irreversible agents need platelet turnover of about 10% per day.

items.title: Which cardiac drugs do you continue and which do you not start before surgery?
items.q: Which cardiac drugs do you continue and which do you not start before surgery?
items.a:
- Continue: beta-blocker, statin, aspirin if stented, calcium channel blocker, nitrates, clonidine.
- Consider withholding on the day: ACEi/ARB, diuretics. Continuation is individualised: AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission for selected hypertension cases and favours continuing compensated-HF therapy; AOA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEi/ARB. Restart when perfusion/renal function permit.
- Stop 3 days before: SGLT2 inhibitor. Current AHA/ACC/FDA interval: ≥72 h for dapagliflozin/empagliflozin/canagliflozin, ≥96 h for ertugliflozin; distinguish this from shorter calendar-day protocols. Restart when stable, eating/drinking and without ketosis.
- Do not start on the day: high-dose beta-blocker (POISE), clonidine and aspirin (POISE-2).

> **Closing point:** Withdrawal of beta-blockers, clonidine and statins is harmful.

items.title: What is MINS and how is it detected?
items.q: What is MINS and how is it detected?
items.a:
- Troponin rise of ischaemic origin within 30 days of surgery, not needing MI criteria.
- VISION Roche hs-troponin T: 20 to under 65 ng/L with absolute change ≥5, or ≥65 ng/L; assay-specific and attributed to ischaemia.
- Over 90% lacked ischaemic symptoms in hsTnT VISION; mortality varies by troponin band and population, not a universal 10%.
- Detect with troponin on days 1 to 3.

> **Closing point:** Most perioperative myocardial injury is silent, so look for it.

items.title: How sensitive is the ECG for intraoperative ischaemia, by lead?
items.q: How sensitive is the ECG for intraoperative ischaemia, by lead?
items.a:
- Lead II alone about 33%.
- V5 alone about 75%.
- II plus V5 about 80%; V4 plus V5 about 90%.
- II, V4 and V5 about 96%.
- Use the diagnostic filter (0.05 Hz).

> **Closing point:** Use a 5-lead system with V5 for at-risk patients.

items.title: What is the approach to a blood pressure of 185/112 before elective surgery?
items.q: What is the approach to a blood pressure of 185/112 before elective surgery?
items.a:
- Confirm the reading and look for end-organ damage and secondary causes.
- Confirm severe BP elevation and assess acute organ injury. AOA/BIHS 2026 uses ≥180/120; AHA/ACC 2024 considers ≥180/110 in selected elevated-risk elective cases. Follow local policy; avoid rapid normalisation without an emergency indication.
- Continue beta-blocker, CCB and clonidine; consider withholding ACEi/ARB and diuretic. Continuation is individualised: AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission for selected hypertension cases and favours continuing compensated-HF therapy; AOA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEi/ARB. Restart when perfusion/renal function permit.

> **Closing point:** In chronic hypertension intraoperative hypotension is the bigger danger.

items.title: Why use a risk tool rather than clinical judgement alone?
items.q: Why use a risk tool rather than clinical judgement alone?
items.a:
- Patients are owed an estimate of risk during consent.
- Tools help target HDU or ICU and limited resources.
- SNAP-2 (22,631 patients): judgement was the only documented tool in 79%.
- Judgement plus a tool estimates risk better than judgement alone.

> **Closing point:** Use a tool to support, not replace, judgement.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.title: Discrimination versus calibration: what is the difference?
items.q: Discrimination versus calibration: what is the difference?
items.a:
- Discrimination: separates patients with and without the outcome (AUROC).
- Calibration: predicted risk matches observed risk.
- Calibration drifts, so tools need periodic recalibration.
- Little evidence yet that risk stratification itself improves outcomes.

> **Closing point:** A good AUROC can still give the wrong absolute risk.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.title: Name the main perioperative risk tools and one feature of each.
items.q: Name the main perioperative risk tools and one feature of each.
items.a:
- ASA-PS: not designed as a score but discriminates mortality well; part of SORT and nzRISK.
- RCRI: six-item cardiac risk.
- ACS NSQIP: 21 variables from about 1.4 million US patients; 30-day mortality and morbidity.
- P-POSSUM and SORT: 30-day mortality.
- nzRISK: New Zealand tool predicting mortality to 2 years.

> **Closing point:** Most tools stop at 30 days; nzRISK looks to 2 years.

Source: Blue Book 2023

items.title: Which definitions of perioperative myocardial injury should you know?
items.q: Which definitions of perioperative myocardial injury should you know?
items.a:
- MINS (VISION): Roche hsTnT 20–<65 ng/L with absolute change ≥5 ng/L, or ≥65 ng/L, attributed to ischaemia within 3 days, judged ischaemic, no clear non-ischaemic explanation. This assay-specific VISION threshold is not a universal threshold for every troponin assay.
- AHA 2021: troponin above the 99th percentile, change in 30 days, symptoms not required.
- Fifth Universal Definition (2026; older studies use the Fourth UDMI): injury can have any cause; infarction needs evidence of ischaemia.

> **Closing point:** Injury is troponin above the assay-specific 99th percentile; acute injury requires a rise/fall, and MI additionally needs evidence of ischaemia.

Source: BJA Educ 2024

items.title: How common is perioperative myocardial injury and what can you do about it?
items.q: How common is perioperative myocardial injury and what can you do about it?
items.a:
- About 20% of high-risk non-cardiac surgery patients.
- Mostly silent; associated with morbidity and mortality.
- Mechanisms mixed: supply-demand, plaque rupture, non-ischaemic.
- No definitive preventative or treatment strategy: correct triggers, surveillance, cardiology.

> **Closing point:** Surveillance finds it; trigger control is the treatment.

Source: BJA Educ 2024

items.title: Should you cancel surgery for a blood pressure above 180/110?
items.q: Should you cancel surgery for a blood pressure above 180/110?
items.a:
- Hypertension alone is not a reason to cancel.
- Decide on overall cardiac risk and end-organ damage.
- AoA/BHS: postpone above 180/110; POQI questions the evidence for a threshold. **Update:** AOA/BIHS 2026 uses clinic ≥180/120 mmHg (and generally continues ACEi/ARB); AHA/ACC 2024 permits considering deferral at ≥180/110 in selected elevated-risk cases. Confirm BP, distinguish chronic damage from acute organ injury, and follow local policy.
- Intraoperative hypotension is the greater danger.

> **Closing point:** The whole patient, not one reading.

Source: BJA Educ 2021

items.title: Define MI and give the ECG criteria for STEMI.
items.q: Define MI and give the ECG criteria for STEMI.
items.a:
- Troponin rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile plus ischaemic symptoms, ECG change, Q waves, imaging evidence, or thrombus.
- Current categories: primary MI from acute coronary pathology (including atherothrombosis, SCAD, vasospasm/embolism), secondary MI from another acute condition causing supply–demand imbalance, and procedure-related MI after cardiac interventions. Older type 1/2 terminology is not an exact mapping.
- STEMI: J-point elevation of 1 mm in two contiguous leads (V2 to V3: 2 mm in men ≥40, 2.5 mm in men <40, 1.5 mm in women).
- Equivalents: new LBBB with Sgarbossa features, posterior MI, de Winter, diffuse subendocardial ischaemia (aVR elevation with widespread ST depression is not specific for left-main occlusion).

> **Closing point:** Correct supply–demand triggers and establish whether acute coronary pathology or another treatable cause is present.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: Match ECG leads to coronary territories.
items.q: Match ECG leads to coronary territories.
items.a:
- Septal V1 to V2 and anterior V3 to V4: LAD.
- Lateral I, aVL, V5 to V6: diagonal or circumflex.
- Inferior II, III, aVF: RCA (80%) or circumflex.
- Posterior: ST depression with tall R in V1 to V3 (confirm V7 to V9).
- RV: V4R.

> **Closing point:** Territory leads to vessel, vessel to complications.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: List the initial management of ACS.
items.q: List the initial management of ACS.
items.a:
- Monitor, 12-lead ECG, titrated opioid; oxygen only if SpO2 below 90%.
- Aspirin 300 mg oral chewed/dissolved (Australian ACS 2025; other guidelines use different loading ranges) and a P2Y12 inhibitor per cardiology.
- Anticoagulation (UFH or enoxaparin); GTN if hypertensive or ongoing pain.
- Beta-blocker only if no heart failure, shock or block; high-intensity statin.
- Early reperfusion.

> **Closing point:** Reperfusion matters more than drugs.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: What are the reperfusion options and why is fibrinolysis a problem after surgery?
items.q: What are the reperfusion options and why is fibrinolysis a problem after surgery?
items.a:
- Primary PCI: first contact to device within 90 minutes (60 if at a PCI centre).
- Fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be done within 120 minutes.
- Recent major surgery is a major contraindication; ESC lists major surgery/trauma/head injury within the previous month as absolute. Use the applicable current lysis checklist.
- Rescue PCI if less than 50% ST resolution.

> **Closing point:** After surgery prefer PCI.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: Define cardiogenic shock and the SCAI stages.
items.q: Define cardiogenic shock and the SCAI stages.
items.a:
- SBP below 90 for 30 minutes or vasopressors needed, with hypoperfusion (lactate above 2, oliguria, cool peripheries) and a cardiac cause.
- Stages: A at risk, B beginning, C classic, D deteriorating, E extremis.
- Mortality about 40 to 50%.

> **Closing point:** Lactate and response to treatment define the stage.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: Which vasoactive drugs for cardiogenic shock?
items.q: Which vasoactive drugs for cardiogenic shock?
items.a:
- Noradrenaline is commonly used for hypotension; SOAP II found fewer arrhythmias than dopamine, with a cardiogenic-subgroup mortality signal rather than definitive dedicated-shock survival proof.
- Dobutamine for low output once MAP restored.
- Milrinone or levosimendan as alternatives.
- Vasopressin to spare catecholamines.
- Lowest dose for the shortest time.

> **Closing point:** Perfusion pressure first, then flow.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.q: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.a:
- IABP: about 0.5 L/min, afterload reduction; no mortality benefit (IABP-SHOCK II).
- Impella: 2.5 to 5.5 L/min; DanGer Shock showed lower mortality in selected STEMI shock; bleeding and limb ischaemia.
- VA-ECMO: full support; no 30-day benefit in ECLS-SHOCK; raises LV afterload; assess for LV distension and add unloading when indicated, not automatically in every patient.

> **Closing point:** Know the exit strategy before insertion.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: How do you read an IABP 1:2 trace?
items.q: How do you read an IABP 1:2 trace?
items.a:
- Inflation at the dicrotic notch; deflation just before systole.
- Diastolic augmentation often exceeds native systole but this is not obligatory; assess timing, assisted pressures and perfusion.
- Assisted end-diastolic and assisted systolic pressures are lower than unassisted.
- Early inflation shortens systole; late deflation raises afterload.

> **Closing point:** Inflate at the notch, deflate before systole.

Source: SS_IC 1.31

items.title: What is the mortality of cardiogenic shock after MI and which treatments have outcome evidence?
items.q: What is the mortality of cardiogenic shock after MI and which treatments have outcome evidence?
items.a:
- Mortality 40 to 70%; about 9% of STEMI.
- Defined by end-organ hypoperfusion, not blood pressure alone.
- Emergency revascularisation is central; DanGer Shock also demonstrated survival benefit with Impella CP in a selected STEMI-shock population, with more adverse events.

> **Closing point:** Revascularise early.

Source: SS_IC 1.31, BJA Educ 2023

items.title: Quote the maximum output of each mechanical circulatory support device.
items.q: Quote the maximum output of each mechanical circulatory support device.
items.a:
- IABP about 0.8 L/min.
- Impella 2.5 to 5.0 L/min.
- TandemHeart 4.0 L/min.
- VA-ECMO up to 7 L/min.
- Use the least support needed.

> **Closing point:** More support means more complications.

Source: SS_IC 1.31, BJA Educ 2023

items.title: Why is noradrenaline contentious in cardiogenic shock after MI?
items.q: Why is noradrenaline contentious in cardiogenic shock after MI?
items.a:
- The syndrome has intense intrinsic vasoconstriction and high SVR.
- A pure vasopressor can raise LV afterload and worsen output.
- Inodilators can reduce afterload but cause hypotension and arrhythmia.
- Titrate carefully with invasive monitoring.

> **Closing point:** Perfusion pressure and afterload pull in opposite directions.

Source: SS_IC 1.31, BJA Educ 2023

items.title: Classify heart failure.
items.q: Classify heart failure.
items.a:
