- By EF: HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41 to 49%, HFpEF 50% or more. ESC 2026 now uses HFrEF <50% and HFpEF ≥50%, retiring HFmrEF; retain older EF bands for historical reports/trial eligibility.
- By severity: NYHA I to IV and ACC/AHA stages A to D.
- By profile: warm/cold and wet/dry.

> **Closing point:** HFpEF is about half of all heart failure.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35

items.title: Name the four pillars of HFrEF therapy.
items.q: Name the four pillars of HFrEF therapy.
items.a:
- ARNI, ACEi or ARB.
- Beta-blocker.
- Mineralocorticoid antagonist.
- SGLT2 inhibitor and, per ESC 2026, an appropriate MRA with potassium/renal monitoring; benefit in HFpEF is mainly fewer HF events.
- All improve survival; restart early after surgery.

> **Closing point:** Hold SGLT2 inhibitors for 3 days before surgery. Current AHA/ACC/FDA interval: ≥72 h for dapagliflozin/empagliflozin/canagliflozin, ≥96 h for ertugliflozin; distinguish this from shorter calendar-day protocols. Restart when stable, eating/drinking and without ketosis.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35

items.title: Compare systolic and diastolic dysfunction.
items.q: Compare systolic and diastolic dysfunction.
items.a:
- Systolic: low contractility, dilated LV, flat Starling curve.
- Diastolic: stiff LV, normal EF, steep pressure-volume curve.
- Diastolic failure: tachycardia and AF are poorly tolerated.
- Both: avoid ischaemia.

> **Closing point:** Diastolic failure is a pressure problem.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35

items.title: How does echo grade diastolic function?
items.q: How does echo grade diastolic function?
items.a:
- Use ASE 2025 integrated mitral inflow, e′, E/e′, TR/PASP and LA volume/strain assessment.
- E/e′ alone cannot assign grades 1–3; pseudonormal inflow can mask impaired relaxation.
- AF, significant MR/MS, pacing and loading changes require modified algorithms and suitable beat averaging.

> **Closing point:** Estimate filling pressure and relaxation together; normal EF does not exclude HFpEF.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35

items.title: State the haemodynamic goals for induction in EF 20%.
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals for induction in EF 20%.
items.a:
- Arterial line first; vasopressor infusing.
- Reduced doses of etomidate or ketamine, or slowly titrated propofol with fentanyl.
- Preload maintained, afterload low-normal, rate individualised without marked rate extremes, sinus rhythm.
- Low mean airway pressure.

> **Closing point:** Pre-empt hypotension with vasopressors.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35

items.title: Outline the management of acute decompensated heart failure with low output.
items.q: Outline the management of acute decompensated heart failure with low output.
items.a:
- Respiratory support: CPAP/NIV; intubation with vasopressor running.
- Perfusion first: noradrenaline, dobutamine or milrinone.
- Decongest: IV furosemide; resistance: thiazide or acetazolamide.
- Mechanical support if refractory; treat the cause (CHAMP).

> **Closing point:** In the cold and wet patient, perfusion comes before decongestion.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35

items.title: When do you stop and restart an SGLT2 inhibitor?
items.q: When do you stop and restart an SGLT2 inhibitor?
items.a:
- Stop 3 days before non-day surgery or bowel preparation (use an explicit last-dose date/time; counting the day of surgery is not equivalent to a full 72-hour interval).
- UK consensus: 2 days, except for prolonged fasting.
- Restart only when eating and drinking normally and the acute illness has resolved.
- Teach a sick-day plan.

> **Closing point:** The danger is euglycaemic DKA: look for ketones, not glucose.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2021

items.title: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure admissions?
items.q: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure admissions?
items.a:
- Benefit within months, regardless of HbA1c or diabetes status.
- Not explained by glucose lowering.
- Proposed: reverse remodelling (lower LV volumes and mass).
- Proposed: less cardiac fibrosis and better myocardial metabolism.

> **Closing point:** The speed of benefit points away from glucose control.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the four phases of diastole?
items.q: What are the four phases of diastole?
items.a:
- Isovolumic relaxation (active, energy-dependent).
- Early rapid filling: suction from LV recoil, a variable proportion of filling, depending on age, rhythm, rate and relaxation.
- Diastasis: filling set by compliance.
- Late filling: atrial contraction (lost in AF).

> **Closing point:** Ischaemia impairs relaxation because relaxation uses ATP.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2017

items.title: Why can diastolic dysfunction not be graded from E/e' alone?
items.q: Why can diastolic dysfunction not be graded from E/e' alone?
items.a:
- Use ASE 2025 integrated mitral inflow, e′, E/e′, TR/PASP and LA volume/strain assessment.
- E/e′ alone cannot assign grades 1–3; pseudonormal inflow can mask impaired relaxation.
- AF, significant MR/MS, pacing and loading changes require modified algorithms and suitable beat averaging.

> **Closing point:** Estimate filling pressure and relaxation together; normal EF does not exclude HFpEF.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2017

items.title: What conditions travel with HFpEF?
items.q: What conditions travel with HFpEF?
items.a:
- 40 to 50% of all heart failure.
- Hypertension (70 to 88%), AF (30 to 37%), coronary disease, diabetes, pulmonary hypertension.
- Commoner in the elderly, obese and women.
- Mortality is higher than in the general population.

> **Closing point:** Normal EF does not exclude heart failure.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2017

items.title: State the anticoagulation targets and plan for an LVAD patient needing surgery.
items.q: State the anticoagulation targets and plan for an LVAD patient needing surgery.
items.a:
Warfarin targets are device- and patient-specific, commonly INR 2.0–3.0 for contemporary durable LVAD care; confirm the VAD centre’s plan. HeartMate 3 patients may omit aspirin under an appropriate protocol (ARIES-HM3), rather than receiving an antiplatelet automatically. If interruption is needed, individualise bridging. Urgent sustained reversal generally uses four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K; coordinate dose, haemostasis and prompt re-anticoagulation with the VAD team.
- Elective: stop warfarin 5 days before; consider bridging only after device/valve-specific specialist assessment of thrombosis versus bleeding; it is not universal.
- Emergency: factor concentrate (Prothrombinex), with IV vitamin K when urgent sustained reversal is required; dose and restart are agreed with the VAD team, to INR below 1.5.

> **Closing point:** Reverse with factor concentrate because warfarin must restart.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the main perioperative problems in a patient with an LVAD?
items.q: What are the main perioperative problems in a patient with an LVAD?
items.a:
- Hypotension is commonest, then AKI, bleeding and arrhythmia.
- Think: haemodynamics, determinants of VAD preload, monitoring, anticoagulation, asepsis.
- Pulsatility may be reduced or absent; NIBP may need Doppler.
- Device-specific EMI plan; asynchronous pacing only if indicated by dependence/EMI, suspend ICD therapies when appropriate and restore before leaving monitoring.

> **Closing point:** Protect the RV and keep the preload up.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2021

items.title: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.q: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.a:
- The heart is denervated: vagal tone is gone.
- Resting rate is 90 to 100 beats/min.
- Antimuscarinic responses are often absent/unreliable, with variable reinnervation; have direct chronotropy and pacing ready.
- Use isoprenaline or a pacemaker for bradycardia.

> **Closing point:** Use reliable direct chronotropic support or pacing; ephedrine has mixed direct/indirect activity.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2019

items.title: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.q: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.a:
- Ephedrine: reduced effect (indirect).
- Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine: exaggerated.
- Phenylephrine and metaraminol: effective, no reflex bradycardia.
- Adenosine: exaggerated bradycardia.
- Neostigmine: bradycardia possible.

> **Closing point:** Titrate catecholamines carefully.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2019

items.title: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.q: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.a:
- No reflex tachycardia; preload dependent.
- Silent ischaemia: no angina.
- Arrhythmia and pacing requirements vary with surgical technique, timing and cohort; investigate new arrhythmia for rejection or vasculopathy.
- Re-innervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months).
- Ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or vasculopathy.

> **Closing point:** No reflex means volume matters most.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, Blue Book 2019

items.title: What is current first-line treatment for HFpEF?
items.q: What is current first-line treatment for HFpEF?
items.a:
- SGLT2 inhibitor and, per ESC 2026, an appropriate MRA with potassium/renal monitoring; benefit in HFpEF is mainly fewer HF events.
- Diuretics for congestion.
- Treat comorbidities: hypertension, diabetes.
- Manage atrial fibrillation aggressively.
- Use current withholding guidance rather than the older review’s shorter interval. Current AHA/ACC/FDA interval: ≥72 h for dapagliflozin/empagliflozin/canagliflozin, ≥96 h for ertugliflozin; distinguish this from shorter calendar-day protocols. Restart when stable, eating/drinking and without ketosis.

> **Closing point:** HFpEF is about 50% of heart failure.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, SS_IC 1.35, BJA Educ 2024

items.title: Give the echo criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
items.q: Give the echo criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
items.a:
- Peak velocity 4 m/s or more.
- Mean gradient 40 mmHg or more.
- Valve area below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6).
- Dimensionless index below 0.25.
- Low-flow low-gradient: use dobutamine stress or CT calcium score.

> **Closing point:** Gradients depend on flow.

Source: SS_CS 1.4

items.title: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic stenosis.
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic stenosis.
items.a:
- Rate 60 to 80; sinus rhythm.
- Preload adequate without congestion.
- SVR and MAP maintained; vasopressor first.
- Contractility preserved.
- Avoid single-shot spinal.

> **Closing point:** Hypotension, tachycardia and AF are the killers.

Source: SS_CS 1.4

items.title: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis.
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis.
items.a:
- AR: rate 80 to 100, euvolaemia without congestion, low-normal afterload.
- MS: rate 60 to 80, sinus rhythm, maintain SVR, avoid raised PVR.
- Avoid IABP in AR.
- MS: tachycardia shortens diastole and raises LA pressure.

> **Closing point:** AR likes it fast and vasodilated; MS likes it slow.

Source: SS_CS 1.4

items.title: State the goals in mitral regurgitation.
items.q: State the goals in mitral regurgitation.
items.a:
- Rate individualised, avoiding tachycardia and marked bradycardia (80 to 90).
- Preload maintained.
- Low-normal afterload.
- Support contractility; keep PVR low.
- EF overestimates LV function.

> **Closing point:** Preserve forward flow: euvolaemia, avoid bradycardia and excess afterload.

Source: SS_CS 1.4

items.title: Give INR targets for mechanical valves and bridging indications.
items.q: Give INR targets for mechanical valves and bridging indications.
items.a:
- Bileaflet aortic without risk factors: 2.5.
- Mitral, tricuspid, or aortic with risk factors: 3.0.
- Bridging is individualised: CHEST 2022 suggests against routine mechanical-valve bridging, whereas AHA/ACC allows selected very-high-risk cases. BRIDGE excluded mechanical valves.
- DOACs are contraindicated.

> **Closing point:** Valve position and type decide risk.

Source: SS_CS 1.4

items.title: Why is warfarin vs heparin a dilemma in pregnancy with a mechanical valve?
items.q: Why is warfarin vs heparin a dilemma in pregnancy with a mechanical valve?
items.a:
- Warfarin: best valve protection; embryopathy at weeks 6 to 12, fetal haemorrhage.
- LMWH/UFH: do not cross placenta; more valve thrombosis; anti-Xa monitoring.
- Switch to LMWH or UFH at about 36 weeks; stop LMWH 24 hours before neuraxial.

> **Closing point:** Maternal valve thrombosis versus fetal harm.

Source: SS_CS 1.4

items.title: Why is mitral stenosis dangerous in labour?
items.q: Why is mitral stenosis dangerous in labour?
items.a:
- Pregnancy raises cardiac output; labour adds pain and tachycardia.
- Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling and raises left atrial pressure.
- Result: pulmonary oedema or AF.
- Risk depends on stenosis severity, PH mechanism and RV function; historical PAH mortality is not a universal estimate for MS.

> **Closing point:** Keep the heart rate slow.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, Blue Book 2023

items.title: How should delivery be planned in rheumatic heart disease?
items.q: How should delivery be planned in rheumatic heart disease?
items.a:
- Vaginal delivery preferred if no obstetric indication.
- mWHO II: spontaneous labour if close to hospital.
- mWHO III or IV: planned delivery in an expert centre with appropriate monitoring, sometimes ICU depending on severity; not obligatory ICU induction for every mWHO III/IV patient.
- Planned caesarean can suit the highest-risk patients.

> **Closing point:** Plan timing, people and place before labour starts.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, Blue Book 2023

items.title: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.q: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.a:
- Pacing at 180 to 220 beats/min.
- Drops systolic pressure to below 50 mmHg for 5 to 10 seconds.
- Used during balloon valvuloplasty and valve deployment.
- Have vasopressors ready for recovery.

> **Closing point:** Pace down, then support up.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, BJA Educ 2021

items.title: List the complications of TAVI.
items.q: List the complications of TAVI.
items.a:
- Femoral artery injury (common).
- Conduction block needing a permanent pacemaker.
- Coronary artery occlusion.
- Stroke.
- Have an emergency bypass plan.

> **Closing point:** Vascular and conduction problems come first.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, BJA Educ 2021

items.title: Primary versus secondary mitral regurgitation?
items.q: Primary versus secondary mitral regurgitation?
items.a:
- Primary: structural leaflet or chordal abnormality.
- Secondary: LV size and geometry changes.
- Moderate or severe MR in about 10% at age 75.
- Transcatheter repair suits high surgical risk.

> **Closing point:** Secondary MR is a disease of the ventricle.

Source: SS_CS 1.4, BJA Educ 2023

items.title: Classify causes of pulmonary oedema by Starling mechanism.
items.q: Classify causes of pulmonary oedema by Starling mechanism.
items.a:
- Raised hydrostatic pressure: LV failure, fluid overload, valve disease.
- Increased permeability: ARDS, sepsis, TRALI, aspiration.
- Mixed: negative pressure, neurogenic, re-expansion.

> **Closing point:** Treat the dominant mechanism.

Source: IT_RT 1.2

items.title: Give the immediate management of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
items.q: Give the immediate management of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
items.a:
- Sit upright; oxygen to SpO2 94% or more.
- CPAP or NIV (3CPO: faster relief).
- GTN if SBP above 100; IV furosemide.
- Treat the cause; avoid routine opioids.

> **Closing point:** CPAP and nitrate treat the pressure.

Source: IT_RT 1.2

items.title: What do B-lines on lung ultrasound mean?
items.q: What do B-lines on lung ultrasound mean?
items.a:
- More than two B-lines per zone, in several zones: interstitial syndrome.
- Causes include pulmonary oedema, pneumonia and ARDS.
- A-lines with lung sliding are normal.
- Combine with echo and the clinical picture.

> **Closing point:** B-lines indicate interstitial syndrome; fibrosis and inflammation as well as fluid can produce them.

Source: IT_RT 1.2, Blue Book 2025

items.title: List the anaesthetic do and do not for HCM with outflow obstruction.
items.q: List the anaesthetic do and do not for HCM with outflow obstruction.
items.a:
- Do: euvolaemia without congestion, slow rate, sinus rhythm, alpha agonist.
- Do not: ephedrine, inotropes, vasodilators, hypovolaemia.
- Single-shot spinal is risky.
- Check the ICD.

> **Closing point:** Adequate filling, controlled rate and preserved perfusion; avoid overloading a stiff ventricle.

items.title: Compare dilated, restrictive and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
items.q: Compare dilated, restrictive and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
items.a:
- Dilated: low EF; treat as HFrEF.
- Restrictive: stiff ventricle, fixed stroke volume; avoid bradycardia and vasodilation.
- Hypertrophic: dynamic obstruction.

> **Closing point:** Is the heart dilated, obstructed or stiff?

items.title: Principles of managing acute RV failure.
items.q: Principles of managing acute RV failure.
items.a:
- Reduce PVR: oxygen, normocarbia, inhaled nitric oxide.
- Perfusion: noradrenaline or vasopressin.
- Preload: avoid overload.
- Contractility: dobutamine or milrinone.

> **Closing point:** The RV needs pressure and a low PVR.

items.title: Which drugs raise pulmonary vascular resistance?
items.q: Which drugs raise pulmonary vascular resistance?
items.a:
- Nitrous oxide and desflurane.
- Large-dose ketamine in adults.
- Hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, hypothermia and pain also raise PVR.
- Etomidate may preserve haemodynamics; agent choice depends on the patient, dose and local availability.

> **Closing point:** Avoid anything that raises RV afterload.

Source: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What ventilator settings protect the right ventricle?
items.q: What ventilator settings protect the right ventricle?
items.a:
- Avoid hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 60) and hypercapnia (the pulmonary vascular response to CO2 varies).
- Tidal volume around 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, adjusted to mechanics; plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O.
- PEEP titrated to recruitment and RV loading, without an absolute 10 cmH2O ceiling cmH2O.
- Ventilate near FRC.

> **Closing point:** Both low and high lung volumes raise PVR.

Source: Blue Book 2021

items.title: Which vasopressors and inotropes suit a failing right ventricle?
items.q: Which vasopressors and inotropes suit a failing right ventricle?
items.a:
- Noradrenaline titrated to systemic perfusion; no universal 0.2/0.5 dose boundary defines pulmonary safety
- Low-dose vasopressin may support systemic pressure with relatively less pulmonary effect; response is dose- and patient-dependent.
- Dobutamine 2 to 5 microgram/kg/min.
- Milrinone 0.25 to 0.5 microgram/kg/min, with a vasopressor.
- Amiodarone, not beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, for arrhythmia.

> **Closing point:** Support perfusion pressure and contractility together.

Source: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the WHO groups of pulmonary hypertension and why do they matter?
items.q: What are the WHO groups of pulmonary hypertension and why do they matter?
items.a:
- 1 PAH; 2 left heart disease; 3 lung disease or hypoxia; 4 CTEPH; 5 multifactorial.
- Cause changes treatment: sildenafil for PAH, valvuloplasty for mitral stenosis, CPAP for OSA.
- Perioperative risk varies with PH group, RV function, functional class, urgency and procedure; no universal percentage.

> **Closing point:** Find the cause, then optimise.

Source: Blue Book 2015

items.title: How is peripartum cardiomyopathy defined and delivered?
items.q: How is peripartum cardiomyopathy defined and delivered?
items.a:
- Heart failure from LV systolic dysfunction (EF below 45%) in late pregnancy or the months after.
- Diagnosis of exclusion; check BNP if orthopnoea or PND.
- Vaginal delivery with neuraxial analgesia where possible.
- Recurrence risk in later pregnancies.

> **Closing point:** Think of it in any breathless postpartum woman.

Source: BJA Educ 2023

items.title: Which TOE view is useful for mid-LV ischaemia monitoring, and what can it miss?
items.q: Which TOE view is useful for mid-LV ischaemia monitoring, and what can it miss?
items.a:
- Transgastric mid short-axis.
- Shows all six mid-ventricular segments.
- New RWMA can precede ECG change but is not invariably earlier or specific.

> **Closing point:** One useful view, with basal/apical blind spots: use an integrated examination.

items.title: When should you suspect infective endocarditis, and how do you investigate it?
items.q: When should you suspect infective endocarditis, and how do you investigate it?
items.a:
- Suspect it with persistent bacteraemia, particularly S. aureus, plus fever, embolic findings, new regurgitation, prosthetic material or unexplained HF.
- Obtain multiple blood-culture sets before antibiotics when feasible; do not delay treatment in an unstable septic patient.
- TTE first, with TOE for suspected left-sided/prosthetic disease, inadequate images or complications. Repeat/add imaging if suspicion remains despite a negative study.
- Integrate microbiology, imaging and current diagnostic criteria; a murmur or incidental mass alone is insufficient.

> **Closing point:** Bacteraemia plus new valve dysfunction needs urgent cardiac and infection-team assessment.

items.title: Which complications of endocarditis require urgent escalation or surgery?
items.q: Which complications of endocarditis require urgent escalation or surgery?
items.a:
- Three major surgical indications: **heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection, and prevention of embolism in selected patients**.
- Acute severe regurgitation with pulmonary oedema/shock can require emergency surgery; do not wait for completion of antibiotics.
- New PR prolongation/AV block suggests perivalvular extension or abscess; involve cardiac surgery and prepare for pacing.
- Look for stroke, infected aneurysm, renal injury and other emboli. Neurological findings influence surgical/anticoagulation timing.
- Anaesthesia follows the valve lesion, ventricular function and septic physiology; plan TOE and postoperative ICU.

> **Closing point:** New conduction delay can be a sign of infection extending beyond the valve.

items.title: What distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from a very high BP reading?
items.q: What distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from a very high BP reading?
items.a:
- **Acute hypertension-mediated organ damage**, not the number alone, defines an emergency.
- Assess chest pain/ischaemia, acute pulmonary oedema, neurological deficit/encephalopathy, retinal changes and acute kidney injury.
- Confirm measurement and review baseline/rate of rise. Check pain, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, urinary retention, drugs and withdrawal.
- Severe hypertension without acute injury generally needs controlled reassessment and oral optimisation, rather than reflex IV normalisation.

> **Closing point:** Treat the patient and organ injury, rather than a threshold in isolation.

items.title: How do you manage hypertensive pulmonary oedema in PACU?
items.q: How do you manage hypertensive pulmonary oedema in PACU?
items.a:
- Call for help; upright position, ECG/SpO2/BP monitoring, IV access and oxygen for hypoxaemia. Obtain ECG, troponin and bedside cardiac/lung assessment.
- Early CPAP/NIV if suitable; intubate for failure or inability to protect the airway.
- Titrate IV GTN when appropriate to reduce preload/afterload; give diuretic for congestion/volume excess. Fluid redistribution may dominate, so diuresis alone is insufficient.
- Treat ACS and reversible triggers; avoid reflex beta-blockade in acute decompensated failure/shock.
- Use condition-specific BP targets and avoid overshoot. The usual initial 20–25% reduction framework is not a rule for every emergency.

> **Closing point:** Support breathing and reduce cardiac loading while preserving perfusion.

items.title: What controls coronary flow beyond aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP?
items.q: What controls coronary flow beyond aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP?
items.a:
- That pressure difference is a useful LV subendocardial approximation; downstream intramyocardial/zero-flow pressure and vascular resistance also matter.
- LV systolic compression favours diastolic perfusion, particularly in the subendocardium; RV flow is less exclusively diastolic.
- Metabolic, myogenic, endothelial/humoral and neural mechanisms regulate resistance vessels.
- Coronary reserve determines the ability to increase flow under stress. Resting flow can be adequate despite poor reserve.
- Oxygen delivery also depends on haemoglobin and saturation; pressure alone does not establish adequate myocardial oxygenation.

> **Closing point:** Coronary driving pressure, reserve and oxygen content must be considered together.

items.title: Why can severe AS cause angina without obstructive coronary disease?
items.q: Why can severe AS cause angina without obstructive coronary disease?
items.a:
- Hypertrophy and high systolic work increase myocardial oxygen demand.
- Impaired relaxation/high LVEDP and intramyocardial compression impair subendocardial perfusion.
- Microvascular dysfunction and reduced coronary reserve limit compensation.
- Tachycardia increases demand while shortening diastole; hypotension, anaemia and hypoxaemia worsen supply.
- Preserve perfusion pressure and oxygen content, avoid tachycardia and fluid extremes, and assess for coexisting CAD rather than assuming it must be present.

> **Closing point:** A supply–demand problem can exist despite unobstructed epicardial arteries.

items.title: Does every mechanical valve need bridging when warfarin is stopped?
items.q: Does every mechanical valve need bridging when warfarin is stopped?
items.a:
- No universal rule: assess valve position/design, previous embolism, AF, LV dysfunction and procedural bleeding risk.
- CHEST 2022 conditionally suggests against bridging for elective mechanical-valve interruption, with very-low-certainty evidence and high-risk implementation considerations.
- AHA/ACC 2024 and ESC/EACTS 2025 support selected high-risk bridging; a mechanical mitral valve warrants specialist individualisation.
- Some minor procedures allow continued warfarin. If interruption is needed, document timing, INR checks, any bridge and postoperative restart.
- BRIDGE excluded mechanical valves. DOACs are unsuitable substitutes.

> **Closing point:** Make an explicit valve-thrombosis versus bleeding decision with the anticoagulation/cardiology team.

items.title: What must the postoperative plan specify for a mechanical valve patient?
items.q: What must the postoperative plan specify for a mechanical valve patient?
items.a:
- When warfarin can restart once haemostasis and enteral administration permit; INR monitoring and who adjusts the dose.
- Whether a therapeutic bridge is indicated and when bleeding risk permits it. After high-bleeding-risk surgery, therapeutic LMWH commonly waits 48–72 h.
- Prophylactic VTE dosing is not equivalent to therapeutic valve protection.
- Coordinate therapeutic anticoagulation with neuraxial insertion/removal intervals; an epidural can delay safe full-dose therapy.
- Monitor bleeding, new dyspnoea, embolic events and prosthetic dysfunction, and provide a written discharge plan.

> **Closing point:** Restart is a planned sequence, not a single instruction to “resume anticoagulation”.

items.title: Why does primary versus secondary MR matter before non-cardiac surgery?
items.q: Why does primary versus secondary MR matter before non-cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Primary MR is leaflet/chordal disease; secondary MR reflects ventricular tethering or atrial/annular dilation.
- Assess symptoms, mechanism/severity, LV size/function, RV function, pulmonary pressure and AF; MR is load dependent.
- EF includes regurgitant flow: in chronic severe primary MR, an EF around 60% can already indicate dysfunction.
- Optimise the underlying disease, especially HF in secondary MR. Discuss independent valve-intervention indications before elevated-risk elective surgery.
- Severe MR alone does not require cancellation of every operation; urgency, symptoms and ventricular response decide the plan.

> **Closing point:** Mechanism and ventricular consequences matter as much as the MR label.

items.title: State the perioperative goals in severe MR without oversimplifying them.
items.q: State the perioperative goals in severe MR without oversimplifying them.
items.a:
- **Preop:** assess stability, optimise congestion/rhythm, review echo and decide whether valve treatment should precede elective surgery.
- **Intraop:** preserve forward flow, euvolaemia and contractility; avoid marked bradycardia, excessive tachycardia, hypertension and hypotension. Protect the RV and avoid raised PVR.
- Titrate technique and fluids. Treat hypotension by cause; use a necessary vasopressor for vasodilation rather than withholding it solely because SVR may rise.
- **Postop:** monitor for congestion, AF, low output and ischaemia; control pain/ventilation and restart medicines when safe.

> **Closing point:** “Fast and vasodilated” is too crude for an ischaemic or failing ventricle.

items.title: Identify four core TTE windows, their landmarks and main clinical uses.
items.q: Identify four core TTE windows, their landmarks and main clinical uses.
items.a:
- **PLAX:** RV near field; interventricular septum, LV and posterior wall, MV, LVOT/AV, aortic root and LA; descending aorta lies posterior to LA. Look for LV size/function, pericardial fluid, AV/MV lesions and aortic root disease.
- **PSAX:** rotate to aortic valve (three cusps), mitral valve (orifice) and mid-papillary level (round LV and regional wall motion). A D-shaped LV suggests RV pressure or volume loading; timing helps distinguish.
- **Apical 4-chamber:** both atria, ventricles, MV/TV; tricuspid insertion is more apical than mitral. Assess RV size/function and chamber proportions. Apical 5-chamber brings LVOT/AV into view for Doppler.
- **Subcostal 4-chamber:** useful in a supine unstable patient for effusion/tamponade, RV and gross biventricular function; IVC view assists RA-pressure interpretation but does **not** prove fluid responsiveness.

> **Closing point:** Name the structure, the physiological question and the view's blind spots; a foreshortened view may mislead.

items.title: Name the essential TOE views and the structures they show.
items.q: Name the essential TOE views and the structures they show.
items.a:
- **ME 4-chamber (0–20°):** both atria/ventricles, MV, TV, septum and gross function.
- **ME 2-chamber (80–100°):** anterior and inferior LV walls, MV, LA/LAA region.
- **ME long-axis (120–160°):** LVOT, AV, MV, LA and proximal ascending aorta.
- **ME AV short-axis (30–60°):** three aortic cusps and valve morphology; **ME bicaval (90–110°)** shows SVC, IVC, RA and interatrial septum.
- **ME RV inflow–outflow (50–70°):** TV, RVOT, pulmonary valve/PA.
- **TG mid-papillary short-axis (~0°):** mid-LV circumferential function (not every segment); **deep TG long-axis (~0–20°)** aligns Doppler across LVOT/AV; descending-aorta SAX/LAX (~0°/90°) for atheroma, dissection and IABP location.
- Angles are **approximate**; manipulate depth, flexion and rotation to acquire an actual diagnostic plane. TOE has a distal ascending-aorta blind spot from intervening airway tissue/air.

> **Closing point:** Explain what decision a view answers; memorising angles is not enough.

items.title: What five questions should focused cardiac ultrasound answer in unexpected cardiovascular collapse?
items.q: What five questions should focused cardiac ultrasound answer in unexpected cardiovascular collapse?
items.a:
- **1.** **Tamponade?** Effusion, chamber collapse and clinical evidence of obstructive physiology.
- **2.** **Severe LV failure or a small hyperdynamic LV?** Assess size, global function and regional wall motion.
- **3.** **RV dilation/pressure overload?** Compare RV:LV size, septal flattening and function; consider PE/PVR/ventilation causes.
- **4.** **Underfilling, dynamic LVOT obstruction or congestion?** Look for small cavity, SAM, filling and venous/lung findings in context.
- **5.** **Major valve lesion or new regional wall-motion abnormality?** Identify urgently management-changing AS, acute MR, AR or ischaemia.

> **Closing point:** Focused echo guides the immediate differential; it does not exclude subtle disease or replace comprehensive assessment.

items.title: Trace the great vessels relevant to TOE, central lines and IABP.
items.q: Trace the great vessels relevant to TOE, central lines and IABP.
items.a:
- LVOT → ascending aorta → arch, whose branches are **brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian** → descending thoracic aorta.
- IABP balloon lies in descending thoracic aorta with the tip just **distal to left subclavian origin**; too proximal may compromise arch vessels, too distal visceral/renal flow.
- PA catheter course: **RA → RV → pulmonary artery → wedged distal PA branch**; SVC/IVC enter RA, four pulmonary veins normally enter LA.
- Descending aorta is well seen on TOE; distal ascending aorta/part of arch is obscured by tracheal air and is a known TOE blind spot.

> **Closing point:** The anatomy matters because a structurally correct image can still omit an important aortic segment.

items.title: How do you distinguish ejection fraction, filling pressure and fluid responsiveness using echo?
items.q: How do you distinguish ejection fraction, filling pressure and fluid responsiveness using echo?
items.a:
- **EF** describes the fraction ejected, not stroke volume or perfusion; a small LV with a normal/high EF may have low output.
- **Filling pressure** is inferred by integrating Doppler (e.g., E/e′), atrial size, pulmonary venous/other measures and the clinical context; a single E/e′ or CVP is insufficient.
- **Fluid responsiveness** means an increase in stroke volume/cardiac output after increasing preload; when feasible, perform a **passive leg raise** and measure **LVOT VTI** before/after (a rise about ≥10% suggests a positive test, subject to measurement and context).
- PPV/SVV require strict conditions (controlled ventilation, no important arrhythmia, adequate tidal volume and suitable thoracic mechanics). IVC size/collapsibility, CVP and EF alone cannot prove fluid responsiveness; responsiveness does not mean fluid is **needed or safe**.

> **Closing point:** Ask both “will output rise?” and “will a fluid bolus harm this heart or lung?”

items.title: Recognise important acute coronary occlusion patterns without conventional ST elevation.
items.q: Recognise important acute coronary occlusion patterns without conventional ST elevation.
items.a:
- **Posterior occlusion:** ST depression V1–V3, often tall R/upright T; record V7–V9 for posterior ST elevation.
- **Right ventricular MI:** inferior infarction (often III > II) with RV ST elevation in V4R; assess preload/RV function and avoid indiscriminate nitrates if hypotensive.
- **de Winter:** upsloping J-point ST depression with large symmetrical precordial T waves, often aVR elevation; consider proximal LAD occlusion.
- **Modified Sgarbossa in LBBB or paced rhythm:** concordant STE ≥1 mm; concordant STD ≥1 mm in V1–V3; or excessively discordant STE relative to S-wave depth (ST/S magnitude ≥0.25). Not all LBBB is occlusion.
- **Wellens:** characteristic biphasic or deeply inverted anterior T waves after pain settles indicate high-risk LAD disease; **avoid stress testing**, arrange urgent cardiology assessment. Diffuse depression plus aVR elevation is high-risk but not uniquely left-main occlusion.

> **Closing point:** The Australian 2025 ACS guideline recognises ACOMI patterns beyond classic STEMI; urgent cardiology/reperfusion assessment may be needed.

items.title: What are the perioperative implications of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy?
items.q: What are the perioperative implications of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy?
items.a:
- Fibrotic/fibrofatty myocardial disease, often involving RV and/or LV, predisposes to **ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden death**, sometimes before severe systolic impairment.
- Ask about exertional syncope, family sudden death, prior VT, ICD, symptoms and exercise; review ECG, rhythm monitoring, echo/CMR and treatment.
- Continue indicated beta-blocker/antiarrhythmic therapy, avoid hypoxaemia, electrolyte disturbance and major catecholamine surges; have defibrillation and ICD management arrangements.
- Device/ICD indication is risk-based—not every patient requires one. Assess ventricular function and haemodynamic reserve separately from arrhythmia risk.

> **Closing point:** Normal-looking EF does not exclude major ventricular arrhythmia risk.

items.title: Why do anthracyclines, trastuzumab and myocarditis matter to the anaesthetist?
items.q: Why do anthracyclines, trastuzumab and myocarditis matter to the anaesthetist?
items.a:
- **Anthracyclines:** dose-related, sometimes delayed LV dysfunction and arrhythmia; toxicity can occur below older “safe” cumulative thresholds.
- **Trastuzumab and other cancer therapies:** may impair LV function; evaluate current EF/strain and concurrent cancer-treatment issues, not merely the last chemotherapy date.
- **Myocarditis:** may cause new ventricular impairment, conduction disease, malignant arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock; active suspected disease warrants specialist investigation/management before elective surgery.
- Preop: symptoms, ECG, echo ± biomarkers and cardio-oncology/cardiology advice where indicated. Intraop: plan around **current physiology** (LV/RV output, rhythm, filling, vasopressor need), not the diagnostic label alone.

> **Closing point:** Past cancer treatment may be relevant years later, and myocarditis may produce electrical instability out of proportion to EF.

items.title: How do you assess and escalate IV loop diuresis in acute heart failure?
items.sub: Acute pulmonary oedema and heart failure
items.eyebrow: Acute pulmonary oedema and heart failure
items.q: How do you assess and escalate IV loop diuresis in acute heart failure?
items.a:
- First decide whether the patient is **congested and perfused**, hypertensive flash oedema, or **cold/wet shock**; restore perfusion in shock and avoid automatic large diuretic or vasodilator doses before reassessing.
- If diuretic-naïve, a typical initial **furosemide 20–40 mg IV**; if already on a loop diuretic, choose an appropriately larger IV dose accounting for the home dose, renal function and severity (commonly about 1–2.5× the oral daily furosemide-equivalent strategy in guidelines/trials).
- Reassess early: urine output, fluid balance, congestion, creatinine, K/Mg, and spot urine sodium at about **2 hours** (often target >50–70 mmol/L; context/local protocol matters). A low early natriuretic response prompts dose escalation.
- If resistant, increase loop dose and consider sequential nephron blockade (thiazide-type agent or **acetazolamide** in appropriate patients). **DOSE** did not establish bolus versus infusion as universally superior; **ADVOR** improved early decongestion, not proven overall mortality.

> **Closing point:** Treat the phenotype and early diuretic response—not an arbitrary fixed furosemide dose.

items.title: What did four landmark studies change in cardiogenic shock and perioperative cardiac care?
items.q: What did four landmark studies change in cardiogenic shock and perioperative cardiac care?
items.a:
- **CULPRIT-SHOCK:** in MI shock with multivessel disease, culprit-only PCI initially (with possible staged PCI) improved a 30-day composite versus routine immediate multivessel PCI.
- **DOREMI:** milrinone versus dobutamine showed **no clear superiority** in the small cardiogenic-shock trial; choose inotrope by physiology, renal function, arrhythmia risk and beta-blockade.
- **IABP-SHOCK II / ECLS-SHOCK:** routine IABP and routine early VA-ECMO, respectively, did **not** confer a demonstrated mortality advantage for unselected MI-related shock; devices still have selected roles.
- **STOP-or-NOT:** continuing versus holding RAAS inhibitors before major non-cardiac surgery yielded similar major postoperative composite outcomes, but continuation caused more intraoperative hypotension; individualise to HF versus hypertension and local policy.

> **Closing point:** State the trial population, comparison and outcome before applying a result to an individual patient.

items.title: Why does peripheral vascular disease alter your cardiac perioperative assessment?
items.q: Why does peripheral vascular disease alter your cardiac perioperative assessment?
items.a:
- PVD suggests **systemic atherosclerosis** and possible coexistent coronary, cerebral and renal disease; don't assess it as limb disease alone.
- Establish angina/ACS symptoms, prior PCI/CABG, functional reserve, strokes/TIAs, renal disease, medications and surgical vascular risk.
- Consider antiplatelet and anticoagulant indications, bleeding risk, BP targets, vascular access limitations, renal protection and postoperative myocardial injury surveillance according to overall risk.
- Test only if results will change management; **stable CAD does not justify prophylactic PCI solely to clear non-cardiac surgery** (CARP).

> **Closing point:** The perioperative risk comes from systemic disease and the proposed operation, not simply the leg symptoms.

items.title: 1. Stepwise cardiac risk assessment before major surgery
items.q: A 68-year-old with known IHD and hypertension is booked for open colectomy. He gets breathless on one flight of stairs. Outline your preoperative cardiac assessment and what would change your management.
items.a:
## 1. Why assess

The purposes are to estimate the risk of major adverse cardiac events (MACE: cardiac death, non-fatal MI, cardiac arrest), to identify patients whose management or timing should change, to optimise treatment, and to inform consent and the choice of anaesthetic technique and postoperative location.

## 2. A stepwise approach (ESC, CCS and ACC/AHA guidelines)

**Step 1: Urgency and active cardiac conditions.**
- Emergency surgery proceeds with risk mitigation; no testing that delays it.
- Active conditions that require treatment first: unstable coronary syndromes, decompensated heart failure, significant arrhythmias, severe symptomatic valve disease.

**Step 2: Surgical risk.**
- Low (below 1% MACE): superficial, cataract, endoscopic.
- Intermediate (1 to 5%): intraperitoneal, orthopaedic, head and neck, carotid.
- High (above 5%): open aortic and major vascular, major thoracic and some emergency surgery.
- Open colectomy is intermediate to high risk.

**Step 3: Patient risk.**
- RCRI: high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine above 177 micromol/L. This patient scores at least 2 (IHD and high-risk surgery), a MACE risk of about 10%.
- Other tools: NSQIP-MICA, ACS NSQIP risk calculator, and frailty assessment.

**Step 4: Functional capacity.**
- Breathlessness on one flight of stairs implies below 4 METs, which is poor. Poor capacity raises risk and limits the usefulness of exercise testing.
- The DASI questionnaire (score below 34 predicts events) and CPET are more reliable than subjective estimates (METS study showed DASI predicted events, and that clinicians' own estimates were not reliable).

**Step 5: Biomarkers and investigations.**
- Resting 12-lead ECG for all intermediate and high-risk patients: baseline, rhythm, ischaemia, LVH, conduction.
- BNP or NT-proBNP before surgery in patients aged 65 or over, or with cardiovascular disease (CCS guidelines): elevated values predict MACE and mortality (BNP of 92 ng/L or more and NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or more indicate higher risk).
- Echocardiography when the cause of breathlessness is unclear, for new symptoms, murmurs, or suspected HF or valve disease, or in patients with unknown LV function and high-risk surgery.
- Non-invasive stress testing (dobutamine stress echo or myocardial perfusion imaging) only when poor function and high risk coincide and the result would alter management.

**Step 6: Revascularisation.**
- CARP (revascularisation before vascular surgery in stable CAD) and DECREASE-V showed no benefit. Revascularisation is indicated only on its own merits (left main disease, ACS, severe multivessel disease with symptoms). It adds delay and DAPT problems.

## 3. What changes management

| Finding | Response |
|---|---|
| Active ACS, HF or arrhythmia | Defer elective surgery, treat first |
| High risk and poor capacity | Multidisciplinary discussion; consider whether surgery is required, whether a less invasive alternative exists |
| Raised BNP | Higher risk category; closer monitoring |
| Ischaemia on stress testing at low threshold | Cardiology input |
| Severe valve disease | Treat or modify technique (see R15) |

## 4. Optimisation and plan

- Continue beta-blocker, statin, and antihypertensives (hold ACEi/ARB on the day). Start a statin if not on one. Check anaemia, electrolytes and renal function.
- Anaesthetic plan: invasive arterial pressure, avoidance of tachycardia and hypotension, normothermia, avoidance of anaemia, a restrictive-to-goal-directed fluid plan.
- Postoperative: HDU, troponin on days 1 and 2 (VISION showed that troponin elevation within 3 days predicts 30 day mortality).
- Consent: discuss the risks of MI, stroke and death in numerical terms.

> **Examiner lens:** testing is justified only when it changes management; do not recommend routine revascularisation.

items.title: 2. Antiplatelet plan for a stented patient needing urgent surgery
items.q: A 72-year-old man has a drug-eluting stent placed 4 months ago for NSTEMI and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He needs a semi-urgent bowel resection. How do you decide what to do with his antiplatelet therapy, and how do you plan the perioperative period?
items.a:
## 1. Framing the problem

- The competing risks are stent thrombosis (catastrophic, with mortality of 20 to 40% when it occurs perioperatively) and surgical bleeding. The surgery is semi-urgent, so the key questions are how long it can safely wait, and what bleeding risk the operation carries.
- Stent thrombosis is driven by: premature cessation of antiplatelet therapy (the strongest predictor), stent placed for ACS, the perioperative prothrombotic and inflammatory state, stent factors (left main, bifurcation, long or overlapping stents, small calibre, under-expansion), and patient factors (diabetes, low EF, renal impairment).
- A DES placed for NSTEMI 4 months ago is still within the high-risk window. Guidelines advise deferring elective surgery for 12 months after ACS (6 months after stable disease with a DES; some newer-generation DES allow 3 months). Surgery between 1 and 6 months after ACS carries a clearly raised MACE rate, which falls progressively with time.

## 2. Decision-making

| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Can surgery wait until 6 months, ideally 12? | Each additional month lowers stent thrombosis risk |
| What is the surgical bleeding risk, and can the operation be done on aspirin alone? | Most abdominal surgery can be done on aspirin; a closed-space operation (neurosurgery, posterior chamber eye) may not |
| Stent characteristics and ACS history | Defines thrombotic risk, via the cardiologist |
| Are there alternatives (non-operative, laparoscopic, staged)? | May reduce risk or delay |

The decision should be made jointly with the surgeon, cardiologist and patient, and documented, including the consent discussion of the risk of MI, stent thrombosis and death.

## 3. Antiplatelet management if surgery cannot wait

- Continue aspirin throughout, unless bleeding risk is prohibitive (in which case discuss with the cardiologist). Aspirin continuation gives most of the protection against stent thrombosis, and POISE-2 showed no benefit to starting it in unselected patients but it does not apply to stented patients.
- Stop the P2Y12 inhibitor at the recommended interval: clopidogrel 5 to 7 days, prasugrel 7 days, ticagrelor 3 to 5 days. Restoring platelet function is the aim.
- Bridging: for very high thrombotic risk (recent stent within 3 months of ACS, left main or multiple overlapping stents, previous stent thrombosis) consider cangrelor, an IV reversible P2Y12 inhibitor with a half-life of 3 to 6 minutes, started 1 to 3 days after stopping the oral agent and stopped about 1 to 6 hours before surgery (BRIDGE trial). Heparin and GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors are alternatives in some centres but have drawbacks. Tirofiban or eptifibatide have been used in some centres.
- Restart the P2Y12 inhibitor as soon as bleeding allows (often within 24 to 48 hours), with a loading dose if the cardiologist advises, to reduce the vulnerable period.

## 4. Perioperative care

- Where: a centre with 24 hour interventional cardiology access (PCI for stent thrombosis is the treatment of choice, with a time-critical goal).
- Monitoring: invasive arterial pressure, five-lead ECG with ST analysis, consider TOE if instability; avoid tachycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, anaemia and pain.
- Anaesthetic technique: both general and regional are acceptable. Neuraxial blockade is only safe after washout (ASRA/ANZCA/ESAIC: clopidogrel 5 to 7 days, ticagrelor 5 to 7 days, prasugrel 7 to 10 days), and aspirin alone is not a contraindication. For this patient general anaesthesia is likely.
- Postoperative: HDU, troponin on days 1 and 2 (and day 3), ECG, early mobilisation, VTE prophylaxis (mechanical first if bleeding risk is high).

## 5. If bleeding or stent thrombosis occurs

- Bleeding on antiplatelet agents: surgical haemostasis, tranexamic acid, desmopressin in some settings; platelet transfusion is only effective after the drug has cleared (active metabolites of clopidogrel and ticagrelor bind transfused platelets), so timing matters.
- Stent thrombosis presents as STEMI. Call the cardiologist for urgent PCI, give aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor, and discuss anticoagulation with the surgeon.

> **Examiner lens:** show that you weigh stent thrombosis against surgical bleeding, keep aspirin, and make it a team decision.

items.title: 3. Perioperative cardioprotective drugs: what works and what harms
items.q: Summarise the evidence for starting or continuing beta-blockers, aspirin, clonidine, statins and ACE inhibitors around non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## 1. Rationale

Perioperative MI is mostly supply-demand mismatch (type 2) triggered by tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia and the stress response, with a minority from plaque rupture (type 1). Drugs have been trialled to blunt these mechanisms. The results show that the details (timing, dose, hypotension) are decisive.

## 2. Evidence by drug

| Drug | Trial and result | Mechanism of the finding | Practical conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Beta-blocker | POISE (8351 patients): metoprolol succinate 100 mg started 2 to 4 hours before surgery and continued for 30 days reduced MI (HR about 0.73) but increased death (HR 1.33) and stroke (HR 2.17), with more hypotension and bradycardia. DECREASE-IV (bisoprolol) was positive but the investigator's work (Poldermans) was discredited, and meta-analyses excluding it show harm | Fixed high dose, no titration, started on the day | Continue in patients already taking them. Do not start high-dose on the day of surgery. If starting, begin at least a week before with titration to heart rate and BP. The 2014 ACC/AHA guideline gave a class III recommendation against day-of-surgery initiation |
| Aspirin | POISE-2 (10010 patients): no reduction in death or MI (HR 0.99), 23% more major bleeding. The prior-stent subgroup was small | Bleeding offsets any ischaemic benefit | Continue for stents and established secondary prevention; do not start for primary prevention |
| Clonidine | POISE-2: no reduction in death or MI, more hypotension and non-fatal cardiac arrest | Hypotension, rebound | Do not start. Continue if already taking (rebound hypertension on withdrawal) |
| Statins | DECREASE-III and observational data suggest benefit; withdrawal is associated with increased MI. LOAD trial: no benefit of high-dose loading | Plaque stabilisation, pleiotropic effects | Continue; reasonable to start before vascular surgery, ideally 2 or more weeks before |
| ACEi / ARB | Observational data link continuation with intraoperative hypotension and AKI. STOP-or-NOT (2024) found no significant difference in composite outcome between continuing and stopping before major non-cardiac surgery; POISE-3 supported a hypotension-avoidance strategy | Vasoplegia under anaesthesia | Reasonable either way. Many hold 24 hours before major surgery if used for hypertension; continue in HFrEF if haemodynamics permit |
| Tranexamic acid (POISE-3) | Reduced bleeding with no increase in composite cardiac events | Antifibrinolysis | Reasonable in patients at risk of bleeding |
| Calcium channel blockers | Small studies show reduced ischaemia with diltiazem or verapamil | Rate control, vasodilation | Continue if on them |

## 3. Common themes

- Hypotension is the common mechanism of harm: a MAP below 60 to 65 mmHg for more than a few minutes raises myocardial injury and AKI (VISION, Sessler, Walsh).
- Withdrawal syndromes (beta-blocker, clonidine, statin) are harmful, so continuation is the rule.
- Starting a new drug on the day of surgery has been shown to be ineffective or harmful.

## 4. Summary rule

Continue established cardiac drugs, avoid starting new cardioprotective agents on the day of surgery, avoid hypotension and tachycardia, and tailor ACEi/ARB handling to the indication and the procedure.

> **Examiner lens:** name the trial, the direction of effect and the mechanism of harm (hypotension).

items.title: 4. MINS, perioperative MI and the troponin rise
items.q: Define perioperative myocardial injury (MINS) and perioperative myocardial infarction. How are they detected, and how do you manage a patient with an asymptomatic troponin rise on postoperative day 1?
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

> **BJA Education:** "Perioperative myocardial injury" (BJA Educ 2024).

## Definitions

Myocardial injury means troponin above the assay’s sex-specific 99th percentile. A rise/fall defines acute injury; persistently elevated values can reflect chronic injury. MINS is the ischaemic postoperative subset, distinct from all perioperative injury.

- **MINS (VISION 2017):** myocardial injury judged ischaemic, detected in the first 3 days in VISION; the clinical MINS definition extends to 30 days, with Roche hsTnT 20–<65 ng/L with absolute change ≥5 ng/L, or ≥65 ng/L, attributed to ischaemia and **no evidence of a non-ischaemic cause** (e.g. myocarditis; AF, PE and sepsis may produce either non-ischaemic injury or secondary MI depending on objective evidence). Ischaemic symptoms or signs are not needed.
- **AHA 2021:** troponin above the 99th percentile with an acute change in the first 30 days (typically within 72 hours), presumed ischaemic, with no overt non-ischaemic cause. Symptoms are not required because sedation and analgesia mask them.
- **Fifth Universal Definition (2026; older studies use the Fourth UDMI):** perioperative myocardial **injury** can have any cause, including extracardiac. **Infarction** additionally requires evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, ECG change, new wall motion abnormality, or thrombus).

## Why it matters

Incidence is about **20% in high-risk patients** having non-cardiac surgery, most without symptoms, and it carries higher morbidity and mortality. The mechanisms are mixed and interact: supply-demand imbalance (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia), plaque rupture, and non-ischaemic causes (sepsis, AF, PE, renal failure).

## Detection

Postoperative troponin surveillance in high-risk patients, usually on days 1 to 3, because most injury is silent. Use the same assay each time and compare with the baseline.

## Managing an asymptomatic rise

- **1.** Examine the patient, take an ECG and review for a non-ischaemic cause.
- **2.** Correct triggers: hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia, pain, hypervolaemia.
- **3.** Echo if the ECG changes or haemodynamics are unstable.
- **4.** Repeat troponin to see the trend.
- **5.** Involve cardiology; consider aspirin and a statin if bleeding risk allows.
- **6.** Review the plan for further surgery and follow-up.

There is no single proven universal treatment for all perioperative injury. Establish the mechanism and treat acute coronary occlusion urgently. MANAGE supports considering dabigatran 110 mg twice daily in selected ischaemic MINS after haemostasis and renal/bleeding review (major vascular events 11% vs 15%; HR 0.72), with high treatment discontinuation and limited generalisability. Aspirin is not automatic for non-ischaemic injury.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.


## Self-marking checklist

- Defines MINS and perioperative MI and distinguishes injury from infarction
- Gives the complete assay-specific VISION threshold and 30-day ischaemic MINS definition; symptoms are not required
- Quotes incidence about 20% and association with poor outcomes
- Explains mechanisms (supply-demand, plaque rupture, non-ischaemic)
- Describes troponin surveillance on days 1 to 3
- Gives a stepwise plan for an asymptomatic rise
- Distinguishes lack of a universal injury treatment from selected ischaemic-MINS evidence (MANAGE) and mechanism-specific ACS treatment

items.title: 5. New ST depression under general anaesthesia
items.q: Thirty minutes into an emergency laparotomy in a patient with known IHD, you see new 2 mm ST depression in V5. Describe your immediate management and how you confirm and treat the cause.
items.a:
## 1. Recognition and verification (first 30 to 60 seconds)

- Announce the finding, ask the surgeon to pause or simplify if the patient is unstable, and call for help early.
- Confirm the change is real: check lead connections and placement, switch the monitor to diagnostic mode (ST analysis in monitor filter mode can distort ST segments), check all leads (II, V5, V4, aVF, V1), look for artefact (diathermy, shivering, movement), and review the rhythm.
- ST depression of 1 mm or more, 60 to 80 ms after the J point, in two leads is the usual criterion. ST elevation of 1 mm or more suggests transmural ischaemia or vasospasm and needs a different approach.
- Sensitivity of leads: V5 alone detects about 75% of ischaemic episodes, II plus V5 about 80%, V4 plus V5 about 90%, and II plus V4 plus V5 about 96% (London). Limitations: LBBB, paced rhythm, digoxin, LVH, hypokalaemia, hypothermia, and posterior or circumflex ischaemia.

## 2. Immediate bedside assessment of supply and demand

| Supply | Demand |
|---|---|
| Hypotension: MAP below 65 or a drop of 20 to 30% from baseline; low diastolic pressure | Tachycardia, hypertension |
| Hypoxia, anaemia (check Hb), hypercarbia | Light anaesthesia, pain, shivering |
| Tachycardia (short diastolic time) | Sympathetic stimulation (laryngoscopy, incision, peritoneal traction) |
| Coronary spasm, embolus, thrombosis | Hypervolaemia, ventricular distension |
| Hypovolaemia, bleeding, vasodilation | Inotropes, exogenous catecholamines |

Check the circuit and ventilation (ETCO2, SpO2, FiO2), temperature, glucose, electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), surgical events (bleeding, retractor pressure on the diaphragm or IVC, pneumoperitoneum, aortic clamping), and recent drugs (vasopressors, ephedrine, adrenaline).

## 3. Immediate treatment (cause directed)

- **Hypotension:** treat promptly with a vasopressor such as phenylephrine or noradrenaline to restore a MAP of at least 65 mmHg (higher in chronic hypertension); a diastolic pressure above 50 to 60 mmHg is useful for coronary flow. Treat bleeding with fluid and blood. Avoid excessive fluid if LV function is poor.
- **Tachycardia:** deepen anaesthesia and analgesia, give esmolol (0.5 mg/kg bolus then infusion) or metoprolol if BP allows, treat AF or SVT with synchronised cardioversion if unstable, amiodarone for rate control.
- **Hypoxia and anaemia:** 100% oxygen, transfuse if Hb is below 80 g/L, or higher with ongoing ischaemia (the threshold of 80 to 100 g/L is guideline-supported).
- **Hypertension and light anaesthesia:** deepen anaesthesia, give an opioid, treat with a short-acting agent.
- **Anti-ischaemic drugs:** GTN infusion (5 to 100 micrograms/min) if the BP is adequate and there is no RV involvement or severe AS; this should not be used to treat hypotension-driven ischaemia. Consider diltiazem for vasospasm.

## 4. Escalation and diagnosis

- Obtain a 12-lead ECG, arterial gas (haemoglobin, lactate, potassium), and an urgent TOE if available: new RWMA in the transgastric mid short-axis view confirms ischaemia, localises the territory and assesses LV and RV function, valves, and tamponade.
- Send troponin, repeating at 3 to 6 hours.
- If ST elevation, haemodynamic collapse, malignant arrhythmia, or persisting ST depression despite treatment: call cardiology early. The options are PCI (consider the antiplatelet requirement and the surgical field), IABP or other mechanical support, and discussion with the surgeon about terminating the operation.
- If the surgery is not time-critical, consider abbreviating it to damage control.

## 5. Afterwards

ICU or HDU, serial ECG and troponin, aspirin and statin if bleeding allows, cardiology review, correction of triggers, and a plan for the antiplatelet and anticoagulant question. Document and disclose to the patient.

> **Examiner lens:** treat the cause before the ECG; know ECG sensitivity (V5 about 75%, II plus V5 about 80%, V4 plus V5 about 90%).

items.title: 6. Blood pressure 185/112 before elective surgery
items.q: A 58-year-old man for elective hip replacement has a clinic blood pressure of 185/112 mmHg. Discuss whether you proceed and how you manage his antihypertensives.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

> **BJA Education:** "Preoperative hypertension" (BJA Educ 2021).

## Should surgery go ahead?

- High blood pressure **in isolation is not a reason to cancel** elective surgery. The decision should rest on his **overall cardiac risk**, not one reading.
- The AoA/BHS statement suggests postponing if the pressure is **above 180/110**; the more recent POQI consensus questions whether there is enough evidence to set a threshold. **Update:** AOA/BIHS 2026 uses clinic ≥180/120 mmHg (and generally continues ACEi/ARB); AHA/ACC 2024 permits considering deferral at ≥180/110 in selected elevated-risk cases. Confirm BP, distinguish chronic damage from acute organ injury, and follow local policy.
- Confirm the reading (repeat, ambulatory or home measurement). Look for end-organ damage (LV hypertrophy, renal impairment, retinopathy, ischaemia) and secondary causes.
- Postpone if there is end-organ damage or if there is time to improve control; avoid rapid lowering.

## Why

Chronic hypertension shifts the autoregulation curve to the right. Intraoperative hypotension is probably more harmful than preoperative hypertension, and preoperative hypotension may itself signal higher risk.

## Medication

- Continue beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and other agents.
- **ACE inhibitors and ARBs:** consider withholding on the morning of surgery because of the risk of vasoplegia; restart when haemodynamically stable. Combination tablets complicate this. Continuation is individualised: AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission for selected hypertension cases and favours continuing compensated-HF therapy; AOA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEi/ARB. Restart when perfusion/renal function permit.
- Diuretics: usually withheld on the day if euvolaemic.
- Do not start a beta-blocker or clonidine immediately before surgery.

## Intraop and postoperative

Avoid hypotension relative to the baseline (aim within 20% of baseline or MAP above 65 to 70), avoid hypertensive surges at intubation, and treat postoperative pain and withdrawal. Restart antihypertensives early.

## Self-marking checklist

- States that hypertension alone is not a reason to cancel and uses overall cardiac risk
- Quotes the 180/110 AoA/BHS threshold and the POQI position **Update:** AOA/BIHS 2026 uses clinic ≥180/120 mmHg (and generally continues ACEi/ARB); AHA/ACC 2024 permits considering deferral at ≥180/110 in selected elevated-risk cases. Confirm BP, distinguish chronic damage from acute organ injury, and follow local policy.
- Assesses for end-organ damage and secondary causes
- Explains autoregulation shift and the danger of intraoperative hypotension
- Manages ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker and diuretic correctly
- Does not start beta-blocker or clonidine acutely
- Gives intraoperative and postoperative blood pressure targets

items.title: 7. Intraoperative hypotension in IHD and hypertension
items.q: Discuss the significance of intraoperative hypotension in a patient with ischaemic heart disease and hypertension. How would you define it, prevent it and treat it?
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Why it matters

Hypotension reduces coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP), cerebral and renal perfusion. In a hypertensive patient with fixed coronary disease and LVH, tolerance is poor because autoregulation is shifted to the right and subendocardial supply is marginal. Observational data (VISION, Sessler, Walsh) link a **MAP below 65 mmHg for more than a few minutes** with myocardial injury, acute kidney injury and death, with risk rising with depth and duration.

## Definition

There is no single definition. Common thresholds are MAP below 65 mmHg, systolic below 90 to 100 mmHg, or a fall of more than 20 to 30% from baseline. In chronic hypertension, relative thresholds (baseline) are more meaningful. Evidence from POISE-3 and other trials does not give a simple proven target, but avoiding prolonged hypotension is accepted practice.

## Causes

Anaesthetic vasodilatation and myocardial depression, hypovolaemia and bleeding, neuraxial sympathectomy, drugs (ACEi/ARB on the morning), positive pressure ventilation, pneumoperitoneum and positioning, arrhythmia, ischaemia, tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, and surgical manipulation.

## Prevention

- Review and consider withholding ACEi/ARB on the morning of major surgery; avoid prolonged fasting and ensure euvolaemia. Continuation is individualised: AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission for selected hypertension cases and favours continuing compensated-HF therapy; AOA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEi/ARB. Restart when perfusion/renal function permit.
- **Arterial line** before induction in high-risk patients; reduced-dose, titrated induction; vasopressor ready or infusing (phenylephrine or noradrenaline).
- Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy, avoiding both hypovolaemia and overload.
- Keep depth of anaesthesia appropriate; use regional techniques with slow titration.

## Treatment

- **1.** Confirm the reading (zero, level, cuff) and check the rhythm and ECG.
- **2.** Look for a cause: bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, arrhythmia, ischaemia, drug error.
- **3.** Reduce anaesthetic depth, give a vasopressor (phenylephrine, metaraminol, noradrenaline), use fluid or blood if hypovolaemic, treat bradycardia.
- **4.** Persistent hypotension with ST change: 12-lead ECG, TOE, and call for help.

## Aim

Keep MAP at or above baseline-related threshold (about 65 mmHg or within 20% of baseline) and maintain heart rate low-normal.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains the physiological consequences of hypotension for coronary, cerebral and renal perfusion
- Cites the association with myocardial injury, AKI and death, and the MAP 65 threshold
- Acknowledges there is no single proven definition or target; uses relative thresholds in hypertension
- Lists causes
- Gives preventive strategies (ACEi/ARB, arterial line, vasopressors, goal-directed therapy)
- Gives a stepwise treatment plan

items.title: 8. Chest pain and ST elevation in PACU
items.q: A 70-year-old man 2 hours after radical prostatectomy has crushing chest pain, BP 90/50, HR 110 and widespread anterior ST elevation. Describe your immediate management and treatment priorities.
items.a:
## 1. Immediate response (the first 5 minutes)
- Call for help: the PACU team, anaesthetic senior, and the on-call cardiologist. Move to a monitored resuscitation space with defibrillator pads attached.
- Standard monitoring, large-bore IV access, supplemental oxygen only if SpO2 is below 90% (AVOID, DETO2X), a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, bedside echocardiography, and bloods (troponin, FBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, group and screen, gas).
- Analgesia: titrated IV opioid (fentanyl), with caution because of hypotension.

## 2. Diagnosis
- Widespread anterior ST elevation with chest pain suggests LAD occlusion. This is a type 1 MI or a type 2 MI with ST elevation (rarer).
- Differential: PE (right heart strain), aortic dissection, tamponade, pericarditis, takotsubo cardiomyopathy, coronary vasospasm, coronary embolus (air, paradoxical), and hyperkalaemia.
- Echo helps: anterior wall akinesia (LAD), RV dilation (PE), effusion (tamponade), aortic root and flap (dissection), and global dysfunction (takotsubo).
- Check for bleeding as a cause of hypotension and tachycardia.

## 3. Haemodynamic stabilisation
- BP 90/50 with a rate of 110 suggests low output or hypovolaemia.
- If hypovolaemia (bleeding, third spacing) is suspected, give small fluid or blood boluses of 250 mL, reassessing after each.
- If cardiogenic, avoid large volumes; use noradrenaline to maintain a MAP of at least 65, with dobutamine if low output persists after pressure is restored (see R8).
- Avoid nitrates while hypotensive.

## 4. Reperfusion strategy: the central decision
| Option | Considerations here |
|---|---|
| Primary PCI | The preferred strategy: door-to-device within 90 minutes (60 if already at a PCI centre). It does not need systemic fibrinolysis, and anticoagulation can be limited to the procedural dose. Femoral or radial access with a haemostasis plan |
| Fibrinolysis | Relatively or absolutely contraindicated by major surgery within 3 weeks (a 2-hour-old surgical wound with risk of haemorrhage, particularly after a prostatectomy). Reserve for situations where PCI is unavailable and the surgeon accepts the bleeding risk |
| CABG | Considered for left main or multivessel disease, or if PCI fails, with the cardiothoracic team |

Communicate with the surgeon about bleeding risk, haemostasis, and drains, and with the cardiologist about the stent choice (a bare-metal or newer DES with short DAPT may be chosen to reduce the duration of dual therapy, and balloon angioplasty alone may be used).

## 5. Antithrombotic therapy in a patient with a surgical wound
- **Aspirin:** 150 to 300 mg loading dose unless surgeon objection is overwhelming. It is the most important agent.
- **P2Y12 inhibitor and heparin:** usually given in the cath lab at the time of PCI; the choice and timing are agreed between cardiologist and surgeon. Options are clopidogrel (less potent, preferred where bleeding risk is high), cangrelor, or a lower heparin dose. GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors increase bleeding.
- Monitor the wound, haemoglobin, and drains.

## 6. Other management
- Beta-blocker only if there is no heart failure, shock or heart block; a high-intensity statin.
- Treat arrhythmias (VF, VT) according to ALS, and electrolytes (potassium above 4, magnesium above 1).
- Cardiogenic shock: see R8, with early consideration of MCS.
- Transfer to the cath lab, then CCU or ICU.

## 7. Priorities, in order
- Recognise and call for help.
- Stabilise haemodynamics and airway.
- Early primary PCI as the reperfusion therapy of choice.
- Minimise bleeding while giving the antithrombotic therapy that is essential.
- Detect and treat complications (shock, arrhythmia, mechanical).
- Communicate with the surgeon, patient and family.

> **Examiner lens:** reperfusion is the priority; explain why lytics are a poor choice after surgery.

items.title: 9. Cardiogenic shock after anterior STEMI
items.q: A 62-year-old man is in cardiogenic shock after an anterior STEMI. Define cardiogenic shock, outline the pathophysiology and discuss your management including mechanical circulatory support.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

> **BJA Education:** "Management of cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction" (BJA Educ 2023).

## Definition and epidemiology

Cardiogenic shock (CS) is end-organ hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia from primary cardiac dysfunction. It is the commonest cause of in-hospital death after ACS (**mortality 40 to 70%**) and complicates about 9% of STEMI.

| Haemodynamic | Clinical |
|---|---|
| Persistent SAP below 80 to 90 (or MAP 30 below baseline) with raised filling pressures | Cardiac index below 1.8 (unsupported); SAP below 90 despite volume plus cool peripheries, oliguria, confusion, narrow pulse pressure, raised lactate or creatinine |

A spuriously normal pressure can hide hypoperfusion because compensatory vasoconstriction is intense. **Diagnosis rests on demonstrating end-organ hypoperfusion.**

## Pathophysiology

LV dysfunction reduces output, triggering sympathetic and neurohormonal activation with high SVR, fluid retention and inflammation. The vicious circle: low output and coronary perfusion, ischaemia, further depression. High afterload worsens LV function.

## Management

- **1.** **Emergency revascularisation is central.** DanGer Shock also found lower 180-day mortality with Impella CP in selected STEMI shock (45.8% vs 58.5%; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55–0.99), with more serious complications. Do not extrapolate to all shock.
- **2.** Monitor invasively (arterial line, lactate, echo, PA catheter if available); early ICU or cardiac ICU.
- **3.** Oxygenation and ventilation: NIV or intubation with vasopressors ready.
- **4.** **Drugs:** noradrenaline is usually first line but contentious because SVR is already high, so titrate carefully. Inodilators (dobutamine, milrinone) can reduce afterload but cause hypotension and arrhythmia. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
- **5.** **Mechanical circulatory support** is a temporising strategy for refractory CS (patient selection, timing, LV/RV phenotype and exit strategy matter; no universal proportion requires it):

| Device | Maximum output |
|---|---|
| IABP | about 0.8 L/min |
| Impella | 2.5 to 5.0 L/min |
| TandemHeart | approximately 4–5 L/min (LA-to-arterial support; configuration-dependent) |
| VA-ECMO | up to 7 L/min |

Use the least support needed; routine IABP and early VA-ECMO trials were neutral for survival; selected Impella CP benefit must be balanced against complications, and complexity and bleeding rise with more support (patients are on DAPT plus anticoagulation).
- **6.** Treat arrhythmia, acidosis, and mechanical complications (septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture).

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines cardiogenic shock with perfusion criteria and quotes mortality 40 to 70%
- Notes that blood pressure alone can mislead
- Explains the vicious circle and high SVR
- Prioritises emergency revascularisation and recognises selected Impella evidence and its limitations
- Discusses vasopressor and inodilator choice and the dilemma of afterload
- Lists MCS devices with output and the principle of least support
- Plans monitoring, ventilation and complications

items.title: 10. Mechanical complications after inferior MI
items.q: Three days after an inferior myocardial infarction a patient develops pulmonary oedema, hypotension and a new systolic murmur. Discuss the differential diagnosis and your immediate management.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Differential

A new murmur with shock after MI is a **mechanical complication until proven otherwise**:

| Complication | Timing | Features | Echo |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Papillary muscle rupture** (acute severe MR) | 2 to 7 days, inferior MI (posteromedial muscle, single supply from the PDA) | Flash pulmonary oedema; murmur may be soft or absent due to rapid pressure equalisation | Flail leaflet, severe eccentric MR, hyperdynamic LV |
| **Ventricular septal rupture** | 3 to 5 days | Loud pansystolic murmur with thrill, biventricular failure | Septal defect with left-to-right shunt |
| **Free wall rupture** | Within 2 weeks | Tamponade, PEA, usually no murmur | Effusion with clot |

Other causes: re-infarction, RV infarction, arrhythmia, LVOT obstruction with SAM, ischaemic MR from ventricular remodelling.

## Immediate management

- **1.** **Resuscitate and call the heart team** (cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, ICU).
- **2.** **Confirm** with TTE/TOE; PA catheter shows giant v waves (papillary rupture) or an oxygen saturation step-up (VSR).
- **3.** **Reduce afterload and improve forward flow:** IABP is the key bridge (reduces afterload and regurgitant or shunt flow, improves coronary perfusion). Cautious nitroprusside or GTN if BP allows; inotropes (dobutamine) if hypotensive; PEEP and ventilation for oedema.
- **4.** **Definitive treatment:** urgent surgery (valve replacement or repair for papillary rupture; patch closure for VSR, delayed if stable). Percutaneous closure for high surgical risk.
- **5.** **Free wall rupture:** emergency surgical repair/resuscitation; controlled pericardial drainage is a rescue bridge for critical tamponade when needed, not routine unrestrained decompression.

## Anaesthetic points

Arterial line and vasopressor/inotrope before induction; keep SVR low-normal in MR and VSR, avoid bradycardia (MR) and raised PVR; TOE for diagnosis and assessment after repair. Mortality is very high without surgery.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies papillary muscle rupture, VSR and free wall rupture with typical timing and murmurs
- Explains the single blood supply of the posteromedial papillary muscle
- Confirms with echo and describes PA catheter findings
- Uses IABP and afterload reduction as a bridge
- States that definitive surgical treatment is urgent
- Gives anaesthetic points for induction in these patients

items.title: 11. Induction with an ejection fraction of 20%
items.q: You must anaesthetise a patient with an ejection fraction of 20% and marginal blood pressure for an emergency laparotomy. Discuss your preparation and induction.
items.a:
