| Monitoring | Pulse oximetry plethysmography or arterial line to confirm mechanical rhythm (ECG is distorted by diathermy); set ECG pacing spike detection on; keep external pacing and defibrillation pads in position; ensure that a defibrillator is immediately available |
| Pacemaker | If not pacing-dependent and surgery is below the umbilicus, no change is needed. For above-umbilical monopolar diathermy in a pacing-dependent patient, use a magnet (asynchronous pacing in most pacemakers, though not all; confirm in advance) or reprogram to an asynchronous mode (VOO/DOO) |
| ICD | A magnet suspends tachyarrhythmia therapies (does not affect bradycardia pacing). Alternatively, the device clinic programs tachy therapies off. Pads on and an external defibrillator are mandatory while therapies are suspended. Some devices have no magnet response |
| CRT | A magnet does not turn off biventricular pacing; check that there is high-percentage biventricular pacing preoperatively; AF or ventricular ectopy can reduce capture, and rate-adaptive pacing may increase heart rate in response to minute ventilation sensors (disable if needed) |
| Rate-responsive sensors | Minute ventilation sensors can be misled by ventilation or monitor signals; consider disabling |

## 4. If an arrhythmia occurs while the ICD is disabled
Treat as normal: defibrillate or cardiovert using pads, with anterior-posterior position, and keeping them at least 8 to 10 cm from the generator.

## 5. Postoperative management
- Re-enable ICD therapies before the patient leaves a monitored environment (never leave therapies disabled in the ward or at home).
- Re-interrogate if there was monopolar diathermy near the device, cardioversion, defibrillation, CPR, or if the device was reprogrammed; pacemakers should be checked within 1 month in other situations according to local policy.
- Monitor the ECG continuously until the device is checked.

## 6. Management of the underlying cardiomyopathy
Treat as HFrEF (see R10 and R11), continue guideline-directed medications, and use invasive monitoring.

## 7. Documentation and communication
Record the pre- and postoperative device status, the programming changes, the equipment used and the person responsible for restoring therapies; inform the patient.

> **Examiner lens:** never leave an ICD with therapies disabled outside a monitored environment.

items.title: 35. Anaesthesia for right ventricular dysfunction
items.q: Outline the principles of anaesthetic management for a patient with right ventricular dysfunction presenting for non-cardiac surgery, including ventilation and drug strategy.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "Right ventricular failure – when the right heart goes wrong" (Falland, Drummond, Wylie).

## Principle

Perioperative RV failure is usually an "at-risk" RV (raised PVR, mitral or tricuspid disease, congenital or ischaemic heart disease) meeting a precipitant that alters preload, afterload or contractility. The RV tolerates **acute afterload rises poorly**, so lower or avoid rises in afterload; it handles preload well when healthy but a failing RV may need contractile support. Ischaemic RV failure needs oxygen supply and demand optimised.

## Preop

## Preparation and monitoring

Optimise preoperatively and continue usual medications. High-risk procedures: venous air, CO2, fat or cement embolism, liver transplant, large rapid infusions and laparoscopy. Use an arterial line, consider a central line (CVP trend, inotrope route; limited reliability for volume), **TOE** for RV function and the septum, and a PA catheter only in experienced centres. Keep the patient warm.

## Anaesthetic technique

Any technique suits if haemodynamics are protected. Neuraxial blocks must be introduced slowly. Avoid nitrous oxide and desflurane (raise PVR); volatiles reduce preload and contractility; propofol and thiopentone reduce contractility and SVR but not PVR; ketamine raises PVR in adults (avoid large doses); opioids judiciously. At induction: preoxygenate, gentle bag-mask ventilation, blunt the sympathetic response, full relaxation before laryngoscopy and vasopressors ready.

## Intraop

## Ventilation

Avoid hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 60 mmHg), hypercapnia (the pulmonary vascular response to CO2 varies; no universal linear pressure conversion applies), acidosis, atelectasis and hyperinflation. Ventilate near FRC with tidal volumes around 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, adjusted to mechanics, plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O and PEEP titrated to oxygenation, recruitment and RV function rather than a fixed 10 cmH2O ceiling.

## Volume, rhythm and drugs

For group 2 PH, pulmonary vasodilation can worsen oedema; prioritise LV/LA pressure and specialist guidance. Continue established PAH therapy and avoid interruption of prostacyclin.

- **Volume:** cautious fluids and minimal transfusion; use passive leg raise because CVP is a poor guide; overdistension lowers contractility.
- **Rhythm:** keep sinus rhythm; DC cardioversion if unstable; amiodarone is the agent of choice (beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers depress the RV).
- **Vasopressors:** titrate noradrenaline or low-dose vasopressin to systemic perfusion and RV coronary driving pressure; there is no universal catecholamine dose boundary or guarantee of PVR neutrality.
- **Inotropes:** dobutamine 2 to 5 microgram/kg/min; milrinone 0.25 to 0.5 microgram/kg/min (nebulised option; needs a vasopressor); levosimendan (costly, 24-hour infusion; correct calcium).
- **Pulmonary vasodilators:** inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin where available.
- **Postop:** analgesia (pain raises PVR), avoid opioid hypoventilation, HDU or ICU.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.


## Self-marking checklist

- States the principle: avoid acute afterload rises and maintain RV perfusion
- Names high-risk procedures and precipitants
- Describes monitoring including TOE and the limits of CVP
- Chooses agents with justification (avoid N2O, desflurane, large-dose ketamine)
- Gives a ventilation strategy (FRC, 6 mL/kg, individualised PEEP, avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia)
- Manages volume cautiously and treats arrhythmia (DCCV, amiodarone)
- Chooses vasopressors and inotropes with doses
- Plans postoperative analgesia and level of care

items.title: 36. Pulmonary hypertension and non-cardiac surgery
items.q: Classify pulmonary hypertension and outline the perioperative risks and anaesthetic management of a patient with pulmonary hypertension for non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2015, "Pulmonary hypertension: An overview for the 'non-cardiac' anaesthetist" (Smith). The chapter says it is aimed at those preparing for the final examination.

## Definition and severity

PH is mPAP >20 mmHg at right-heart catheterisation; precapillary PH additionally requires PAWP ≤15 mmHg and PVR >2 Wood units. Postcapillary PH has PAWP >15; classify by cause and RV/clinical risk, not old mPAP-only mild/moderate/severe bands.

## WHO classification (five groups)

- **1.** Pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease)
- **2.** Left heart disease
- **3.** Lung disease or hypoxia
- **4.** Chronic thromboembolic (CTEPH)
- **5.** Unclear or multifactorial

Knowing the group matters: PAH may need sildenafil or other vasodilators, mitral stenosis may need valvuloplasty or replacement, and obstructive sleep apnoea needs CPAP. Risk differs between groups.

## Perioperative risk

Historical series reported substantial mortality/morbidity, but risk varies markedly by PH group, RV function, urgency and surgery. Do not apply a universal 10–15% mortality estimate.

## Preop

## Management

- Preoperative: identify the group, functional class and RV function (echo, BNP), continue pulmonary vasodilators (avoid interruption), plan HDU or ICU.
- Avoid triggers of high PVR: hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain, light anaesthesia and sympathetic stimulation, nitrous oxide.
- Maintain SVR and RV coronary perfusion (vasopressor ready); avoid fluid overload.
- Treat acute RV failure as in the right ventricular failure item: vasopressor plus inotrope, inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin, TOE guidance.
- Postoperative analgesia and monitoring.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.


## Self-marking checklist

- Defines PH using current mPAP, PAWP and PVR criteria; avoids old pressure-only severity bands
- Notes a failing RV may not generate high pressures
- Lists the five WHO groups
- Explains why the cause changes management
- Explains that PH risk varies by group, RV function, urgency and surgery; avoids a universal mortality percentage
- Avoids precipitants of raised PVR and continues pulmonary vasodilators
- Plans haemodynamic support and postoperative care

items.title: 42. Inferior ST elevation: vessel, territory and echo views
items.q: During a laparotomy you see new ST elevation in the inferior leads with hypotension. Link the likely culprit vessel, the structures it supplies, and the echo views you would use to confirm the diagnosis.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## From ECG to vessel

ST elevation in II, III and aVF indicates an inferior infarct. The **RCA** is the culprit in about 80% (right-dominant circulation) and the circumflex in the rest. ST elevation in III greater than II with ST depression in I and aVL favours the RCA; II greater than III with lateral extension (V5 to V6) favours the circumflex. ST elevation in V4R confirms RV involvement (proximal RCA). Tall R waves and ST depression in V1 to V3 suggest posterior extension.

## RCA anatomy and territory

Origin from the right sinus of Valsalva, running in the right AV groove. Branches: conus, **SA nodal** (60%), acute marginals, **AV nodal** (about 90%), posterior descending (in the 85% who are right dominant) and posterolateral. Supplies: the RV free wall, inferior LV wall, posterior third of the septum, SA and AV nodes and the posteromedial papillary muscle (single supply).

## Echo views

| View | Use |
|---|---|
| **TOE transgastric mid short-axis** | Mid-LV wall motion from several territories; useful for inferior/inferoseptal comparison but misses basal/apical disease. Use multiple views and compare baseline; one view cannot exclude ischaemia. |
| ME four-chamber | RV size and function (TAPSE, S'), septal movement |
| ME two-chamber | Anterior and inferior walls |
| ME long axis | Anteroseptal and inferolateral walls, LVOT, MR jet |

Use the 17-segment AHA model and rate each segment normal, hypokinetic, akinetic or dyskinetic; a new RWMA can precede ECG change but is not invariably earlier or specific.

## Associated complications

- **RV infarction:** hypotension with clear lungs and raised JVP; assess underfilling versus congestion; give small reassessed fluid only if underfilled, avoid nitrates and diuretics, support with dobutamine, maintain AV synchrony.
- **Bradycardia/AV block** (nodal supply): atropine, pacing.
- **Papillary muscle rupture** (single supply) and arrhythmia.

## Management

Confirm with a 12-lead including V4R and V7 to V9, TOE, troponin; support perfusion pressure; call cardiology for emergency PCI and agree antithrombotic therapy with the surgeon.

## Self-marking checklist

- Links inferior ST elevation to the RCA (or circumflex) and notes how to distinguish them
- Describes RCA branches and structures supplied (nodes, RV, posteromedial papillary muscle)
- Names the TG mid short-axis view as best for ischaemia and lists other views
- Uses the 17-segment model and notes RWMA precedes ECG change
- Lists complications (RV infarct, AV block, papillary muscle rupture)
- Gives immediate management

items.title: 2023.2 Q6: Treatment strategies for chronic heart failure
items.q: Outline the treatment strategies for chronic heart failure.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2023.2 report verified: prioritise therapies, distinguish prognosis versus symptom benefit, grade severity, and include rehabilitation/risk-factor treatment and ICD/CRT.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Classify first

Chronic heart failure is a clinical syndrome of dyspnoea, fatigue and congestion due to structural or functional cardiac abnormality. Treatment depends on **ejection fraction** (HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41 to 49%, HFpEF 50% or more), severity (NYHA I to IV) and cause (ischaemic, hypertensive, valvular, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia). ESC 2026 now uses HFrEF <50% and HFpEF ≥50%, retiring HFmrEF; retain older EF bands for historical reports/trial eligibility.

## General measures

- Education, self-management plan, daily weights, salt restriction, vaccination, stop smoking, limit alcohol.
- Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation.
- Treat the cause and precipitants (ischaemia, AF, anaemia and iron deficiency, thyroid disease, infection, non-adherence); avoid NSAIDs and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

## Drug therapy in HFrEF

Four classes reduce mortality and admissions and are started early and up-titrated:

| Class | Notes |
|---|---|
| ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan), or ACE inhibitor/ARB | ARNI preferred (PARADIGM-HF); monitor BP, K, creatinine |
| Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) | Start low once euvolaemic |
| Mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone) | Monitor K and creatinine |
| SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) | Fewer heart failure admissions within months, with or without diabetes and independent of glucose lowering (reverse remodelling, less fibrosis proposed) |

Symptomatic and add-on therapy: **loop diuretic** for congestion (primarily relieves congestion; use the lowest dose maintaining euvolaemia rather than withholding necessary decongestion); ivabradine if sinus rhythm with HR 70 or more on maximal beta-blocker; hydralazine plus nitrate if ACEi/ARB/ARNI not tolerated; digoxin for symptoms or AF; anticoagulation if AF.

## HFpEF and legacy HFmrEF

ESC 2026 also recommends an MRA across symptomatic EF phenotypes with renal/potassium monitoring. Composite benefit in HFpEF is largely driven by fewer HF events and should not be described as proven mortality reduction for every agent.

HFpEF is about half of all heart failure and is often accompanied by hypertension, AF, diabetes and obesity. The **SGLT2 inhibitor is first-line**, with diuretics for congestion and control of hypertension, AF, obesity and ischaemia; the other mortality-reducing classes have weaker evidence. Avoid tachycardia and loss of sinus rhythm, since filling depends on diastolic time and atrial contraction.

## Devices and procedures

- **ICD** in eligible patients with persistent low EF despite ≥3 months of therapy, considering symptoms, aetiology, ≥40-day post-MI timing and meaningful survival >1 year; EF alone is insufficient.
- **CRT** in eligible symptomatic low-EF patients despite therapy, with strongest evidence for LBBB/QRS ≥150 ms; consider rhythm, pacing and life expectancy.
- Revascularisation for established coronary indications; viability alone does not prove outcome benefit, valve intervention (for example transcatheter mitral repair for secondary MR), AF ablation.

## Advanced disease

Inotropes, LVAD (bridge or destination) or transplantation in selected patients, and early palliative care.

## Anaesthetic relevance

Continue beta-blocker, individualise loop diuretic and RAAS/ARNI management according to congestion, BP, renal function and drug indication, check any device, and **stop the SGLT2 inhibitor 3 days before** surgery (UK consensus omits the day before and day of surgery (a different protocol, not 48 h in every case)) because of euglycaemic DKA, restarting once eating normally. Continuation is individualised: AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission for selected hypertension cases and favours continuing compensated-HF therapy; AOA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEi/ARB. Restart when perfusion/renal function permit. Current AHA/ACC/FDA interval: ≥72 h for dapagliflozin/empagliflozin/canagliflozin, ≥96 h for ertugliflozin; distinguish this from shorter calendar-day protocols. Restart when stable, eating/drinking and without ketosis.

Includes general measures: education, salt, rehabilitation, avoiding harmful drugs, treating precipitants
Lists the four mortality-reducing classes (ARNI/ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor)
Places loop diuretics as symptomatic therapy and mentions add-ons (ivabradine, hydralazine and nitrate, digoxin)

items.title: 2023.1 Q1: Coronary arteries, territories, ECG leads and NSTEMI
items.q: List the branches of the coronary arteries and the myocardial territories and structures they supply. Outline the ECG leads that correspond to the blood supply. Describe the ECG changes in a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarct (NSTEMI).
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2023.1 report verified: name major branches plus at least one supplied structure/territory; give anterior/inferior/lateral leads and at least two NSTEMI features. Better answers recognised overlap.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Coronary arteries, branches and territories

| Artery | Branches | Supplies |
|---|---|---|
| **Right coronary (RCA)** | Conus; sinoatrial nodal (about 60%); acute marginals; AV nodal (about 90%); posterior descending (PDA, in the 85% who are right dominant); posterolateral | RA, RV, inferior LV wall, posterior third of septum, SA and AV nodes, posteromedial papillary muscle |
| **Left main** | Divides into LAD and circumflex (sometimes a ramus) | Most of the LV |
| **Left anterior descending (LAD)** | Septal perforators; diagonals | Anterior LV wall and apex, anterior two thirds of septum, bundle branches, anterolateral papillary muscle |
| **Circumflex (LCx)** | Obtuse marginals; posterolateral; PDA in left-dominant hearts (about 8%); SA nodal in about 40% | Lateral and posterior LV wall, LA |

The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single supply (PDA), so it is more prone to ischaemic rupture. Dominance is defined by the origin of the PDA.

## Leads corresponding to territory

| Territory | Leads | Usual vessel |
|---|---|---|
| Septal | V1 to V2 | LAD |
| Anterior | V3 to V4 | LAD |
| Lateral | I, aVL, V5 to V6 | Diagonal or LCx |
| Inferior | II, III, aVF | RCA (80%) or LCx |
| Posterior | Reciprocal ST depression and tall R in V1 to V3; confirm with V7 to V9 | RCA or LCx |
| Right ventricle | V4R | Proximal RCA |

Supply overlaps between RCA and circumflex, so leads suggest rather than prove the culprit.

## ECG changes in NSTEMI

NSTEMI is diagnosed by acute troponin rise/fall above the assay’s sex-specific 99th percentile plus evidence of ischaemia; the ECG may be normal and changes are often dynamic.

- **ST depression** (new horizontal or downsloping, 0.5 mm or more in two contiguous leads).
- **T-wave inversion** (new, 1 mm or more in leads with a dominant R wave), including deep symmetrical anterior T waves (Wellens pattern).
- ST depression in many leads with **ST elevation in aVR** suggests global subendocardial ischaemia, which may accompany multivessel disease or supply–demand imbalance; it does not specifically diagnose left-main occlusion.
- ST depression V1 to V3 with a dominant R wave suggests posterior infarction (a STEMI equivalent).
- Ischaemia can also show as **pseudonormalisation** (an inverted T wave becoming upright). Q waves are not required. Repeat the ECG serially.

## Clinical points

Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in III greater than II suggests RCA, whereas II greater than III with lateral involvement suggests circumflex. Right ventricular infarction is preload dependent, so avoid preload reduction if hypotensive; give small reassessed fluid only when underfilled, not routine loading of a congested RV.

Mentions dominance and SA/AV nodal supply
Gives correct leads: septal V1 to V2, anterior V3 to V4, lateral I, aVL, V5 to V6, inferior II, III, aVF
Mentions posterior and right ventricular leads
Describes NSTEMI changes: ST depression, T-wave inversion, dynamic or normal ECG
Mentions aVR elevation/left main pattern or posterior equivalent

items.title: 2023.1 Q6: Mechanical aortic valve through pregnancy and delivery
items.q: Discuss the implications of anticoagulation as well as an appropriate anticoagulant management strategy for a 25-year-old with a mechanical aortic valve for the duration of pregnancy, delivery and the postpartum period.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2023.1 report verified: continued valve protection until close to delivery, fetal teratogenic/haemorrhage risks, neuraxial implications and major bleeding were core requirements.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## The problem

A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation and pregnancy is hypercoagulable, with changing drug requirements (higher volume of distribution, increased renal clearance). Every option trades **maternal valve thrombosis, stroke and death** against **fetal harm and bleeding**. Care is by a pregnancy heart team (cardiology, obstetrics, anaesthesia, haematology) with the patient's informed choice.

## Agents and implications

| Agent | Maternal efficacy | Fetal and practical issues |
|---|---|---|
| **Warfarin** | Most effective | Crosses the placenta: teratogenic in the first trimester (embryopathy at weeks 6 to 12, lower risk if dose 5 mg/day or less), fetal intracranial haemorrhage, miscarriage |
| **LMWH** (twice daily) | Better fetal outcomes but more valve thrombosis than warfarin | Does not cross the placenta; needs anti-Xa monitoring (peak about 0.8 to 1.2 IU/mL for aortic valve) because weight-based dosing is inaccurate as fluid state changes |
| **UFH** (aPTT guided) | Effective but hard to keep in range | No placental transfer; used peripartum; HIT, osteoporosis |
| **DOACs** | Contraindicated (mechanical valve and pregnancy) | |

## Suggested strategy

- **First trimester:** after informed discussion, continue warfarin if dose is 5 mg/day or less (European and US guidance), otherwise twice-daily LMWH or UFH for the first trimester (the Australian rheumatic heart disease approach), then back to warfarin from about week 13. There is no consensus on the optimal regimen.
- **Second and third trimester:** warfarin (valve-specific INR (often target 2.5 for a bileaflet aortic valve without extra risk; higher for relevant valve/patient factors)) or LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring; echo surveillance. Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception, which adds thrombotic risk.
- **From about 36 weeks:** change to LMWH or IV UFH so the fetus is not anticoagulated at delivery, and plan delivery.
- **Delivery:** planned induction at 38 to 39 weeks. Stop therapeutic LMWH at least 24 hours before neuraxial block or delivery (use IV UFH, stopped 4 to 6 hours before). If labour starts on warfarin, caesarean section is advised because of fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk.
- **Postpartum:** restart anticoagulation according to bleeding, valve risk and neuraxial timing; distinguish prophylactic from therapeutic dosing. Therapeutic LMWH usually waits ≥24 h after lower-risk surgery or 48–72 h after high-risk surgery; remove catheter ≥4 h before first dose and wait ≥24 h from needle placement. All are compatible with breastfeeding.

## Anaesthetic implications

- Neuraxial block needs normal coagulation (INR normalised to the local laboratory range for neuraxial insertion; catheter removal generally requires INR <1.5; 24 hours after therapeutic LMWH; UFH off with normal aPTT) and observance of catheter removal intervals. Alternatives are remifentanil PCA or general anaesthesia.
- Avoid tachycardia and hypotension (aortic valve disease); slow epidural top-ups; oxytocin by infusion.
- Anticoagulation raises the risk of peripartum haemorrhage, so prepare for postpartum haemorrhage with early surgical management, and for reversal (protamine for heparins, vitamin K and PCC for warfarin). General anaesthesia is needed for caesarean section if anticoagulation cannot be stopped.
- **Valve thrombosis** (new dyspnoea, embolism, loss of the valve click) is an emergency needing urgent transfer for TOE-guided thrombolysis or surgery.

Compares warfarin (embryopathy, fetal haemorrhage), LMWH (anti-Xa monitoring, less effective) and UFH; notes DOACs are contraindicated
Gives a staged plan including the switch at about 36 weeks
Explains delivery planning and caesarean if on warfarin in labour

Covers postpartum restart, bleeding, reversal and valve thrombosis

items.title: 2022.2 Q1: Detecting myocardial ischaemia under anaesthesia
items.q: Evaluate the methods for detection of myocardial ischaemia in the anaesthetised patient.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2022.2 report verified: evaluate clinical signs, ECG and echo. Omitting clinical methods prevented a pass; a list without appraisal was insufficient.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Principle

Ischaemia is a supply and demand imbalance. Under general anaesthesia the patient cannot report angina and ischaemia is often silent, so we depend on monitoring. No single method is both sensitive and specific; combine them and interpret them with the haemodynamics.

## Methods and evaluation

| Method | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Clinical signs** (unexplained hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, rising filling pressures, pulmonary oedema; chest pain or dyspnoea in awake patients) | Immediate; symptoms may support diagnosis in awake patients but may be absent or nonspecific | Late and non-specific; masked by GA, opioids, beta-blockers, diabetes |
| **ECG with ST analysis** | Continuous, cheap, standard, trend display | Sensitivity depends on leads; false positives (electrolytes, hypothermia, position) and false negatives (posterior, circumflex, subendocardial ischaemia); uninterpretable with LBBB, pacing, LVH, digoxin; needs diagnostic filter |
| **Transoesophageal echo** | **New regional wall motion abnormality** appears before ECG change; mid-papillary short-axis view covers all three territories | Invasive, needs training and equipment, intermittent; not specific (loading, pacing, stunning) |
| **PA catheter** | Direct pressures (raised PAOP, v waves) | Insensitive and late; invasive; not recommended for detection |
| **Troponin** | Detects silent myocardial injury (MINS) and predicts outcome | Not real time |

## ECG detail

- **Lead sensitivity:** V5 alone about 75%, II plus V5 about 80%, V4 plus V5 about 90%, II, V4 and V5 about 96%. Lead II alone mainly detects inferior ischaemia. Practical lead selection includes **II plus V5 (or V4)**, **V4 plus V5** if high risk, and II, V4 and V5 if three leads can be displayed.
- **Technique:** V5 sits at the anterior axillary line in the horizontal plane of V4 (not along the intercostal space). Misplacement by more than 2 to 3 cm changes morphology, and Mason-Likar (torso) limb electrodes shift lateral ST changes into the inferior leads.
- **Criteria:** distinguish monitor ST alarms (often ≥1 mm depression) from formal diagnostic 12-lead criteria: new horizontal/downsloping ST depression ≥0.5 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads; J-point elevation ≥1 mm except V2–V3 (men ≥40: ≥2 mm; men <40: ≥2.5 mm; women: ≥1.5 mm), without confounding LVH/BBB. New LBBB alone is not diagnostic; use validated Sgarbossa/modified criteria in context. T-wave changes, arrhythmia and conduction changes are supportive but nonspecific.

## Overall

ECG is the backbone, with a 5-lead system and ST trending (V5 plus II) in at-risk patients, an arterial line, and **TOE for high-risk or unstable patients**. Agree a response plan for ST change. Respond early to haemodynamic prompts, and confirm postoperatively with ECG and troponin on days 1 to 3, because most myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (Roche hsTnT 20–<65 ng/L with absolute change ≥5 ng/L, or ≥65 ng/L, attributed to ischaemia) is silent.
rubric: Explains the supply and demand principle and why ischaemia is often silent under anaesthesia
Includes clinical signs
Describes ECG detection with ST criteria and lead sensitivity (V5, II plus V5, V4 plus V5)
States ECG limitations (LBBB, pacing, LVH, filters, posterior/circumflex ischaemia)
Describes TOE regional wall motion abnormality as a potentially early finding, not invariably earlier or specific, with its limitations
Mentions PA catheter and troponin
Evaluates strengths and weaknesses rather than listing, and gives an overall approach

items.title: 2022.1 Q8: IABP pressure trace at 1:2 augmentation
items.q: Identify the points labelled A to F on this intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) pressure-time trace at the commencement of 1:2 augmentation. (30%) Outline the aims of IABP placement and discuss the underlying physiological principles. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2022.1 report verified: A was accepted as assisted/unassisted systole; B notch, C unassisted end-diastole, D augmentation, E assisted end-diastole, F assisted systole. The labels below refer to **this exact original examination figure**.

![Original ANZCA Final 2022.1 Q8 IABP pressure-time waveform showing points A to F, red arterial pressure and blue balloon timing](set11-saq-iabp.png)

> Original ANZCA 2022.1 Q8 figure, supplied by the user. Cover the model answer, identify A–F, then explain counterpulsation in the 1:2 trace.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## The trace at 1:2 assist (figure reproduced above)

| Point | Identification |
|---|---|
| A | Assisted/unassisted systole accepted in the original report; identify against the supplied figure |
| B | Dicrotic notch (balloon inflation point) |
| C | Unassisted aortic end-diastolic pressure |
| D | Diastolic augmentation |
| E | Assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure (lower than C) |
| F | Assisted systolic pressure (lower than A) |

In this labelled trace E should be below C and F below A; D often exceeds native systole, but this is not a universal requirement.

## Aims

- **1.** **Improve myocardial oxygen supply** by raising diastolic aortic pressure and coronary perfusion pressure.
- **2.** **Reduce myocardial oxygen demand** by reducing afterload and LV wall tension.
- **3.** Modestly improve cardiac output (up to about 0.8 L/min, compared with 2.5 to 5 L/min for Impella and up to 7 L/min for VA-ECMO) and organ perfusion.
- **4.** Bridge to definitive treatment (revascularisation, surgery, recovery or advanced support).

## Physiological principles

- A 30 to 50 mL helium-filled balloon sits in the descending thoracic aorta, tip just distal to the left subclavian artery. Helium is used because of its low density (rapid inflation and deflation). It is triggered by the ECG R wave or arterial pressure.
- **Inflation at the dicrotic notch** (aortic valve closure, start of diastole) displaces blood proximally, raising diastolic root pressure and coronary flow (coronaries fill in diastole), and distally, improving peripheral perfusion.
- **Deflation just before systole** produces a sudden fall in aortic volume and end-diastolic pressure, so the LV ejects against lower afterload, reducing wall tension, oxygen demand and LVEDP.
- Net effect: improved supply to demand ratio.
- It needs a regular trigger rhythm (poor with AF or tachycardia), some LV function and a competent aortic valve.

## Use, contraindications and complications

Indications include cardiogenic shock bridge (although routine use after MI has not improved outcome: IABP-SHOCK II showed no 30-day mortality benefit), mechanical complications of MI (acute MR, VSD), refractory ischaemia, high-risk PCI/CABG. **Contraindications/cautions:** significant AR and aortic dissection; aneurysm and vascular disease require anatomical/device-specific assessment, severe peripheral vascular disease. Complications: limb ischaemia, aortic injury, thrombocytopenia, bleeding, infection, balloon rupture.

## Timing errors and weaning

Early inflation (before the notch) causes premature aortic valve closure and reduces stroke volume. Late inflation loses augmentation. Early deflation loses the unloading effect; late deflation raises afterload as the LV ejects against the inflated balloon. Wean by lowering the ratio (1:1, 1:2, 1:3) while watching haemodynamics, and monitor limb perfusion, platelets and urine output.
rubric: Correctly identifies **A** (the report accepted assisted/unassisted systole), **B** dicrotic notch, **C** unassisted aortic end-diastolic pressure, **D** diastolic augmentation, **E** assisted end-diastolic pressure and **F** assisted systole from the supplied figure
States the aims: improved coronary perfusion, reduced afterload and oxygen demand
Describes balloon position, helium and triggering
Explains inflation at the dicrotic notch and deflation before systole, with effects
Mentions limits (rhythm, LV function, competent aortic valve)
Lists indications, contraindications (aortic regurgitation, dissection) and complications
Comments on limited evidence in cardiogenic shock

items.title: 2021.1 Q5: Post-laparotomy ECG in PACU
items.q: This is the standard 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) of a 56-year-old man in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) two hours after an emergency laparotomy for bowel obstruction. He is complaining of shortness of breath, abdominal pain and has a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg. He has a history of hypertension controlled with atenolol and hydrochlorothiazide. The preoperative ECG is missing. The anaesthetic assessment only notes that it showed sinus rhythm. Considering all the clinical information, interpret this ECG and outline the appropriate management of this patient in PACU.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report emphasis:** 2021.1 report and ECG verified (report p13): identify ischaemia and territory, provide analgesia/oxygenation, Hb/troponin, cardiology advice and appropriate therapies. Address hypertension; unqualified thrombolysis after laparotomy was a safety concern.

![Original ANZCA Final 2021.1 Q5 twelve-lead PACU ECG](set11-saq-ecg.png)

> Original ANZCA 2021.1 Q5 ECG, supplied by the user. Interpret rate, rhythm, axis, intervals and ST–T abnormalities before revealing the model answer.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Interpretation (ECG reproduced above)

Read systematically: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, then ST segments and T waves lead by lead, naming the territory. The tracing has a regular **sinus rhythm**, prominent precordial QRS voltage, **inferior T-wave inversion (particularly III/aVF)** and **lateral ST–T abnormalities (notably V5–V6)**; the changes raise concern for **inferolateral myocardial ischaemia** in the symptomatic postoperative patient. The conspicuous anterior repolarisation/voltage pattern also deserves attention. Hypertensive LVH with secondary repolarisation changes is a possible competing explanation, and the tracing alone neither proves a new infarction nor uniquely establishes a culprit artery. The missing baseline is important. State that:

- Without a baseline ECG you cannot establish which changes are new: treat the **symptomatic patient and suspicious changes** as potentially acute while obtaining serial and prior ECGs.
- Mimics and contributors must be considered: LV hypertrophy with strain, electrolyte disturbance, pulmonary embolism (T-wave inversion also occurs in PE, HCM, pericarditis and raised intracranial pressure), pulmonary oedema, and beta-blocker withdrawal (a missed atenolol dose causes tachycardia and hypertension).

## Management in PACU

- **1.** **Call for help**; sit upright; monitor with defibrillator pads; large-bore IV access; oxygen for hypoxaemia, titrated to the clinical target; in ACS give routinely below 90% and avoid >96% on oxygen.
- **2.** **Analgesia** for the abdominal pain (titrated opioid, regional block) because pain drives hypertension and tachycardia.
- **3.** **Reduce demand and optimise supply:** treat hypertension (GTN infusion if ischaemic; resume beta-blocker, for example esmolol or metoprolol, if no heart failure or bronchospasm), treat tachycardia, correct anaemia, hypoxia and electrolytes (K, Mg).
- **4.** **Investigate:** repeat 12-lead ECG in 15 to 30 minutes, serial high-sensitivity troponin, haemoglobin, electrolytes, gas, chest X-ray, bedside echo for new wall motion abnormality or pulmonary oedema.
- **5.** **Antiplatelet therapy:** aspirin is reasonable but discuss with the surgeon given the fresh laparotomy; avoid anticoagulation without surgical agreement.
- **6.** **If ST elevation or ongoing ischaemia:** urgent cardiology review for angiography/PCI. **Recent major surgery may prohibit fibrinolysis (ESC: major surgery/trauma/head injury within the previous month is an absolute contraindication)**.
- **7.** **Disposition:** HDU/ICU with continuous ECG and serial troponin, then secondary prevention.

## Further points

Treat the hypertension as a contributor and a consequence: pain, beta-blocker withdrawal, fluid overload and ischaemia all raise BP. Check that atenolol was given. An acute troponin change plus convincing new ischaemic ST depression may establish MI; the mechanism cannot be assumed to be secondary/type 2 solely from this presentation; manage the supply-demand cause and arrange cardiology input before any anticoagulation. Document that the baseline ECG was unavailable and obtain old tracings from the GP or previous admissions.

items.title: 2020.1 Q10: Mitral stenosis for laparoscopic hernia repair
items.q: Outline your peri-operative management of a patient with mitral stenosis scheduled for a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2020.1 Q10:** Distinguish stenosis from regurgitation, classify severity accurately, and explain how transabdominal, extraperitoneal or open repair changes management. Replace vague phrases such as “gentle induction” with specific drugs, titration and haemodynamic responses.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Pathophysiology and severity

Mitral stenosis (usually rheumatic) obstructs LA to LV flow, raising LA pressure with pulmonary congestion, pulmonary hypertension, RV failure and AF. The LV is underfilled. **Tachycardia is poorly tolerated** because shorter diastole raises the gradient and LA pressure. Severe MS (BJA Education): valve area **below 1.0 cm2**, mean gradient above 10 mmHg, pressure half-time 220 ms or more (moderate: 1.0 to 1.5 cm2, gradient 5 to 10 mmHg). Up to 40% of patients with severe MS develop AF. Severe MS limits flow reserve through a rate- and flow-dependent inflow obstruction; its physiology is not identical to AS. Current ESC intervention terminology uses clinically severe/significant rheumatic MS at MVA ≤1.5 cm²; gradients depend on rate/flow and PHT on compliance, so report the area and framework rather than applying one number alone.

## Preop

- Symptoms (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, embolism), rhythm, and a **current echo** (area, gradient, PA pressure, RV function).
- Severe symptomatic MS warrants specialist consideration of valve intervention before elective surgery; establish whether this hernia repair can safely be deferred.
- Continue rate control (beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker); anticoagulate (target INR 2 to 3) only if AF, previous embolism or left atrial thrombus; anxiolytic premedication to avoid tachycardia. PASP <50 mmHg and absence of symptoms may be reassuring but do not guarantee safety; assess severity, RV function and surgical stress.
- Discuss technique with the surgeon: open repair under local or regional avoids pneumoperitoneum; if laparoscopic, clarify transabdominal versus totally extraperitoneal insufflation. Both can impair venous return and cause CO2 absorption; effects depend on pressure, positioning and technique, so an extraperitoneal approach does not guarantee haemodynamic stability.

## Haemodynamic goals

| Variable | Goal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | Below 70, sinus rhythm | Maximise diastolic filling time; treat tachycardia and arrhythmia aggressively |
| Preload | Normovolaemia: fluid boluses can cause pulmonary oedema | LV underfilled but lungs congested; use vasopressors rather than volume for hypotension |
| SVR | Maintain | Fixed output |
| PVR | Keep low: avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, N2O | Protect the RV |

## Intraop

- Arterial line and 5-lead ECG; do not use PAC routinely; LA/PAOP may be high despite a low LVEDP in MS, and selected complex cases may still benefit from invasive data; consider TOE; defibrillator pads.
- Slow titrated induction with opioid to blunt laryngoscopy; avoid ketamine, pancuronium and other causes of tachycardia.
- Low-pressure pneumoperitoneum (10 to 12 mmHg), slow insufflation, minimal tilt, ventilation adjusted for CO2 absorption.
- Treat hypotension with phenylephrine or noradrenaline rather than fluid boluses; treat fast AF early (cardioversion if unstable, otherwise beta-blocker or amiodarone).

## Postop

Monitored recovery (HDU if severe), with instructions to recovery staff to avoid fluid boluses and to call anaesthetic review for any hypotension. Multimodal analgesia with regional block and minimal opioid, avoid pain and shivering, restart rate control and anticoagulation, watch for pulmonary oedema (venous return improves with desufflation). Neuraxial block is not chosen lightly because of the sympathetic block and any anticoagulation.
rubric: Defines MS without confusing it with MR; recognises clinically significant MS at valve area ≤1.5 cm² and very severe narrowing at ≤1.0 cm²; interprets gradients and pressure half-time in their flow/rate context

items.title: 2018.2 Q14: HCM in pregnancy, labour and delivery
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and how this is affected by pregnancy, labour, and vaginal delivery.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2018.2 Q14:** Link septal hypertrophy and dynamic obstruction to the changing loading conditions of pregnancy, labour and vaginal delivery; describing HCM alone does not answer the whole question.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Pathophysiology of HCM

- Autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutation (more than 11 genes; about 1 in 500 adults) with asymmetric **septal hypertrophy**, myocyte disarray and fibrosis.
- **Dynamic LVOT obstruction** (about 70%; gradient above 30 mmHg at rest in a third, only on provocation in a third): the narrowed outflow tract accelerates flow and the anterior mitral leaflet is drawn into it (**systolic anterior motion**), causing obstruction and mitral regurgitation.
- **Diastolic dysfunction** is the major abnormality: a stiff ventricle with preserved or high EF, dependent on diastolic filling time and atrial contraction, so AF is poorly tolerated.
- **Ischaemia** despite normal coronaries (high wall tension, small-vessel disease) and **arrhythmia** (AF, VT/VF, sudden death).

Obstruction is **worsened** by low preload, low afterload, high contractility and tachycardia, and **reduced** by the opposite.

## Effects of pregnancy, labour and delivery

| Phase | Change | Effect on HCM |
|---|---|---|
| **Pregnancy** | Blood volume up 40 to 50%, cardiac output up, SVR down, heart rate up | Larger preload reduces obstruction (helpful); lower SVR and tachycardia increase it (harmful); most women tolerate pregnancy |
| **Late pregnancy** | Aortocaval compression | Reduced venous return worsens obstruction |
| **Labour** | Pain and catecholamines raise heart rate and contractility; contractions autotransfuse 300 to 500 mL | Tachycardia harmful; autotransfusion helpful |
| **Second stage** | Valsalva lowers venous return | Worsens obstruction |
| **Delivery** | Blood loss, oxytocin (vasodilation, tachycardia), relief of caval compression | Hypovolaemia and hypotension increase obstruction |
| **Postpartum** | Fluid shifts | Pulmonary oedema (diastolic dysfunction) and AF |

## Implications

Early, slowly titrated epidural with phenylephrine ready, left lateral tilt, fluid to maintain preload, assisted second stage to avoid prolonged pushing, oxytocin by slow infusion only (it vasodilates and causes tachycardia), avoid ergometrine, carboprost, sympathomimetic uterotonics and tocolytics, continue beta-blocker, keep sinus rhythm, and deliver where cardiology and ICU are available.

## Risk and counselling

Women with HCM and low-risk features (no severe symptoms, mild gradient, no arrhythmia) usually do well; predictors of poor outcome are severe LVOT gradient, symptoms before pregnancy, and AF. The disease is dominantly inherited, so offer genetic counselling and consider screening of the baby. Epidural analgesia is usually helpful because pain control reduces catecholamines, provided hypotension is prevented with a vasopressor. If caesarean section is needed, a slowly titrated epidural or CSE is preferred to a single-shot spinal, or a general anaesthetic with the same principles.

items.title: 2018.1 Q6: Urgent cancer surgery three weeks after MI
items.q: A 63-year-old patient presents for urgent cancer surgery three weeks following myocardial infarction. Discuss the risk assessment of this patient for this surgery. (50%) How would you optimise this patient for surgery? (50%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2018.1 Q6:** The report expected recognition of competing priorities, major cardiac risk, nonsurgical cancer options, and both pharmacological and non-pharmacological optimisation. It specifically discouraged significant delay without weighing the cancer urgency. This is a reasoned risk decision, not a blanket instruction to operate despite active instability.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Preop

### Risk assessment (50%)

The competing priorities are cancer progression with delay and the elevated early risk of reinfarction and death. Three weeks is a high-risk interval; risk does not normalise at six weeks and depends on the MI, treatment, recovery and proposed surgery. The decision is shared among patient, surgeon, oncologist, cardiologist and anaesthetist.

**The MI:** type (STEMI, NSTEMI, type 2), culprit and extent, revascularisation (stent type, antiplatelet requirement), residual ischaemia, LV function, and complications (arrhythmia, heart failure).

**Current status:** angina, dyspnoea, functional capacity (METs/DASI), ECG, echo, troponin/BNP, rhythm, haemoglobin, renal function, diabetes.

**Surgery:** type of cancer surgery (intermediate or high risk), urgency, blood loss, duration, and whether a **less invasive or briefly delayed alternative** exists (neoadjuvant therapy, smaller procedure).

**Quantify:** use a tool alongside clinical judgement (RCRI for cardiac risk; NSQIP, SORT or nzRISK for mortality), remembering they do not capture a recent MI well and mostly predict only to 30 days; consider cancer anaemia, hypercoagulability and chemotherapy cardiotoxicity.

### Optimisation (50%)

- **Medications:** continue aspirin and beta-blocker (do not start a high dose on the day), statin, ACE inhibitor (consider omitting on the morning), treat heart failure and hypertension. Continuation is individualised: AHA/ACC 2024 allows omission for selected hypertension cases and favours continuing compensated-HF therapy; AOA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEi/ARB. Restart when perfusion/renal function permit.
- **Antiplatelets:** if a stent was placed, agree the P2Y12 inhibitor plan with the cardiologist (interruption soon after PCI is especially hazardous, with risk determined by timing, ACS indication and procedural complexity); continue aspirin if the bleeding balance permits.
- **Revascularisation:** only if independently indicated (residual high-risk ischaemia), as it adds DAPT and delay.
- **Other:** correct anaemia, electrolytes, glucose and nutrition.
- **Setting:** agree rescue PCI access and the postoperative level of care before proceeding.
- **Consent:** discuss specific risks and alternatives, and document the shared decision.

### Timing of surgery

Recent MI timing is individualised by residual ischaemia, recovery, ventricular function, urgency, PCI and antithrombotics. A historical 60-day interval without PCI does not establish normal risk. After DES, elective surgery requiring interruption is generally delayed ≥12 months after ACS or ≥6 months after chronic-disease PCI; selected time-sensitive surgery may be considered ≥3 months. A universal six-week DAPT rule is inappropriate. Agree the acceptable oncological delay with the surgeon.

## Intraop

Arterial pressure monitoring and 5-lead ECG with ST analysis as appropriate to severity; avoid tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia and hypothermia. Titrate fluids to perfusion and congestion, and provide regional or other multimodal analgesia within antithrombotic constraints.

## Postop

Plan HDU/ICU according to risk, continuous ECG and hs-troponin surveillance over the first 48–72 hours when indicated. Most perioperative myocardial injury is silent. Reassess bleeding, oxygenation, pain, perfusion and congestion; restore indicated medication and antiplatelets promptly when safe.

Assesses current functional status and tests
Considers the surgery and less invasive/delayed alternatives
Uses risk tools and notes they underestimate risk after recent MI
Optimises medications and antiplatelet plan with the cardiologist

Includes consent and balances cancer urgency, nonsurgical options and a justified acceptable delay

items.title: 2017.1 Q11: HCM with a femoral fracture
items.q: A 60-year-old female patient with known hypertrophic cardiomyopathy requires semi-urgent surgery for a femoral fracture. Describe the perioperative haemodynamic goals and justify your anaesthetic technique.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2017.1 Q11:** Prioritise heart rate, volume and afterload goals, then justify the chosen technique against those goals. Secondary assessment details should not displace the two main tasks.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Haemodynamic goals and reasons

HCM causes dynamic LVOT obstruction (SAM) and diastolic dysfunction. Obstruction worsens with low preload, low afterload, high contractility and tachycardia.

| Variable | Goal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Preload** | Euvolaemia: correct demonstrated deficit/blood loss in reassessed increments, avoid unnecessary venodilation | A larger cavity separates septum and mitral valve |
| **Heart rate** | Low-normal (50 to 70) | Longer diastole, less obstruction and ischaemia |
| **Rhythm** | Sinus; cardiovert unstable AF; individualise stable rhythm/rate management | Atrial kick fills the stiff ventricle |
| **Afterload** | Maintain or raise | Holds the leaflet away; coronary perfusion |
| **Contractility** | Low-normal; avoid inotropes | Hypercontractility raises the gradient |

## Preop

Symptoms, family history of sudden death, echo (gradient, SAM, MR), ECG, continue beta-blocker or verapamil, check any ICD (pads, reprogramme for diathermy). Replace volume, correct electrolytes and treat pain early with a **fascia iliaca block**, because pain causes tachycardia. Surgery within 24 to 48 hours.

## Intraop

## Technique and justification

- **General anaesthesia** permits controlled titration but has not been proven universally safer than neuraxial anaesthesia in HCM: arterial line before induction, **phenylephrine infusion** running, slow titrated induction (etomidate or reduced-dose propofol with opioid), no ketamine, low-dose volatile (negative inotrope), maintain volume, avoid light anaesthesia and tachycardia, avoid high intrathoracic pressures.
- **Neuraxial:** a conventional single-shot spinal causes abrupt sympathectomy (fall in SVR and preload) and is **avoided**. A low-dose or titrated CSE/epidural with phenylephrine infusion is acceptable in experienced hands and avoids airway instrumentation.
- A fascia iliaca or femoral block reduces opioid and anaesthetic requirements with either technique.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line, 5-lead ECG, TOE if unstable.
- **Hypotension:** phenylephrine, with a small reassessed fluid bolus only if underfilled (first line) or vasopressin, reduce volatile; **avoid ephedrine**, adrenaline and dobutamine, which worsen obstruction and MR. TOE guides volume and gradient.
- Be ready for cement-related hypotension. Postoperatively use HDU, continue beta-blocker, and give thromboprophylaxis.

## Further points

Aim for rapid mobilisation after surgery. Clearly communicate the risk of hypotension and obstruction to the theatre team and avoid transfer or positioning changes that reduce preload (head-up tilt, sudden sitting). Treat pain with a fascia iliaca block in the emergency department and replace demonstrable deficits cautiously rather than loading routinely. If an anaesthetic is needed for cementing, anticipate the drop in systemic vascular resistance and have a vasopressor running.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.
rubric: States the pathophysiology (dynamic LVOT obstruction, SAM, diastolic dysfunction)

items.title: 2016.2 Q4: Frothy secretions and dyspnoea in PACU
items.q: A 55-year-old male is in the post-anaesthesia care unit after nasal surgery. He is conscious, dyspnoeic, and is coughing up frothy secretions. List your differential diagnosis AND how this would direct subsequent management.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2016.2 Q4:** The borderline answer recognised pulmonary oedema and airway obstruction, including throat pack or clots, and managed both appropriately. An extensive differential does not replace immediate assessment and relief of obstruction.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Immediate response

Call for help, sit upright, high-flow oxygen, full monitoring, suction. **Inspect the oropharynx for blood, clot or a retained throat pack**, check the surgical site and nasal packs, and examine the chest, JVP and heart sounds.

## Differential diagnosis and how it directs management

| Cause | Clues | Management |
|---|---|---|
| **Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema** (ischaemia, arrhythmia, hypertension, fluid overload, valve disease) | Raised JVP, bilateral crackles, ECG change | Sit up, CPAP/NIV (avoid if SBP below 85), GTN, IV loop diuretic, treat cause, ECG, troponin, echo; opioid only for distress |
| **Negative-pressure pulmonary oedema** | Laryngospasm or airway obstruction at emergence | Relieve obstruction, oxygen, CPAP/PEEP; resolves in 12 to 48 hours |
| **Airway obstruction from blood, clot or throat pack** | Stridor, noisy breathing, blood in pharynx | Suction, remove pack, reintubate or surgical airway, ENT help |
| **Aspiration of gastric contents or blood** | Regurgitation, wheeze | Suction, oxygen, CPAP, supportive |
| **Anaphylaxis** | Bronchospasm, flushing, hypotension | Adrenaline, fluids, tryptase |
| **TACO or TRALI, fluid overload** | Recent blood or large fluid load | Stop transfusion, diuretic or supportive |
| **Others** | Bronchospasm, pneumothorax, PE, residual neuromuscular block | Specific treatment |

## Investigation and escalation

12-lead ECG, chest X-ray or lung ultrasound (diffuse B-lines in several zones indicate interstitial syndrome but not the cause), blood gas, troponin/BNP (BNP <100 ng/L makes acute HF less likely, but obesity/flash oedema can yield low values), bedside echo. Trial CPAP/NIV; intubate if exhausted, hypoxic or drowsy (vasopressor ready); admit to HDU/ICU; review fluid balance and inform the surgeons.

## Reasoning behind the first-line diagnosis

Frothy, often pink-tinged secretions are characteristic of alveolar flooding. After nasal surgery the commonest explanations are airway obstruction with negative-pressure oedema, fluid overload, or aspirated blood. A young fit man points to negative-pressure oedema; an older man with hypertension points to cardiogenic oedema. Check that no throat pack has been left in place, and look for features of anaphylaxis (rash, wheeze, hypotension) because reversal and antibiotic drugs are common triggers.

items.title: 2016.2 Q13: Antiplatelet therapy with a coronary stent
items.q: A 70-year-old man scheduled for major surgery presents to the pre-anaesthesia assessment clinic. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and coronary stent insertion, and is on aspirin and clopidogrel. Outline the considerations when managing his antiplatelet therapy.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2016.2 Q13:** The report explicitly prioritised risk assessment over a generic management protocol: why antiplatelets are needed, what stent, when it was placed, and when surgery is planned. Weigh the consequence of bleeding against stent thrombosis before proposing interruption.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Preop

### The core issue

**Stent thrombosis** (potentially catastrophic MI or death; a single mortality percentage is not portable across settings) versus **surgical bleeding**. Four questions drive the decision:

- **1.** **Does the surgery need to happen now, and can it wait?**
- **2.** **What stent?** Drug-eluting or bare-metal, location (left main, bifurcation), number and length.
- **3.** **When was it placed and why?** Acute coronary syndrome carries higher risk than stable disease.
- **4.** **How bleeding-prone is the surgery?** Neurosurgery, spinal and posterior eye surgery are high risk; many abdominal, orthopaedic and vascular operations can be done on aspirin.

### Minimum delay before elective surgery

| Situation | Delay |
|---|---|
| Balloon angioplasty alone | About 2 weeks |
| Bare-metal stent | At least 1 month (ideally 3) |
| Drug-eluting stent, stable disease | At least 6 months (3 if surgery is time-sensitive and delay is more harmful, with MDT agreement) |
| Drug-eluting stent after ACS | at least 12 months for elective surgery requiring interruption; selected time-sensitive surgery from 3 months after DES if delay is more harmful |

### Antiplatelet decision

- **Defer elective surgery** until the minimum period is complete.
- **If it cannot wait:** continue aspirin; stop the P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel 5 to 7 days, prasugrel 7–10 days, ticagrelor 3 to 5 days) by joint decision of surgeon, cardiologist and anaesthetist.
- **High thrombotic risk:** consider bridging with IV cangrelor (reversible, short half-life) or a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor under cardiology advice. Heparin does not protect the stent.
- **If clopidogrel must continue:** accept more bleeding, have tranexamic acid and platelets available (platelets work once active metabolite has cleared); neuraxial block requires washout.
- **Restart** the P2Y12 inhibitor within 24 to 48 hours once bleeding is controlled.
- **Environment:** a hospital with a 24-hour cath lab, arterial line, ST monitoring, avoid tachycardia, hypotension and anaemia, postoperative troponin.
- Discuss both risks with the patient and document the decision.

## Intraop

Use ST monitoring and maintain coronary perfusion, oxygenation, haemoglobin and temperature. Agree haemostatic measures and access to rescue PCI. Bridging is exceptional and requires a specialist protocol rather than routine heparin substitution.

### Practical points

Neuraxial and deep nerve blocks need clopidogrel washout of 5 to 7 days, so discuss the anaesthetic plan early. Use of a PPI with clopidogrel should favour pantoprazole over omeprazole. Document who made the decision and the plan for restarting. The patient should know the symptoms of stent thrombosis (chest pain, breathlessness) and where to seek help.

## Postop

Monitor ECG, symptoms, bleeding and haemoglobin, with troponin surveillance where indicated. Restart the P2Y12 inhibitor as soon as haemostasis permits, commonly within 24–48 hours, with any loading dose and neuraxial-catheter plan agreed in advance. Provide a named team responsible for restarting therapy and an urgent PCI escalation pathway.

items.title: 2014.1 Q6: Chest pain in PACU after femoro-popliteal bypass
items.q: A patient is complaining of central chest pain in the post anaesthesia care unit (PACU) following femoro-popliteal artery bypass surgery. Outline the diagnostic criteria for acute myocardial ischaemia on an ECG? (30%) Describe your management of acute myocardial ischemia in PACU in this patient. (70%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2014.1 Q6:** Describe acute ischaemic ECG changes rather than relying on infarction findings such as Q waves. Tailor management to vascular surgery, intraoperative heparin, and the patient’s usual blood pressure; an apparently “normal” pressure may be a substantial fall from baseline.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## ECG criteria for acute ischaemia (30%)

Compare with the preoperative tracing; changes are new and dynamic.

- **ST elevation:** new J-point elevation of 1 mm or more in two contiguous leads (V2 to V3: 2 mm or more in men aged 40 or over, 2.5 mm in men under 40, 1.5 mm in women); or new LBBB with Sgarbossa features.
- **ST depression:** new horizontal or downsloping depression of 0.5 mm or more in two contiguous leads.
- **T-wave change:** new inversion of 1 mm or more in leads with a dominant R wave, hyperacute T waves, or pseudonormalisation of a previously inverted T wave.
- Posterior infarction: ST depression with tall R in V1 to V3. ST elevation in aVR with diffuse depression suggests global subendocardial ischaemia; it is not specific for left-main occlusion.
- Q waves indicate established infarction, not acute ischaemia.

## Management in PACU (70%)

Assume ischaemia is likely in a patient with peripheral vascular disease, but consider PE, dissection, pneumothorax, bleeding and graft problems.

**Immediate:** call for help and inform the surgeon; sit up; monitoring with defibrillator pads; 12-lead ECG (repeat in 15 to 30 minutes); oxygen for SpO2 <90% in ACS, titrated without hyperoxia; large-bore access; titrated opioid analgesia.

**Restore supply and demand balance:**
- Treat tachycardia and hypertension (beta-blocker, GTN if BP allows); avoid and treat hypotension (phenylephrine, noradrenaline).
- Correct anaemia, hypoxia, hypothermia, shivering, electrolytes (K, Mg) and hypovolaemia.
- Check graft and limb perfusion.

**Investigate:** serial high-sensitivity troponin, FBC, electrolytes, gas, chest X-ray, bedside echo for new wall motion abnormality, effusion or dissection.

**Antithrombotic therapy tailored to this patient:** he has a fresh arterial graft and has had heparin. Aspirin is reasonable unless bleeding; further antiplatelets or anticoagulation need the vascular surgeon's agreement.

**Definitive:** urgent cardiology review; primary PCI is preferred for STEMI. Recent major surgery may prohibit fibrinolysis; ESC lists major surgery/trauma/head injury in the preceding month as an absolute contraindication, so check the current applicable contraindication list. Then HDU/ICU, continuous ECG, troponin surveillance, statin and secondary prevention.

## Specific considerations after femoro-popliteal bypass

Intraoperative heparin, vasodilatation and a long operation raise the possibility of bleeding, hypotension and anaemia as contributors. Check the wound and graft pulses. A rising troponin with no symptoms is still myocardial injury and should prompt the same supply and demand review. Beta-blockers are generally preferred, but avoid them if there is hypotension, bradycardia or acute heart failure.

items.title: 2012.2 Q2: Antiplatelets eight months after a drug-eluting stent
items.q: A 75-year-old man presents for right hemicolectomy for an obstructing lesion of the ascending colon that has failed to settle with conservative management. He had a drug-eluting stent placed eight months ago, and is currently on clopidogrel and aspirin. Discuss and justify your plan for perioperative management of his antiplatelet therapy?
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2012.2 Q2:** Balance bleeding, stent occlusion and the feasibility of rescue PCI/revascularisation, including delay or transfer to a suitable centre. The report’s concern about stopping DAPT before 12 months reflects its 2012 context; apply current ACS/chronic-coronary-disease timing rather than a universal historical DES interval.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Preop

### Framing

Stent thrombosis versus surgical bleeding. A DES at 8 months is beyond the 6-month minimum for stable disease (close to the 12 months advised after ACS), so the thrombotic risk has fallen. The obstruction makes the surgery urgent rather than elective, as delay risks perforation and sepsis.

### Factors to weigh

- Urgency and how long surgery can safely wait (can clopidogrel washout of 5 to 7 days be achieved, or is decompression possible as a bridge?).
- The stent: indication (ACS or stable), location (left main, proximal LAD, bifurcation), length, generation.
- Bleeding risk: major abdominal surgery, anaemia from the lesion, age, renal function.
- Rebound hypercoagulability after stopping antiplatelets, and the surgical stress response.
- Availability of 24-hour PCI for rescue.

### Plan and justification

- **1.** **Multidisciplinary decision** (surgeon, cardiologist, anaesthetist, patient), documented.
- **2.** **Continue aspirin** throughout: it protects the stent and bleeding is manageable.
- **3.** **Stop clopidogrel 5 to 7 days before** surgery if the surgery can wait (irreversible binding, platelets regenerate about 10% per day). At 8 months, risk depends on ACS versus chronic-disease PCI, complexity, ventricular/renal function and antiplatelet interruption; do not declare it automatically low.
- **4.** **If surgery cannot wait:** operate on both agents with meticulous haemostasis, tranexamic acid, blood and platelets available (platelets are effective once clopidogrel's active metabolite has cleared), accepting more bleeding.
- **5.** **Bridging** with cangrelor only for very high-risk stents, under cardiology advice.
- **6.** **Anaesthesia:** general anaesthesia with rapid sequence induction for obstruction (neuraxial insertion is avoided with residual clopidogrel effect; apply the 5–7-day interval and other ASRA requirements; use TAP or rectus sheath blocks); arterial line, ST analysis; avoid tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia; continue beta-blocker and statin.
- **7.** **Postop:** HDU, ECG and troponin surveillance, restart clopidogrel at 24 to 48 hours once haemostasis is secure, and an urgent PCI pathway if stent thrombosis occurs.

### Patient communication

Explain the patient-specific risks of stent thrombosis, delay and bleeding, without assuming their relative sizes, and that the plan will be revised if the situation changes. If surgery proceeds on clopidogrel, the surgeon should be told so haemostasis is meticulous, and drains should be checked early. Postoperative ECG and troponin monitoring is advised, with a clear escalation pathway.

## Intraop

Treat this as bowel obstruction requiring aspiration precautions. Use the agreed antiplatelet plan, meticulous haemostasis and blood-conservation measures; maintain coronary perfusion and oxygen supply, monitor ST trends and activate rescue PCI promptly for suspected stent thrombosis.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.

items.title: 2012.2 Q4: Natural history and echo features of aortic stenosis
items.q: 1. What is the natural history of aortic stenosis? (30%) 2. What are the key echocardiographic features in haemodynamically significant aortic stenosis? (70%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2012.2 Q4:** Cover aetiology-dependent natural history, symptom onset and prognosis, then qualitative and quantitative echo findings. Include LV adaptation, raised left-atrial-pressure manifestations, post-stenotic dilatation, late LV/RV changes and diastolic dysfunction, rather than giving valve-area cut-offs alone.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## 1. Natural history (30%)

- **Causes:** age-related calcific degeneration (commonest), congenital bicuspid valve (presents a decade earlier), and rheumatic disease.
- **Long latent phase** of years to decades with slow progression (peak velocity rises about 0.3 m/s per year, valve area falls about 0.1 cm2 per year) while the LV compensates with concentric hypertrophy.
- **Asymptomatic phase:** risk varies; older untreated cohorts reported sudden death around 1%/year, but this does not justify dismissing severe AS.
- **Symptoms are the turning point:** historical untreated cohorts: angina (average survival about 5 years), syncope (about 3 years), heart failure (about 1 to 2 years). Without valve replacement, mortality is about 50% at 2 years after symptom onset. Treatment is surgical or transcatheter (TAVI) valve replacement.
- Late: LV decompensation, pulmonary hypertension, AF, endocarditis. Treatment is surgical or transcatheter valve replacement.

## 2. Key echo features of significant AS (70%)

**Morphology:** thickened, calcified, restricted leaflets with reduced opening; bicuspid valve; post-stenotic aortic dilatation.

**Severity (Doppler):**

| Parameter | Severe AS |
|---|---|
| Peak jet velocity (CW Doppler) | 4 m/s or more |
| Mean gradient | 40 mmHg or more |
| Valve area (continuity equation) | Below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6 cm2/m2) |
| Dimensionless index (LVOT VTI / AV VTI) | Below 0.25 |

**LV and consequences:** concentric LV hypertrophy, preserved EF early then reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction, dilated LA, pulmonary hypertension, associated MR or AR.

**Pitfall: low-flow low-gradient AS.** Valve area below 1.0 cm2 with mean gradient below 40 mmHg. In the classic form (low EF) use **low-dose dobutamine stress echo** to distinguish true from pseudo-severe AS; in the paradoxical form (normal EF, stroke volume index below 35 mL/m2) a CT calcium score supports severity. Gradients depend on flow, so align the beam and measure the LVOT carefully.

## Anaesthetic relevance

Severe AS limits the heart's ability to increase output, so hypotension and tachycardia are poorly tolerated. This is why echo grading matters before surgery: severe symptomatic AS should be treated (valve replacement or balloon valvuloplasty as a bridge) before elective non-cardiac surgery.

Gives quantitative criteria: Vmax 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, AVA below 1.0 cm2, dimensionless index below 0.25

items.title: 2011.2 Q14: Anterior ST elevation on emergence
items.q: A 70-year-old man has undergone radical prostatectomy under general anaesthesia. On emergence he has crushing central chest pain, is restless, and has cold, clammy skin. His blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg, pulse rate 110/minute and SpO2 is 95% on oxygen via a Hudson mask. A twelve-lead ECG shows widespread ST segment elevation across the anterior chest leads. a. Describe your immediate management. (50%) b. What are the treatment priorities for this patient? (50%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2011.2 Q14:** Treat the cause while limiting myocardial damage; assess other causes of hypotension, oxygen supply/demand, haemoglobin, serial ECG/biomarkers, imaging, monitoring and destination. Reperfusion/invasive evaluation and the postoperative anticoagulation dilemma must be explicit.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Diagnosis

Chest pain, shock and anterior ST elevation indicate an **acute anterior MI (LAD) with early cardiogenic shock**: end-organ hypoperfusion (cold, clammy, restless, lactate), not blood pressure alone. Mortality is 40 to 70%, and Emergency revascularisation is central; selected STEMI-shock patients also benefited from Impella CP in DanGer Shock, with more complications. Consider other causes of hypotension and ST change (haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, tamponade, dissection, pneumothorax, takotsubo), but treat as MI.

## a. Immediate management (50%)

- **Call for help** (anaesthetic colleague, cardiologist, ICU); defibrillator pads; full monitoring; arterial line; two large-bore IV cannulae.
- Oxygen to maintain SpO2 94 to 98%; titrated IV opioid for pain.
- **Haemodynamics:** keep MAP at least 65 mmHg with **noradrenaline**; small fluid boluses only if hypovolaemia or bleeding is suspected; avoid nitrates while hypotensive; do not give beta-blockers while in shock.
- **Aspirin** 300 mg chewed/dissolved unless contraindicated, with immediate surgical/cardiology discussion of fresh operative bleeding.
- **Confirm and exclude:** repeat ECG including right-sided and posterior leads, troponin, haemoglobin, electrolytes, gas, chest X-ray, bedside echo (wall motion, RV, effusion, mechanical complication); check wound and drains.

## b. Treatment priorities (50%)

- **1.** **Early reperfusion:** primary PCI is preferred; call the cath lab. **Recent major surgery may prohibit fibrinolysis (ESC: major surgery/trauma/head injury within the previous month is an absolute contraindication)**;  if PCI is unavailable, weigh risks with surgeon and cardiologist.
- **2.** **Antithrombotic therapy balanced against surgical bleeding:** aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor and heparin chosen with cardiologist and surgeon.
- **3.** **Support the circulation:** noradrenaline (first line, titrated, since noradrenaline raises vascular resistance and also has beta activity), dobutamine for low output, and early mechanical support if refractory (IABP up to about 0.8 L/min, Impella 2.5 to 5 L/min, VA-ECMO up to 7 L/min; the least support needed, as complications rise with support).
- **4.** **Treat complications:** VF/VT (defibrillate, amiodarone, correct K and Mg), pulmonary oedema (CPAP or ventilation), mechanical complications.
- **5.** **ICU/CCU admission** and secondary prevention (statin, antiplatelets, beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor when stable).

## Additional points

Arrange primary PCI transfer early because delay worsens outcome; time to reperfusion is the key variable. If the ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V3 only with reciprocal inferior changes, consider an anterior MI with proximal LAD occlusion. Anticoagulants carry a high surgical bleeding risk after radical prostatectomy (pelvic bleeding), so agree the regimen with the urologist. Document the discussion.
