items.title: 2010.2 Q11: Mitral regurgitation with pulmonary hypertension
items.q: A 78-year-old female presents for fixation of a displaced femoral fracture. She has longstanding mitral regurgitation and is known to have a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 60 mmHg. She reports orthopnoea but is not short of breath at rest. (a) What are the issues of concern in your preoperative assessment? (50%) (b) How would you manage pulmonary vascular resistance perioperatively? (50%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2010.2 Q11:** Recognise severe PH, MR and possible biventricular failure, and explain optimisation, specialist input and consent. The fracture itself matters: haemorrhage, pain, cause of the fall and cementing. Better answers used preop/intraop/postop organisation and addressed the trade-off between reducing PVR and preserving SVR/RV perfusion. Historical blanket drug exclusions should be interpreted using current physiology and specialist guidance.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Preop

### a. Preoperative assessment (50%)

- **Mitral regurgitation:** mechanism (primary or secondary), severity (severe: regurgitant fraction 50% or more, orifice area 0.4 cm2 or more, volume 60 mL/beat or more), LV size and EF (EF may appear preserved despite impaired contractile function in MR; ≤60% is a concerning dysfunction threshold in severe primary MR), LA size, AF and anticoagulation. Orthopnoea suggests left-sided congestion.
- **Severe pulmonary hypertension** (mean PAP 60 mmHg): likely post-capillary from MR, but look for a pre-capillary component (lung disease, thromboembolism). Assess **RV size and function** (TAPSE, septal position, TR) and signs of right heart failure.
- **Risk:** individualise by PH group, RV dysfunction, functional class, urgency and operation; historical high-risk series are not a universal estimate. In MR-associated PH, treat high LA pressure and avoid pulmonary vasodilators that worsen oedema.
- **The fracture:** blood loss and hypovolaemia, pain (tachycardia, raised PVR), cause of the fall (syncope, arrhythmia, ischaemia), anaemia, renal function, delirium, and cement or reaming causing **embolisation and a sudden rise in PVR**.
- **Timing:** surgery within 24 to 48 hours; optimise in parallel (diuretics, rate control, oxygen, fluids, early fascia iliaca block).
- Investigations: ECG, chest X-ray, echo, BNP, FBC, electrolytes.
- **Consent and setting:** discuss major cardiac/RV failure risk, postoperative ventilation or intensive care, benefits of timely fixation and realistic alternatives with the patient; involve cardiology/PH and orthogeriatric teams.

### b. Managing PVR — preop principles (part b totals 50%)

In MR-associated postcapillary PH, reduce LA pressure and optimise LV/valve function. Pulmonary vasodilators can worsen pulmonary oedema; use only with specialist haemodynamic guidance. Maintain established PAH treatment when appropriate.

**Principle:** avoid rises in PVR and support the RV, without letting systemic pressure fall.

## Intraop

### b. Managing PVR — intraop

| Measure | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Avoid triggers** | Hypoxia (high FiO2), hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain and light anaesthesia, nitrous oxide, desflurane, large-dose ketamine, high airway pressure; tidal volume 6 mL/kg, plateau below 30 cmH2O, PEEP titrated to recruitment and RV loading, without an absolute 10 cmH2O ceiling, ventilate near FRC |
| **Pulmonary vasodilators** | Inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol (selective), sildenafil, milrinone; avoid IV vasodilators that drop SVR |
| **Support the RV** | Low-dose vasopressin (relatively less pulmonary effect, not universally PVR-neutral) or noradrenaline titrated to perfusion and RV response to maintain systemic perfusion and RV coronary driving pressure; SBP >PASP is not an absolute target and preserve RV coronary perfusion; dobutamine 2 to 5 or milrinone 0.25 to 0.5 microgram/kg/min for RV failure; amiodarone for arrhythmia; maintain sinus rhythm; avoid both hypovolaemia and overload |

**Monitoring:** arterial line, CVP, TOE for RV function (PAC is selected for complex/refractory cases rather than used routinely).

**Technique:** fascia iliaca or femoral block with careful titrated neuraxial or a haemodynamically stable GA (opioid, vasopressor ready, low-dose volatile). In MR, forward flow is helped by a normal to high heart rate (80 to 90) and low-normal afterload. Avoid excessive fluid (the RV dilates, the septum shifts and LV filling falls). Early surgery is still preferred for hip fractures, with stabilisation and planning in parallel.

## Postop

### b. Managing PVR — postop

ICU/HDU, oxygen and effective multimodal analgesia; prevent hypoventilation, acidosis, hypothermia and sympathetic surges. Continue established pulmonary-hypertension treatment where appropriate to the PH group, with specialist oversight; MR-related PH does not justify routine PAH therapy. Monitor for cement/embolisation-related RV deterioration, arrhythmia, bleeding and pulmonary oedema.


Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.

items.title: 2010.1 Q6: HOCM for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: A 40 year old man with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) presents for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. a. Describe the principles of intraoperative haemodynamic management for this patient. (40%) b. How would you manage hypotension post induction of general anaesthesia in this patient? (60%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2010.1 Q6:** Part (b), worth 60%, needs a differential and simultaneous diagnosis/treatment, not repetition of haemodynamic goals. Include crisis escalation, rhythm treatment, oxygen supply/demand, echo and, if surgery has begun, desufflation or reversal of head-up positioning when contributing to instability.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## a. Principles of intraoperative management (40%)

Dynamic LVOT obstruction (SAM) is worsened by **low preload, low SVR, high contractility and tachycardia**. Before the case, assess symptoms, echo (gradient at rest and with Valsalva, SAM, MR), rhythm, drugs (continue beta-blocker or verapamil) and any ICD.

**Goals: adequate filling without congestion, controlled rate, preserved perfusion.**
- **Adequate filling:** maintain euvolaemia without congestion, avoid dehydration and venodilators.
- **Preserve systemic perfusion without excessive vasoconstriction:** phenylephrine or vasopressin.
- **Slow heart rate** (50 to 70) and **low contractility:** adequate analgesia and depth; avoid inotropes, ephedrine and ketamine.
- **Sinus rhythm:** treat AF early.

**Technique:** arterial line before induction, phenylephrine infusion ready, slow titrated induction, avoid light anaesthesia.

**Laparoscopy:** insufflation raises SVR, but raised intra-abdominal pressure and head-up tilt reduce venous return, and CO2 absorption causes sympathetic stimulation. Use slow insufflation, low pressure (10 to 12 mmHg), modest tilt and correction of demonstrated volume deficit; watch for hypotension at desufflation.

## b. Hypotension after induction (60%)

**Mechanism:** loss of preload and SVR increases the LVOT gradient and reduces cardiac output.

**Differential:** worsening obstruction (commonest), ischaemia, arrhythmia (AF, VT), anaphylaxis, bleeding, tension pneumothorax, equipment or drug error.

**Management:**
- **1.** Call for help, 100% oxygen, check circuit, capnography and rhythm.
- **2.** **Reduce or stop the volatile agent.**
- **3.** **Alpha agonist:** phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms boluses then infusion, or vasopressin.
- **4.** **Reassessed small fluid bolus if underfilled**, with the alpha agonist; use leg raise or reverse head-up positioning when appropriate. If insufflation has begun and contributes to collapse, ask the surgeon to release pneumoperitoneum.
- **5.** Slow the heart rate (esmolol) once pressure is restored; ensure adequate anaesthesia.
- **6.** **Avoid** ephedrine, adrenaline, dobutamine, nitrates and IABP.
- **7.** Confirm with TOE (SAM, gradient, volume status); cardiovert AF/VT; defibrillate if VF. Inotropes can precipitate pulmonary oedema and collapse.
- **8.** If refractory, escalate vasopressors, consider VA-ECMO, and postpone surgery.

## Additional points

Elective surgery in HOCM should be performed where invasive monitoring, TOE, vasopressors and ICU are available. Avoid premedication that causes anxiety and tachycardia. During laparoscopy, release of pneumoperitoneum can cause hypotension, so be ready with phenylephrine and keep preload up. After surgery, continue beta-blocker and monitor in a high-dependency area if the gradient is severe.

items.title: 2009.2 Q1: Clopidogrel and bare-metal stents in trauma laparotomy
items.q: There is a 70-year-old female on your emergency list for an urgent laparotomy. She was involved in a motor vehicle accident this morning and sustained multiple trauma. Her medications include clopidogrel to cover the insertion of bare metal stents into her coronary arteries 2 months ago. 1. Describe the mechanism and duration of action of clopidogrel. (30%) 2. What are the major considerations for the perioperative period in view of the patient's stent? (70%)
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2009.2 Q1:** Apply the answer to this elderly patient with multiple trauma: systematic trauma assessment, bleeding from irreversible platelet inhibition, and stent thrombosis if antiplatelets are stopped or reversed. Quoting stent guidelines without applying them to the injuries did not earn adequate credit. The report’s approximate five-day duration refers to functional recovery; irreversible inhibition persists for the affected platelet’s lifespan.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## 1. Clopidogrel (30%)

- An oral thienopyridine **prodrug**. About 85% is hydrolysed to an inactive metabolite; the remainder is activated in the liver (CYP2C19 and others) to an active thiol metabolite.
- The active metabolite **irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor** on platelets, preventing ADP-mediated activation of the GP IIb/IIIa complex and platelet aggregation.
- **Duration:** the effect lasts for the life of the platelet (7 to 10 days), not the drug half-life. Platelet function recovers about 10% per day; stop 5 to 7 days before elective surgery. CYP2C19 variants and omeprazole reduce the effect.

## 2. Perioperative considerations (70%)

### Preop

Two competing problems apply to **this patient**: life-threatening trauma needing haemorrhage control now, and a recent stent needing antiplatelet protection.

**Trauma:** systematic EMST/ATLS approach (airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation with haemorrhage control, disability, exposure). Damage-control principles: avoid hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, massive transfusion protocol with tranexamic acid, rapid sequence induction with haemodynamically stable drugs, arterial line, large-bore access, warming.

**Bleeding risk from clopidogrel:** the platelet defect cannot be reversed quickly. Platelet transfusion works only once the active metabolite has cleared, so give platelets for bleeding with several hours' separation from the last dose; use TXA when indicated and consider desmopressin only in selected circumstances; routine viscoelastic tests do not measure clopidogrel effect adequately. Do not delay life-saving surgery for washout.

**Stent thrombosis risk:** bare-metal stents at 2 months are beyond the minimum 1 month of DAPT, so the highest-risk early window has passed, but stopping still requires indication-, anatomy- and bleeding-based assessment. **Continue aspirin** if bleeding allows, and restart antiplatelets as soon as bleeding is controlled. Trauma and surgery are prothrombotic, so watch for ECG change, chest pain or unexplained hypotension (stent thrombosis) and ensure access to 24-hour PCI.

### Intraop

**Anaesthetic plan:** arterial line, 5-lead ECG with ST analysis, avoid tachycardia, hypotension and anaemia, ICU postoperatively, troponin surveillance, avoid neuraxial techniques while the antiplatelet effect and coagulopathy persist.

## Additional points

Aspirin continuation reduces the stent risk but adds to bleeding, so the decision is individual. Stent-related risk persists beyond one month and depends on ACS indication, anatomy and antiplatelet interruption. After haemorrhage control, restart aspirin within 24 hours and clopidogrel within a few days once bleeding risk allows, after discussion with cardiology. Avoid hypothermia, acidosis and calcium deficiency, which worsen coagulopathy and platelet function.

### Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.

items.title: 2009.1 Q9: Beta-blockers before femoro-popliteal bypass
items.q: A 65-year-old male presents in your preadmission clinic. He is scheduled for femoral-popliteal bypass surgery for peripheral vascular disease in 4 days time. He has ischaemic rest pain in his leg. Evaluate the usefulness of initiating therapy with beta-blockers to reduce the incidence of perioperative myocardial infarction in this man.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2009.1 Q9:** The report accepted either starting or not starting beta-blockade if the reasoning addressed this patient. It expected appraisal of MI benefit versus mortality/stroke, contraindications, dose, four-day lead-in and monitoring. Current recommendations and later concerns about DECREASE data supersede older blanket indications and contraindication lists.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Context

Femoro-popliteal bypass in a patient with rest pain signals substantial vascular and cardiac risk; the report used a historical ≥5% estimate, but a contemporary individual estimate requires the planned procedure, comorbidities and a validated risk tool. Perioperative MI is usually a supply-demand event driven by tachycardia and hypertension, so slowing the heart should help in theory. He is not already on a beta-blocker (existing therapy should be continued).

## Evidence

| Evidence | Findings | Appraisal |
|---|---|---|
| Mangano 1996 (atenolol) | Reduced cardiac events and mortality | Small |
| DECREASE-I, IV (bisoprolol) | Fewer cardiac deaths and MIs in high-risk vascular patients | Data integrity concerns; unreliable |
| **POISE (2008)**, 8,351 patients, metoprolol CR 100 mg started 2 to 4 hours before surgery | Fewer MIs but **more deaths and strokes**, with hypotension and bradycardia | Large and well designed; criticised for high fixed dose started on the day of surgery |

Meta-analyses without DECREASE show fewer MIs but more death and stroke when beta-blockers are started late and at high dose.

## Evaluation for this patient

- **Potential benefit:** fewer MIs, offset by hypotension/bradycardia; benefit of prophylactic initiation in an individual patient is uncertain.
- **Harm:** hypotension, bradycardia and stroke, plus bronchospasm; bleeding or sepsis impairs compensatory tachycardia.
- **Timing:** 4 days is better than day-of-surgery but too short for careful titration. Guidelines favour starting at least a week before, low dose, titrated to a heart rate of 60 to 80 with SBP above 100.
- Contraindications/cautions: shock, symptomatic bradycardia, advanced AV block without pacing, hypotension and active bronchospasm; stable COPD or a remote stroke alone is not an absolute contraindication. Individualise cardioselective beta-blockade.

## Conclusion

Do not start beta-blockade solely for prophylaxis four days before surgery. If there is a new independent cardiac indication, discuss whether time permits safe titration; avoid high fixed-dose or day-of-surgery initiation. Continue established therapy and optimise other triggers.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.

items.title: 2007.1 Q8: Using the ECG to monitor for ischaemia
items.q: Describe how the ECG should be used to monitor for intraoperative myocardial ischemia in a patient with ischemic heart disease.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2007.1 Q8:** Balance technical and clinical use of the ECG. The report allocated 1 mark to clinical context/other monitors, 2 to technical considerations and 7 to clinical interpretation and lead choice. It favoured multiple leads (an inferior lead plus two precordial leads when available) and warned against spending the answer on general IHD management. Historical monitor thresholds differ from formal diagnostic 12-lead criteria.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Role

The ECG is the standard continuous monitor for ischaemia. It is used **with other monitors** (arterial pressure, heart rate, SpO2, TOE where available) and interpreted in clinical context. It detects only some ischaemic episodes.

## Technical use

- Good skin preparation and accurate electrode placement (V5 at the anterior axillary line level with V4; misplacement over 2 to 3 cm changes morphology; Mason-Likar limb placement shifts ST change into the inferior leads); record a **baseline before induction** and compare with the preoperative 12-lead.
- Select the **diagnostic filter (0.05 Hz)**, not the monitoring filter (0.5 Hz), which distorts the ST segment.
- Use ST-segment trending and alarms, and review the trace manually.

## Lead selection

| Leads | Approximate sensitivity |
|---|---|
| Lead II alone | About 33% |
| V5 alone | About 75% |
| II plus V5 | About 80% |
| V4 plus V5 | About 90% |
| II, V4 and V5 | About 96% |

Use a 5-lead system with an inferior lead and V4/V5. Practical lead selection includes **II plus V5 (or V4)** for general anaesthesia, **V4 plus V5** if at high risk of ischaemia, and II, V4 and V5 if three leads can be shown. If only one precordial lead is available, choose the one that best matches the patient's known ischaemic territory. The CM5 lead (right arm electrode on the manubrium, left arm at V5, lead I displayed) is an alternative, but recent supporting data are lacking.

## Interpretation

- **Criteria:** distinguish monitor ST alarms (often ≥1 mm depression) from formal diagnostic 12-lead criteria: new horizontal/downsloping ST depression ≥0.5 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads; J-point elevation ≥1 mm except V2–V3 (men ≥40: ≥2 mm; men <40: ≥2.5 mm; women: ≥1.5 mm), without confounding LVH/BBB. New LBBB alone is not diagnostic; use validated Sgarbossa/modified criteria in context. T-wave changes, arrhythmia and conduction changes are supportive but nonspecific.
- **Limitations:** LBBB, pacing, LVH, digoxin, electrolyte change, hypothermia and positioning; posterior and circumflex ischaemia may be missed.

## Action if changes occur

- **1.** Confirm they are real (electrodes, filter, rhythm).
- **2.** Check supply and demand: blood pressure, heart rate, haemoglobin, oxygenation, depth of anaesthesia, volume.
- **3.** Treat the cause (vasopressor, beta-blocker, GTN, transfusion, oxygen).
- **4.** Consider TOE and a 12-lead ECG; follow with troponin on days 1 to 3.

items.title: 2006.2 Q11: Beta-blockers to prevent perioperative MI
items.q: Critically evaluate the use of Beta blockers in the perioperative period to prevent myocardial infarction.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis — 2006.2 Q11:** Identify which patient groups should receive treatment and critically assess the evidence; listing physiological benefits alone was insufficient. POISE (2008), DECREASE-IV and later guidelines post-date this examination: they are included below to make this a current revision answer, not attributed to the 2006 examiner report.

> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

## Rationale

Perioperative MI is mostly a supply-demand event driven by tachycardia, hypertension and the catecholamine surge. Beta-blockers lower heart rate and contractility, lengthen diastole and may stabilise plaque, so they should reduce ischaemia and MI.

## Evidence (critically appraised)

| Study | Findings | Appraisal |
|---|---|---|
| Mangano 1996 (atenolol) | Reduced mortality and ischaemia | Small, single centre |
| DECREASE-I and IV (bisoprolol) | Fewer cardiac events in high-risk vascular patients | Data integrity concerns; unreliable |
| **POISE (2008)**, metoprolol CR 100 mg on the day of surgery | Fewer MIs but **more deaths and strokes**, more hypotension and bradycardia | Large, well designed; fixed high dose, no titration, same-day start |
| Meta-analyses | Fewer MIs but more death and stroke when started on the day of surgery | Harm from late, high-dose, un-titrated use |
| Observational data | Benefit in high-risk (RCRI 3 or more), harm in low-risk patients | Confounded |

## Critical points

- Benefit from initiating perioperative beta-blockade is uncertain; high calculated risk alone does not mandate initiation. Continue chronic treatment; if a new independent indication exists, start optimally >7 days before surgery and titrate to tolerance.
- Harm arises from hypotension, bradycardia and loss of compensatory tachycardia in bleeding or sepsis, leading to stroke and death.
- Trials differ in drug, dose, timing and population.
- **Withdrawal** of chronic beta-blockers causes rebound tachycardia and ischaemia.

## Which patients?

- **Already on beta-blockers:** continue.
- **Known IHD, inducible ischaemia or high RCRI with high-risk surgery:** if independently indicated, start optimally >7 days (ideally longer) before surgery at low dose, titrated to heart rate 60 to 80 and SBP above 100.
- **Low risk, or day-of-surgery start:** no benefit and risk of harm; avoid.
- Contraindications/cautions: shock, symptomatic bradycardia, advanced AV block without pacing, hypotension and active bronchospasm; stable COPD or a remote stroke alone is not an absolute contraindication. Individualise cardioselective beta-blockade.

## Conclusion

Beta-blockers reduce non-fatal MI but increase death and stroke when started inappropriately. Continue them in current users and start them selectively, early, low and titrated, in high-risk patients. Avoiding hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia and hypothermia, and using statins, matter at least as much.

## Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.
rubric: Gives the physiological rationale (reduced demand, longer diastole)
Critically evaluates the evidence (Mangano, DECREASE integrity, POISE benefit and harm)
Explains why POISE found harm (dose, timing, hypotension)
Identifies which patients should receive beta-blockers and which should not
Discusses dose, timing and titration, and the danger of day-of-surgery initiation
Lists contraindications and reaches a conclusion

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
> The following are the principal evidence and teaching references used to construct the chapters independently. Older BJA Education articles remain useful for physiology and clinical frameworks; when thresholds or medication advice differ, the **newer guideline controls the contemporary recommendation**. Guideline recommendations may differ legitimately across countries and societies; the relevant differences are identified in the chapters. Sources are cited here using the same bracketed reference IDs embedded in the notes.

## Current perioperative, cardiology and anaesthesia guidelines

- **R1 —** [2026 ACC/AHA perioperative cardiovascular management guideline (reaffirmed 2024 guideline)](https://www.jacc.org/doi/full/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017). Primary reference for risk stratification, cardiac testing, PCI-to-surgery timing, perioperative antiplatelets, beta-blockers, BP targets and MINS surveillance. [Official reaffirmation notice](https://professional.heart.org/en/science-news/2026-guideline-for-perioperative-cardiovascular-management-for-noncardiac-surgery).
- **R2 —** [Association of Anaesthetists/British and Irish Hypertension Society: peri-operative BP (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082). Guidance on measured BP, acceptable elective-surgery thresholds, postoperative BP and renin–angiotensin inhibitor continuation. Particularly important where it differs from ACC/AHA policy.
- **R3 —** [Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026)](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/universal-definition-myocardial-infarction/). New acute injury/MI taxonomy, objective ischaemia criteria, troponin interpretation; older trials still use type-1/type-2 terminology.
- **R6 —** [National Heart Foundation of Australia/CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndromes Guideline (2025)](https://www.heartfoundation.au/for-professionals/acs-guideline). Australasian recognition, oxygen and antithrombotic management, acute coronary occlusion patterns, reperfusion and secondary prevention. [Peer-reviewed publication](https://doi.org/10.5694/mja2.70127).
- **R8 —** [2026 ESC guidelines for the management of heart failure](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag100). Updated HF phenotype definitions (HFrEF LVEF <50%, HFpEF ≥50%), stages, treatment, decongestion and acute deterioration; understand that older trials use older EF eligibility bands.
- **R9 —** [ASE 2025 Recommendations for evaluating LV diastolic function](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.echo.2025.03.011). Integrated echo interpretation; E/e′, e′, LA and pulmonary variables must be interpreted together, not as isolated diagnostic thresholds.
- **R11 —** [ESC/EACTS 2025 guidelines on valvular heart disease](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194). Severity interpretation, intervention indications, treatment selection and antithrombotic issues for native and prosthetic valves.
- **R13 —** [CHEST 2022 guideline: perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chest.2022.07.025). Perioperative VKA/DOAC decisions and evidence limitations regarding bridging, including in mechanical-valve populations.
- **R14 —** [ASRA Evidence-Based Guidelines, fifth edition (2025)](https://asra.com/the-asra-family/special-interest-groups/neuromodulation-sig/neuromodulation-sig-article-item/guidelines/2025/01/31/regional-anesthesia-in-the-patient-receiving-antithrombotic-or-thrombolytic-therapy-american-society-of-regional-anesthesia-and-pain-medicine-evidence-based-guidelines-%28fifth-edition%29). Separate neuraxial/deep-block timing from general surgical bleeding timing for antiplatelets and anticoagulants.
- **R16 —** [2024 AHA/ACC guideline for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.014). Assessment of obstruction, gradients, symptoms, myosin inhibitors and sudden-death/ICD risk.

- **Hypertension (end-organ damage table) —** [2018 ESC/ESH guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/39/33/3021/5079119). Criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, arterial stiffness, albuminuria and retinopathy, with the cardiac consequences of hypertension.
- **Hypertension (end-organ damage table) —** [2023 ESH guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension](https://iris.unibs.it/bitstream/11379/603005/1/2023_ESH_Guidelines_for_the_management_of_arterial%20HT.pdf). Current organ-damage criteria and why damage in any organ raises risk.
- **Hypertension (brain) —** [White matter lesions and cognitive impairment as silent cerebral disease in hypertension](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5917262/). Review of silent cerebral small-vessel disease, stroke and dementia in hypertension.

## BJA Education — targeted reading with purpose

- **R4 —** [Hughes C, Ackland G, Shelley B. Perioperative myocardial injury. BJA Education (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.06.001). Best for the diagnostic distinction between injury, MINS and MI, postoperative surveillance and the limitations of intervention evidence.
- **R5 —** [Tait A, Howell SJ. Preoperative hypertension: perioperative implications and management. BJA Education (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.07.002). Explains hypertension physiology, target-organ effects and assessment. Use the 2026 guidelines for the latest postponement and ACEi/ARB policies.
- **R7 —** [Milne B, Dalzell J, Kunst G. Cardiogenic shock. BJA Education (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.01.006). For shock phenotypes, haemodynamic logic and selection of drug versus mechanical support; trials published later refine device decisions.
- **R10 —** [Shah K, Sabharwal N, Day J. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: implications for anaesthesia. BJA Education (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.02.003). Particularly useful for diastolic dysfunction, fluid sensitivity and why a normal EF does not imply low risk.
- **R12 —** [Holmes K, Gibbison B, Vohra H. Mitral valve disease and anaesthesia. BJA Education (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw032). Strong explanation of how stenosis and regurgitation differ, including atrial rhythm and pulmonary vascular consequences. Supplement with newer guideline thresholds.
- **R15 —** [Ibrahim M, Sharma S. Cardiomyopathy and anaesthesia. BJA Education (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkx022). Core physiology of dilated, hypertrophic and restrictive phenotypes and why induction/afterload management differs.

## ANZCA curriculum, Blue Book and examiner reports

- **C1 —** ANZCA anaesthesia training programme curriculum, Appendix Five: Final Examination learning outcomes. The user-provided **training program curriculum.pdf** is the authoritative wording; Set 11 selections and priorities come from the uploaded **Prioritised LEarning Sets(3).xlsx**. [ANZCA training programme](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program).
- **B1 —** [Kim and Lau. B-lines and beyond: Lung ultrasound for the perioperative clinician. Australasian Anaesthesia (ANZCA Blue Book, 2025)](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1378). Useful for the ultrasound interpretation of interstitial syndrome, distinguishing diffuse B-lines from a specific diagnosis and linking lung findings to cardiac and respiratory management. [Blue Book home](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29).
- **E1 —** ANZCA Final Examination Chair’s Report 2022.2, supplied in this project. The coronary-stent/antiplatelet anaesthesia viva and other cardiac scenarios illustrate the expectation of practical risk assessment, drug strategy and management of ischaemia. [ANZCA trainee/exam resources](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-trainee-toolkit).
- **E2 —** ANZCA Final Examination Chair’s Report 2023.1, supplied in this project. Includes the mechanical-valve-in-pregnancy SAQ and the importance of haemodynamic and anticoagulation specifics. [ANZCA trainee/exam resources](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-trainee-toolkit).
- **E3 —** ANZCA Final Examination Chair’s Reports 2024.1, 2025.2 and 2026.1, supplied in this project. Used to target severity/stability assessment, investigational interpretation, optimisation, valve disease and high-risk perioperative cardiac problems. [ANZCA exam resources](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-and-pathways/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-trainee-toolkit).

> **Scope and verification note.** The document deliberately follows the nine Set 11 master-workbook LO rows; associated shared learning outcomes are addressed only for their Set 11 components. The Blue Book chapter above is a specific confirmed ANZCA chapter; other recommendations come from the linked guidelines and original studies. Reference titles and outcomes are paraphrased for teaching rather than copied verbatim. Recommendations may require local protocol adaptation and clinical judgement.

## Evidence and source key (Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content)

Clinical review: November 2026. Sources below support the topic corrections; no claim is made that every chapter or entire guideline was reviewed cover to cover. Numerical teaching targets require clinical context. Historical labels and estimates are distinguished from current recommendations. Aortic-dissection management remains in Set 14; RV/PH/transplant/VAD prompts are retained as supporting cross-set practice rather than a new LO allocation.

- [Perioperative cardiac assessment, PCI timing and drug continuation — AHA/ACC 2024](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/09/23/04/15/2024-aha-acc-perioperative-guideline-gl)
- [Perioperative BP — AOA/BIHS 2026 (distinguish UK thresholds from local policy)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12893837/)
- [Myocardial injury — Hughes, Ackland, Shelley. BJA Education 2024;24:352–360](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11522720/)
- [MI classification — Fifth Universal Definition 2026](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/universal-definition-myocardial-infarction/)
- [ACS — Australian guideline 2025](https://www.heartfoundation.org.au/for-professionals/acs-guideline)
- [HF — ESC 2026; older EF categories remain relevant to historical trial entry criteria](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/heart-failure)
- [HFpEF anaesthesia — Shah, Sabharwal, Day. BJA Education 2024;24:155–163](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11026937/)
- [Diastolic assessment — ASE 2025](https://www.asecho.org/guideline/left-ventricular-diastolic-function-by-echo/)
- [Valve intervention — ESC/EACTS 2025](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/)
- [Pregnancy, valves and cardiomyopathy — ESC 2025](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/cardiovascular-diseases-during-pregnancy-management-of/)
- [Neuraxial antithrombotic intervals — ASRA fifth edition 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/)
- [Mechanical-valve bridging — CHEST 2022 (compare selected high-risk AHA/ACC exceptions)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35964704/)
- [RV imaging — ASE 2025](https://www.asecho.org/guideline/right-heart-in-adults-pulmonary-hypertension/)
- [Shock after ACS — Milne, Dalzell, Kunst. BJA Education 2023;23:172–181](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140595/)
- [Transcatheter mitral repair — BJA Education 2023;23:189–195](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140472/)
- [ANZCA Blue Book archive — use chapter titles quoted in each question; older drug intervals and pressure thresholds are superseded where indicated](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

items.title: 37. Infective endocarditis with new valve regurgitation and heart failure
items.q: A 57-year-old with persistent Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia develops a new murmur, pulmonary oedema and PR prolongation. Discuss the diagnosis, complications and management of suspected infective endocarditis, including anaesthetic considerations if urgent valve surgery is required.
items.a:
### Recognition and physiological problem

Infective endocarditis (IE) involves infection of the endocardial surface, usually a native or prosthetic valve. In this patient, bacteraemia plus new valve dysfunction makes IE likely. Pulmonary oedema suggests acute severe regurgitation; **new PR prolongation or AV block raises concern for perivalvular extension/abscess**, particularly with aortic infection. Neither sign alone establishes the diagnosis.

Complications include valve destruction and heart failure, systemic emboli (stroke, splenic/renal infarction, limb ischaemia), septic pulmonary emboli with right-sided infection, perivalvular abscess/fistula, conduction block, persistent sepsis, kidney injury and infected arterial aneurysms. Neurological injury may affect surgical timing and the safety of anticoagulation for bypass.

### Preop

- **Stabilise and involve the team:** assess airway, breathing, perfusion and lactate; seek early cardiology, cardiac surgery, infectious diseases/microbiology and ICU input. This is an urgent Endocarditis Team problem, not a routine elective assessment.
- **Microbiology:** obtain multiple peripheral blood-culture sets, ideally three before antibiotics when feasible. Do not delay effective treatment in an unstable septic patient merely to achieve a sampling interval. Start local empiric IV therapy after cultures, then tailor to organism, susceptibility, valve type, renal function and source; involve microbiology for persistent or culture-negative infection.
- **Imaging and diagnosis:** urgent TTE, with TOE for suspected left-sided/prosthetic infection, inadequate images or complications. Persistent suspicion after a negative study requires repeat or additional imaging. Use the current diagnostic framework (e.g. 2023 Duke-ISCVID/ESC criteria); combine microbiology, imaging and clinical findings rather than relying on a murmur or vegetation alone.
- Assess valve lesion, LV/RV function, congestion, pulmonary pressure, rhythm and organ dysfunction. ECG/telemetry, blood count, renal/electrolyte/liver tests and coagulation guide preparation. Image neurological or other embolic complications according to findings; do not assume all altered consciousness is sepsis.
- **Surgery:** the three principal indications are heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection and prevention of embolism in selected patients. Refractory pulmonary oedema/shock may require emergency surgery; other urgent indications need prompt specialist assessment. Do not wait for completion of antibiotics when a surgical indication exists. Intracranial haemorrhage or major stroke requires individual multidisciplinary timing.
- Correct hypoxaemia, severe electrolyte disturbance and anaemia where possible. Arrange blood products, pacing capability, invasive monitoring and postoperative ICU. Discuss the risks of sepsis, embolism, organ failure and prolonged support.

### Intraop

The dominant lesion determines the haemodynamic plan. Acute severe MR/AR generally requires preserving forward output, avoiding marked bradycardia and excessive afterload, and avoiding both underfilling and congestion. **A septic, hypotensive patient may still need vasopressors**; unqualified vasodilation is unsafe.

Use a titrated induction with vasoactive support prepared; consider arterial monitoring before induction when feasible. Avoid hypoxaemia, acidosis and large abrupt changes in preload/SVR. TOE defines lesion severity, ventricular function and complications and assesses the repair/replacement. Anticipate conduction block, difficult separation from bypass, vasoplegia and bleeding. Coordinate antibiotics, renal protection and coagulation management with the cardiac team.

### Postop

ICU care includes haemodynamic/ventilatory support, rhythm and pacing surveillance, renal and neurological assessment, and review for residual infection. Continue the organism-directed antibiotic course and obtain follow-up cultures as indicated. Agree antithrombotics after valve intervention according to valve type, bleeding and neurological complications. Plan follow-up, source control, oral health and prevention advice.

**Pitfall:** treatment of active IE, routine surgical prophylaxis and future IE prophylaxis are different decisions. Apply NZ/Australian prevention guidance to the cardiac condition and procedure; “all valve disease needs prophylaxis” is incorrect.

### Self-marking checklist

- Recognises IE from bacteraemia plus new valve dysfunction and identifies acute regurgitation/heart failure
- Recognises new conduction delay as a warning of perivalvular extension
- Obtains cultures without delaying urgent antibiotics in an unstable patient
- Uses TTE/TOE and integrated diagnostic criteria; a negative initial study does not always exclude IE
- Covers cardiac, embolic, neurological, septic and renal complications
- Gives the three main surgical indications and distinguishes emergency from urgent assessment
- Tailors anaesthesia to valve physiology, sepsis and ventricular function, with pacing/TOE/ICU planning
- Covers postoperative antibiotics, organ surveillance, antithrombotics and prevention advice

**Sources:** [Charlesworth et al. Infective endocarditis. BJA Education 2023;23:144–152](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10028394/); [ESC endocarditis guideline 2023](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/endocarditis/); [NZ Heart Foundation IE prevention guidance](https://www.heartfoundation.org.nz/resources/prevention-of-infective-endocarditis).

items.title: 38. Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema in PACU
items.q: A 68-year-old develops a blood pressure of 225/125 mmHg, chest discomfort and acute breathlessness in PACU. Explain how you distinguish a hypertensive emergency from severe hypertension without acute organ injury, and outline your management.
items.a:
### Definition and immediate priorities

A **hypertensive emergency is hypertension with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage**. The BP number alone does not define it: the rate of rise, baseline pressure and clinical findings matter. Severe asymptomatic hypertension without acute injury generally requires reassessment and controlled longer-term treatment, not reflex IV normalisation.

This patient's chest symptoms and breathlessness raise concern for ACS and hypertensive acute heart failure/pulmonary oedema. Other possibilities include pain/anxiety with unrelated PE, aspiration or pneumothorax. Do not assume hypertension explains all symptoms.

### Preop — baseline and reversible causes

Review the preoperative BP, usual antihypertensives, cardiovascular/renal disease and the anaesthetic record. Check for omitted beta-blocker/clonidine, inadequate analgesia, agitation, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, shivering, urinary retention and iatrogenic sympathomimetics. Correcting a trigger is necessary but does not replace treatment of established organ injury. Defer any further elective procedure while an emergency is investigated and stabilised.

### Intraop — immediate perioperative/PACU treatment

- **1.** **Call for help and assess ABC.** Sit upright if appropriate, monitor ECG/SpO2 and repeat BP with a correct cuff; consider an arterial line for titrated IV treatment. Assess work of breathing, perfusion, mental status and urine output. Give oxygen for hypoxaemia and establish IV access.
- **2.** **Look for acute organ injury:** ECG and serial troponin for ischaemia; bedside heart/lung ultrasound and chest imaging for pulmonary oedema; renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis and blood count. Neurological symptoms require focused examination and appropriate brain imaging. Fundoscopy may identify haemorrhage/papilloedema where feasible. Investigation must not delay stabilisation.
- **3.** **Treat the phenotype.** For hypertensive cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, use titrated IV GTN when appropriate and early CPAP/NIV if tolerated; intubate if ventilation/airway protection fails. Give loop diuretic when congestion/volume excess is present. Abrupt fluid redistribution can produce pulmonary oedema without major total-body fluid gain, so diuresis alone is insufficient.
- **4.** **If ACS is suspected**, reduce myocardial workload while maintaining coronary perfusion and activate the ACS pathway, including cardiology and a bleeding-aware antithrombotic/reperfusion plan. Avoid reflex tachycardia. Beta-blockade may suit selected hypertensive ischaemic patients but is unsafe as a reflex treatment in acute decompensated failure, shock or important bradycardia/block.
- **5.** **Choose a titratable drug and target.** GTN suits the cardiac presentation; nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol may suit other phenotypes, subject to availability and contraindications. Avoid sublingual immediate-release nifedipine and uncontrolled bolus-driven overshoot.

### How quickly should pressure fall?

Use condition-specific targets. A common framework for an emergency without a special target is an initial MAP reduction of **no more than about 20–25% over the first hour**, followed by slower reduction if stable. This is not a universal prescription: pulmonary oedema/ACS, stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, pregnancy and acute aortic syndromes require their own pathways. Acute aortic-dissection management is covered in Set 14.

Chronic hypertension can shift autoregulation; excessive reduction may cause cerebral, coronary or renal hypoperfusion. Reassess symptoms, perfusion and organ function rather than treating the monitor to a “normal” number.

### Postop

Admit to a monitored area/HDU/ICU according to respiratory support, IV drug requirement and organ injury. Continue ECG/troponin, renal and fluid-balance review; identify secondary causes when indicated. Transition to oral therapy and restart omitted medicines when safe. Document the diagnosis, revised medication plan and follow-up BP assessment.

### Self-marking checklist

- Defines emergency by acute organ injury rather than a BP threshold alone
- Confirms the measurement and checks perioperative reversible causes
- Investigates cardiac, neurological and renal injury without delaying stabilisation
- Treats pulmonary oedema with respiratory support and appropriate vasodilation; individualises diuresis
- Recognises ACS and balances treatment against surgical bleeding
- Selects titratable therapy, names relevant contraindications and avoids rapid uncontrolled lowering
- Explains the usual initial reduction framework and condition-specific exceptions
- Plans monitored postoperative care, oral transition and follow-up

**Sources:** [Davies et al. Hypertensive emergencies. BJA Education 2024;24:371–380](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11522727/); [NICE NG136, severe hypertension and same-day assessment](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations); [Australian ACS guideline 2025](https://www.heartfoundation.org.au/for-professionals/acs-guideline). This question concerns acute organ injury, not elective cancellation thresholds.

items.title: 41. Coronary blood flow: determinants, regulation and the effects of AS and LVH
items.q: Explain the determinants and regulation of coronary blood flow. How are they altered by aortic stenosis and left ventricular hypertrophy, and how does this influence perioperative management?
items.a:
### Determinants of flow

Coronary blood flow reflects the pressure gradient across the coronary circulation divided by vascular resistance, modified by phasic external compression. The LV myocardium already extracts a high proportion of delivered oxygen at rest; increased oxygen demand is met mainly by increasing flow rather than greatly increasing extraction.

| Determinant | Explanation and clinical implication |
|---|---|
| **Driving pressure** | Aortic root pressure drives flow. Aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP is a useful bedside approximation for LV subendocardial perfusion, not an exact universal formula: intramyocardial/zero-flow pressure also matters. Low diastolic pressure or high LVEDP reduces the effective gradient. |
| **Extravascular compression** | Systolic contraction compresses intramural vessels, especially the LV subendocardium. LV perfusion is therefore predominantly diastolic; RV flow is less exclusively diastolic because normal RV systolic pressure is lower. |
| **Diastolic duration** | Tachycardia shortens diastole while increasing oxygen demand, creating a double disadvantage. |
| **Vascular resistance and reserve** | Epicardial obstruction, microvascular disease, endothelial dysfunction and exhausted vasodilator reserve limit the ability to increase flow during stress. A normal resting flow does not establish adequate reserve. |
| **Arterial oxygen content** | Haemoglobin concentration and saturation determine oxygen delivery at a given flow; adequate pressure does not compensate reliably for severe anaemia or hypoxaemia. |

### Regulation

- **Metabolic:** local oxygen demand and metabolites promote resistance-vessel dilation; coronary flow usually increases with work.
- **Myogenic/autoregulatory:** changes in arteriolar tone buffer pressure changes within a variable operating range. Avoid presenting one MAP interval as valid for every diseased heart.
- **Endothelial/humoral:** nitric oxide and prostacyclin influence dilation; endothelin and other mediators influence constriction. Endothelial dysfunction impairs normal responses.
- **Neural:** sympathetic activation has direct vascular effects but also increases rate/contractility and metabolic demand; the net flow response cannot be inferred from an alpha/beta label alone.

Anaesthetic agents may reduce demand but simultaneously lower perfusion pressure and depress contractility. A reduced BP after induction is not automatically protective merely because heart rate or workload has fallen. Coronary steal describes redistribution away from a vulnerable region in particular vascular/collateral configurations; it is not an inevitable effect of every vasodilator.

### Why AS/LVH is vulnerable

Pressure overload produces hypertrophy and impaired relaxation. Greater muscle mass and systolic work increase demand; high LVEDP and intramyocardial compression reduce subendocardial perfusion. Microvascular dysfunction and reduced flow reserve add risk. **Angina/ischaemia can occur even without obstructive epicardial coronary disease.** Hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia and loss of atrial contribution can expose this limited reserve.

### Preop

Assess symptoms, functional capacity, AS severity, ventricular function, rhythm, anaemia and coexistent CAD. Identify whether a valve intervention or other optimisation is indicated before elective surgery. Treat relevant disease rather than requesting routine coronary intervention purely to “clear” the patient.

### Intraop

Preserve effective coronary driving pressure and oxygen content; avoid tachycardia, major hypotension, abrupt sympathetic surges and severe underfilling or congestion. Titrate induction and ventilation to the physiology. Use ECG/ST monitoring and additional invasive/echo monitoring according to risk. New ischaemia prompts correction of supply–demand triggers and assessment for an acute coronary event; simply raising MAP without considering LV filling pressure, output and afterload may be insufficient.

### Postop

Control pain, shivering and hypoventilation; monitor rhythm and congestion. Use ECG/troponin surveillance when indicated by cardiac risk or symptoms, and respond to silent myocardial injury as well as chest pain.

### Self-marking checklist

- Relates flow to driving pressure, resistance and extravascular compression
- Explains predominant LV diastolic perfusion and subendocardial vulnerability
- Explains why tachycardia both increases demand and reduces perfusion time
- Covers metabolic, myogenic, endothelial/humoral and neural regulation
- Distinguishes resting flow from coronary reserve and pressure from oxygen delivery
- Explains AS/LVH ischaemia despite unobstructed epicardial coronaries
- Describes competing anaesthetic effects and qualifies coronary steal
- Translates physiology into preoperative assessment, intraoperative goals and postoperative surveillance

**Sources:** [Pathania and Clark. The coronary circulation in healthy and diseased states. BJA Education 2024;24:210–216](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11096616/); [Goodwill et al. Regulation of coronary blood flow. Comprehensive Physiology 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28333376/); [AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guideline 2024](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285).

items.title: 39. Mechanical mitral valve and warfarin for elective colorectal surgery
items.q: A 64-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and requires elective major colorectal surgery. Discuss your perioperative assessment and anticoagulation plan, including bridging, neuraxial implications and postoperative restart.
items.a:
### The competing risks

Interrupting anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis and systemic embolism; continuing it or using therapeutic heparin increases surgical and neuraxial bleeding. A mechanical mitral valve generally carries greater thrombotic risk than a contemporary bileaflet aortic valve without additional risk factors. **Neither “bridge all mechanical valves” nor “never bridge” is a satisfactory individual plan.**

### Preop

**Establish the valve and patient risk.** Confirm valve position, design/date, valve card and prescribed INR target; identify previous thrombosis/embolism, recent stroke, AF, severe LV dysfunction, hypercoagulability and multiple/older valves. A usual target INR is 3.0 for a mechanical mitral valve; use the patient's device-specific prescribed range. Review symptoms and echo for obstruction/regurgitation, ventricular function and PH. New symptoms require investigation, not merely an anticoagulation schedule.

**Define procedural risk.** Discuss urgency, expected bleeding and consequences of bleeding, postoperative oral absorption and any epidural plan with surgeon, cardiology/anticoagulation service and anaesthesia. Check INR, blood count, renal function and interacting medicines. Some minor low-bleeding-risk procedures can proceed with therapeutic warfarin; major colorectal surgery usually requires interruption.

**State the guideline difference.** CHEST 2022 conditionally suggests against bridging when mechanical-valve patients require elective VKA interruption, with very-low-certainty evidence and high-risk implementation considerations. AHA/ACC 2024 and ESC/EACTS 2025 support consideration of bridging in selected high-risk valve patients. This mechanical-mitral patient needs a documented specialist decision balancing thrombotic features against major abdominal bleeding risk. The BRIDGE trial excluded mechanical valves and cannot settle this question for them.

**Illustrative elective schedule if interruption and bridging are agreed:**

| Step | Plan |
|---|---|
| Warfarin | Usually stop about 5 days before surgery; check INR before the procedure and correct a persistently excessive INR through the agreed pathway. The required INR depends on the intervention. |
| Bridge, if indicated | Start therapeutic LMWH or IV UFH as INR becomes subtherapeutic. Select dose/agent for weight, renal function, monitoring and reversibility; UFH may suit severe renal impairment or closely controlled inpatient management. |
| Before surgery | Last therapeutic LMWH at least 24 h beforehand; stop IV UFH 4–6 h beforehand and confirm coagulation has recovered. Longer intervals may be needed with impaired clearance or residual anticoagulant effect. |
| Urgent reversal alternative | For surgery that cannot await warfarin clearance, consider four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K with specialist guidance; balance bleeding urgency against valve thrombosis and plan re-anticoagulation. |

DOACs are not substitutes for warfarin in mechanical valves. Do not add aspirin automatically without a separate indication and bleeding assessment.

### Intraop

Confirm the last anticoagulant doses, INR/coagulation and documented plan before intervention. **A neuraxial procedure adds its own safety requirements:** stop warfarin and normalise INR to the local laboratory range for needle insertion; respect therapeutic LMWH/UFH intervals and catheter-removal rules. An epidural may complicate early therapeutic re-anticoagulation; discuss alternative analgesia before placing it.

Maintain oxygenation, perfusion and haemostasis. Monitoring depends on residual valve/ventricular disease and surgical stress. Mechanical-valve status alone does not identify the haemodynamic goals of an otherwise normally functioning prosthesis.

### Postop

Restart warfarin when haemostasis and enteral administration permit, often the evening of surgery or next day if appropriate; its effect is delayed. If therapeutic bridging was selected, restart only when bleeding risk allows—commonly 48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk surgery for therapeutic LMWH, rather than automatically at 24 h. Use earlier prophylactic VTE prevention when safe; **prophylaxis is not equivalent to therapeutic valve protection**.

Coordinate all doses with epidural removal: therapeutic LMWH generally requires at least 24 h from needle placement, catheter removal at least 4 h before its first postoperative dose, and the appropriate interval since any preceding anticoagulant. Apply the full ASRA/local protocol, not these intervals in isolation. Continue any agreed bridge until the INR is therapeutic. Watch for bleeding and for new dyspnoea, embolism or prosthetic dysfunction; document discharge INR testing and responsibility for dose adjustment.

### Self-marking checklist

- Defines thrombotic and bleeding risks and confirms valve type/position and prescribed INR
- Assesses valve function, prior embolism, rhythm, LV function and procedural risk
- Explains the guideline disagreement and makes an individual specialist bridging decision
- States that BRIDGE excluded mechanical valves and DOACs are unsuitable substitutes
- Gives a coherent interruption, monitoring and conditional bridging schedule
- Covers renal function, UFH/LMWH timing and an urgent-reversal alternative
- Includes neuraxial insertion/removal and analgesic implications
- Distinguishes postoperative prophylaxis from therapeutic anticoagulation and plans safe restart/INR follow-up

**Sources:** [CHEST perioperative antithrombotic guideline 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35964704/); [AHA/ACC perioperative guideline 2024](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285); [ESC/EACTS valve guideline 2025](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194); [ASRA fifth edition 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39880411/). Supporting Blue Book reading: Emanuel, Intravenous heparin and non-cardiac anaesthesia, 2023, pp81–90, in the [2023 volume](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/f1a580a9-36db-4c77-aa46-37d9f7e88f0b/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/blue_book_combined_digital_v2.pdf).

items.title: 40. Primary versus secondary mitral regurgitation for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A 72-year-old with severe mitral regurgitation is scheduled for major non-cardiac surgery. Discuss how primary versus secondary MR influences your assessment and outline your perioperative management.
items.a:
### Physiology and mechanism

In MR, part of LV stroke volume enters the LA during systole. Total LV ejection fraction includes regurgitant as well as forward flow and can look reassuring despite impaired myocardial performance. Chronic compensation involves LV/LA dilation; progressive disease causes congestion, AF, pulmonary hypertension and ventricular dysfunction. Acute severe MR is less well tolerated because the LA has not adapted.

| Mechanism | Assessment and treatment implication |
|---|---|
| **Primary MR** | Leaflet/chordal disease, such as prolapse or flail leaflet. Assess the structural lesion, repairability and evidence of LV consequences. In chronic severe primary MR, an EF around 60% can already signal impaired LV function; a generic “EF >50% is normal” rule is misleading. |
| **Secondary MR** | Altered ventricular geometry/tethering or atrial/annular dilation, rather than primary leaflet damage. Define ventricular versus atrial phenotype, ischaemia, LV/RV function and rhythm. Optimise underlying HF and consider CRT/revascularisation or valve intervention when indicated. |

### Preop

- **Symptoms and stability:** exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, oedema, recent admissions and treatment changes. Examine congestion, perfusion and rhythm. Decompensated HF, a new severe lesion or suspected IE needs treatment and specialist review before elective surgery.
- **Echo:** establish mechanism/severity using an integrated study, LV size and systolic function, LA size, RV function, estimated pulmonary pressure and associated lesions. Eccentric jets and loading conditions can mislead. Suspected moderate/severe regurgitation warrants an appropriate preoperative echo; repeat testing is driven by clinical change and adequacy of the existing assessment.
- **Proceed or intervene first:** combine surgical urgency/stress with symptoms, ventricular response and pulmonary pressure. Severe MR alone does not mandate cancellation of all surgery. Stable asymptomatic patients with preserved LV function may proceed with a suitable plan; symptomatic disease, adverse ventricular findings or an independent indication for valve treatment warrants Heart Team discussion before elevated-risk elective surgery.
- **Optimise:** treat congestion without excessive depletion, control AF and relevant ischaemia, and review renal function, electrolytes and haemoglobin. Manage HF drugs and any anticoagulants by indication and the planned procedure. Discuss risks, monitoring, postoperative destination and escalation limits.

### Intraop

**The aim is adequate forward flow, not merely a higher total EF.**

| Variable | Goal and justification |
|---|---|
| Rate/rhythm | Avoid marked bradycardia, which can favour a larger regurgitant volume, but do not chase tachycardia, especially with ischaemia or limited filling. Individualise to baseline, rhythm and ventricular function. Maintain AV synchrony where possible. |
| Preload | Euvolaemia: avoid underfilling and avoid loading a congested LV/LA. Reassess small fluid challenges rather than administering routine large boluses. |
| Afterload | Avoid excessive SVR/hypertension, which impedes forward ejection. Also avoid hypotension that compromises systemic/coronary perfusion. |
| Contractility | Preserve ventricular function. Use inotropy only for demonstrated low output; inodilators can aggravate hypotension. |
| RV/PVR | Avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis and excessive airway pressures; PH/RV dysfunction substantially changes risk. |

Choose GA, regional or combined techniques according to surgery, anticoagulation, PH and ventricular reserve. Titrate induction and neuraxial sympathectomy carefully. Consider an arterial line for major surgery/significant disease; TOE is useful for unexplained instability when expertise is available, rather than mandatory for every MR patient.

Treat hypotension by mechanism: reduce excessive anaesthetic effect, correct genuine underfilling, use a titrated vasopressor for vasodilation and support contractility for low output. Do not withhold a necessary vasopressor solely because it raises SVR. Anaesthetic unloading may reduce the apparent MR severity; interpret echo alongside BP/loading and the awake baseline.

### Postop

Plan monitored recovery/HDU/ICU according to symptoms, LV/RV function, PH and operation. Avoid pain, shivering, hypoventilation and fluid overload. Assess pulmonary oedema, AF, low output and ischaemia promptly. Resume HF medicines and indicated anticoagulation when haemostasis, renal function and intake allow. Arrange cardiology follow-up for significant untreated MR.

### Self-marking checklist

- Distinguishes primary, ventricular secondary and atrial secondary mechanisms
- Explains regurgitant versus forward flow and why EF can overestimate LV performance
- Assesses symptoms, echo severity, LV/RV function, PH, rhythm and surgical urgency
- Gives a reasoned proceed/optimise/Heart Team decision rather than automatic cancellation
- Sets individualised rate, preload, afterload, contractility and PVR goals
- Justifies technique, monitoring and mechanism-based treatment of hypotension
- Recognises loading-dependent MR and possible underestimation during anaesthesia
- Plans postoperative monitoring, fluid/respiratory care and medication restart

**Sources:** [AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guideline 2024 — official slide set, chronic aortic and mitral regurgitation](https://professional.heart.org/en/-/media/PHD-Files-2/Science-News/2/2024/2024-Guideline-for-Perioperative-Cardiovascular-Management-slide-set.pdf); [ESC/EACTS valve guideline 2025](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194); [Anaesthesia for transcatheter mitral valve repair. BJA Education 2023;23:189–195](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140472/). This answer addresses non-cardiac surgery; the existing TEER question covers procedural anaesthesia.

items.title: 25. Focused TTE/TOE for sudden hypotension and hypoxaemia
items.q: An anaesthetised patient develops sudden hypotension and hypoxaemia. Outline a focused TTE/TOE examination, naming the views, structures and management-changing findings you would seek.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: the systematic cardiac anatomy and focused echo approach in the revised Set 11 teaching notes; ASE focused-ultrasound guidance. Ultrasound is interpreted alongside clinical and haemodynamic data, not as a stand-alone volume or shock diagnostic test.

## Initial approach

Call for help; assess airway/circuit, ECG/rhythm, oxygenation, blood loss, arterial trace and capnography, and begin immediate resuscitation. Obtain the fastest adequate view (TTE or TOE according to surgery, access, operator competence and contraindications). Use several views rather than making a diagnosis from a single off-axis image.

## Views and anatomical landmarks

| View | Key structures to identify | Highest-yield questions |
|---|---|---|
| PLAX TTE | RV anterior, septum, LV/posterior wall, MV, LVOT/AV, root, LA and descending aorta behind LA | LV function/size, AV/MV pathology, pericardial fluid, root |
| PSAX TTE at papillary level | Circular LV, septum and opposing LV walls; RV crescent | New regional wall-motion abnormality, globally impaired LV, D-shaped LV with RV loading |
| Apical 4/5-chamber TTE | RA/RV, LA/LV, MV/TV (TV more apical); 5-chamber adds LVOT/AV | Relative RV/LV size, gross systolic function, valve regurgitation and LVOT Doppler |
| Subcostal 4-chamber/IVC | Pericardial space, chambers and IVC–RA junction | Effusion, gross RV/LV function; IVC supports venous-pressure assessment only |
| ME 4-chamber TOE (0–20°) | Both ventricles, atria and AV valves | Global function, RV/LV comparison, effusion |
| ME 2-chamber / long-axis TOE (80–100° / 120–160°) | Anterior/inferior LV walls; LVOT/AV/MV in long axis | Regional change, dynamic LVOT obstruction, major valvular mechanism |
| TG mid-papillary SAX TOE (~0°) | LV mid-level circumferential wall motion | Severe global impairment, new regional dysfunction (not all segments) |
| ME bicaval / RV inflow–outflow TOE | Interatrial septum/SVC/IVC; TV, RVOT, PV and PA | Catheter/PFO questions, RV/PA findings |

Know the descending-aortic TOE long/short-axis views and the **distal ascending-aortic TOE blind spot**. For comprehensive valve gradients, select the correctly aligned Doppler view; an off-axis colour jet cannot establish valve severity.

## Five immediate decisions

- **1.** **Tamponade?** Effusion with appropriate clinical/chamber-collapse features → urgent cause-specific drainage/escalation, not an automatic fluid diagnosis.
- **2.** **Severe LV impairment or dynamic LVOT obstruction?** A globally poor LV may need inotropy/revascularisation; a small hyperdynamic ventricle with SAM/LVOTO can worsen with catecholamine inotropy and excessive underfilling.
- **3.** **RV strain/failure?** Dilated RV, septal shift and poor RV function prompt PE, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, PEEP/airway pressure, ischaemia or pulmonary hypertension assessment; avoid unnecessary fluid overload.
- **4.** **True underfilling versus raised filling pressure?** EF, filling pressure, and responsiveness are distinct. Where safe, assess change in **LVOT VTI with passive leg raising**; IVC size or CVP alone cannot prove fluid responsiveness.
- **5.** **Acute valve disease or ischaemia?** New regional abnormalities, acute MR/AR or severe AS may change need for emergency cardiology/surgical management.

## Interpretation limits and disposition

A negative limited scan does not exclude pulmonary embolism, regional ischaemia or dissection. Image quality, loading, mechanical ventilation, tachycardia, pacing and operator skill influence interpretation. Treat reversible causes immediately, repeat/upgrade to comprehensive echo when unclear, and plan appropriately monitored postoperative care.

## Self-marking checklist

- Begins with resuscitation and a physiological differential rather than an isolated image diagnosis
- Identifies PLAX, PSAX, A4C, subcostal TTE landmarks and one useful question per view
- Names ME 4C, 2C, long-axis, TG SAX and an additional bicaval/RV TOE view with approximate angles
- Lists the five life-threatening echo questions: tamponade, LV, RV, filling/obstruction, valve/regional wall motion
- Distinguishes EF and filling pressure from fluid responsiveness, and explains LVOT VTI/PLR versus IVC limitations
- Recognises the TOE distal ascending-aorta blind spot and limitations of a single view
- Links echo findings to different haemodynamic treatments and escalation

**Sources:** revised Set 11, section 9; [ASE focused cardiac ultrasound recommendations](https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/FCU.pdf); [ASE right-heart assessment 2025](https://www.asecho.org/guideline/right-heart-in-adults-pulmonary-hypertension/).

items.title: 26. Severe ischaemia and instability in PACU after emergency abdominal surgery
items.q: A patient develops severe ischaemia and haemodynamic instability in PACU immediately after emergency abdominal surgery. Urgent coronary angiography and possible PCI are planned. Discuss your anaesthetic and peri-procedural management.
items.a:
> Evidence framework: ANZCA 2021.1 Q5 examiner priorities, the updated Set 11 acute coronary chapter, and the Australian 2025 ACS guideline; fresh surgery changes the bleeding and antithrombotic decisions.

## Establish urgency and diagnosis

Call for senior anaesthesia, cardiology/interventional and surgical support. Reassess the airway, consciousness, work of breathing, rhythm, perfusion, surgical bleeding and abdominal complication. Obtain **serial 12-lead ECGs**, compare with old traces if available, troponin trend, FBC, gas/lactate, electrolytes, renal function and urgent focused echo for LV/RV function, RWMA, acute MR and other shock causes. A normal or nondiagnostic ECG does not exclude acute coronary occlusion: consider posterior, high lateral, RV, de Winter or modified Sgarbossa patterns when appropriate. Distinguish an acutely occluded vessel from supply–demand injury and non-ischaemic causes; do not delay an indicated emergency catheterisation solely while waiting for serial troponins.

## Before transfer to the catheter laboratory

- Correct reversible demand/supply problems: hypoxaemia, pain, tachyarrhythmia, severe hypertension or hypotension, anaemia/haemorrhage and electrolyte imbalance. Oxygen for hypoxaemia; do not routinely deliver excess oxygen to a normally saturated patient.
- Establish monitors, functioning IVs, defibrillation/pacing availability and a resuscitation/transport plan. Consider an arterial catheter and vasoactive infusion in shock, without delaying emergency reperfusion.
- Confirm operation, haemostasis, drains and bleeding risk with surgeon. Discuss aspirin/P2Y12/IV anticoagulant and **access-site** choices with interventional cardiology; drug selection and timing should reflect coronary urgency, bleeding risk and whether PCI occurs. Recent laparotomy makes **fibrinolysis hazardous/usually contraindicated**; unqualified thrombolysis is inappropriate.

## Anaesthesia in the cath lab

- **Technique:** local anaesthesia with minimal sedation if cooperative and stable; GA if unstable airway/oxygenation, inability to remain still, profound shock or long complex intervention. Decide jointly; cath-lab sedation is not risk-free in pulmonary oedema or low output.
- **Induction:** preoxygenate while watching preload/RV effects, prepare noradrenaline and titrate a haemodynamically suitable agent (e.g. carefully titrated etomidate or an alternative based on circumstances). Avoid propofol boluses causing major vasodilation and avoid unnecessary tachycardia; choose analgesia with minimal haemodynamic disruption.
- **Maintenance:** maintain coronary perfusion and adequate arterial pressure (usually MAP ≥65 mmHg as a starting point, individualised), correct rhythm, preserve oxygenation and normocapnia, limit excessive PEEP/airway pressure and give **small reassessed fluids only if truly underfilled**. Use inotropes for proven low output rather than reflexively treating every low BP with fluid.
- **Mechanical complications/shock:** seek urgent echo, shock-team discussion and cause-specific treatment; select IABP/Impella/VA-ECMO only for an appropriate phenotype and expertise, acknowledging no routine device benefit in unselected patients.

## After PCI

Communicate culprit anatomy, stent/antithrombotic plan, access complications and bleeding risk explicitly to the receiving ICU/HDU and surgical team. Monitor ECG, perfusion/lactate, renal function, haemoglobin, surgical-site bleeding, pulmonary oedema and recurrent ischaemia. Reconcile DAPT/anticoagulation urgently with the risk of fresh surgery and any regional catheter. Plan follow-up/secondary prevention and assess when staged procedures can safely occur.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises that postoperative ischaemic ECG/biomarkers need mechanism-specific evaluation; considers occlusion despite nonclassic ECG
- Calls cardiology, surgery and senior anaesthesia early and decides urgency of angiography/reperfusion
- Addresses haemorrhage and fresh-laparotomy limitations on anticoagulation, DAPT and fibrinolysis
- Selects monitored sedation versus GA based on haemodynamics, airway and cath-lab practicalities
- Describes haemodynamically cautious induction, coronary perfusion, rhythm, fluids/vasopressors and ventilation
- Recognises need to investigate mechanical MI complications and use MCS selectively
- Gives a specific ICU/HDU handover covering stent antithrombotics, bleeding and recurrent ischaemia

**Sources:** ANZCA Final 2021.1 Q5 examiner report (user-supplied); [Australian 2025 ACS guideline](https://www.heartfoundation.org.au/for-professionals/acs-guideline); [BJA Education: cardiogenic shock after ACS (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140595/); revised Set 11, sections 1, 3, 4 and 9.
